administration.name: administration
administration.desc: 'And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles, and those with gifts of healing, helping, administration, and various tongues.' (1Cor 12:28).

apostles.name: apostles
apostles.desc: 'And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles, and those with gifts of healing, helping, administration, and various tongues.' (1Cor 12:28).

baptized_into_his_death.name: baptized into His death
baptized_into_his_death.desc: 'Or aren't you aware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death?' (Rom 6:3).

blessed_is_the_man.name: Blessed is the man
blessed_is_the_man.desc: 'Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked' (Ps 1:1). The Psalter opens with it, and Psalms 32 and 112 open the same way: the one 'whose transgressions are forgiven' (32:1), the one 'who fears the LORD' (112:1).

coveting.name: coveting
coveting.desc: 'You shall not covet your neighbor's house. You shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.' (Exod 20:17).

dead_to_sin_alive_to_god.name: dead to sin, but alive to God
dead_to_sin_alive_to_god.desc: 'So you too must count yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.' (Rom 6:11).

debauchery.name: debauchery
debauchery.desc: 'The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery;' (Gal 5:19).

discord.name: discord
discord.desc: 'idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions,' (Gal 5:20).

distinguishing_between_spirits.name: distinguishing between spirits
distinguishing_between_spirits.desc: 'to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues.' (1Cor 12:10).

drunkenness.name: drunkenness
drunkenness.desc: 'and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like. I warn you, as I did before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.' (Gal 5:21).

dying_and_rising_with_christ.name: dying and rising with Christ
dying_and_rising_with_christ.desc: 'all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death' (Rom 6:3), 'buried with Him', so that 'we too may walk in newness of life' (6:4). Galatians 2:20, Colossians 2:12 and 3:9-10, and Ephesians 4:22-24 are set beside it, and John 3:3 and 2 Corinthians 5:17 are gathered with them here; the card gathers them and does not say they teach one thing.

items.label: speaks of
items.name: dead to sin, but alive to God

items.label: speaks of
items.name: the old self and the new self

encouraging.name: encouraging
encouraging.desc: 'if it is encouraging, let him encourage; if it is giving, let him give generously; if it is leading, let him lead with diligence; if it is showing mercy, let him do it cheerfully.' (Rom 12:8).

evangelists.name: evangelists
evangelists.desc: 'And it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers,' (Eph 4:11).

factions.name: factions
factions.desc: 'idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions,' (Gal 5:20).

false_witness.name: false witness
false_witness.desc: 'You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.' (Exod 20:16).

giving.name: giving
giving.desc: 'if it is encouraging, let him encourage; if it is giving, let him give generously; if it is leading, let him lead with diligence; if it is showing mercy, let him do it cheerfully.' (Rom 12:8).

grain_offering.name: grain offering
grain_offering.desc: 'When anyone brings a grain offering to the LORD, his offering must consist of fine flour. He is to pour olive oil on it, put frankincense on it,' (Lev 2:1).

guilt_offering.name: guilt offering
guilt_offering.desc: 'If someone acts unfaithfully and sins unintentionally against any of the LORD's holy things, he must bring his guilt offering to the LORD: an unblemished ram from the flock, of proper value in silver shekels according to the sanctuary shekel; it is a guilt offering.' (Lev 5:15).

helping.name: helping
helping.desc: 'And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles, and those with gifts of healing, helping, administration, and various tongues.' (1Cor 12:28).

idolatry.name: idolatry
idolatry.desc: 'idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions,' (Gal 5:20).

image_belt_of_truth.name: the belt of truth
image_belt_of_truth.desc: 'Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness arrayed,' (Eph 6:14).

image_breastplate_of_righteousness.name: the breastplate of righteousness
image_breastplate_of_righteousness.desc: 'Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness arrayed,' (Eph 6:14).

image_helmet_of_salvation.name: the helmet of salvation
image_helmet_of_salvation.desc: 'And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.' (Eph 6:17).

image_readiness_of_the_gospel_of_peace.name: the readiness of the gospel of peace
image_readiness_of_the_gospel_of_peace.desc: 'and with your feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace.' (Eph 6:15).

image_shield_of_faith.name: the shield of faith
image_shield_of_faith.desc: 'In addition to all this, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one.' (Eph 6:16).

image_sword_of_the_spirit.name: the sword of the Spirit
image_sword_of_the_spirit.desc: 'And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.' (Eph 6:17).

impurity.name: impurity
impurity.desc: 'The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery;' (Gal 5:19).

interpretation_of_tongues.name: the interpretation of tongues
interpretation_of_tongues.desc: 'to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues.' (1Cor 12:10).

jealousy.name: jealousy
jealousy.desc: 'idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions,' (Gal 5:20).

leading.name: leading
leading.desc: 'if it is encouraging, let him encourage; if it is giving, let him give generously; if it is leading, let him lead with diligence; if it is showing mercy, let him do it cheerfully.' (Rom 12:8).

lev_1_5.name: the offerings
lev_1_5.desc: 'When any of you brings an offering to the LORD' (Lev 1:2): the burnt offering, the grain offering, the peace offering, the sin offering and the guilt offering, each given its own law, beginning in Leviticus 1-5.

matt_5_3_12.name: the Beatitudes
matt_5_3_12.desc: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven' (Matt 5:3), and further sayings in the same form follow it (Matt 5:4-11), at the opening of the Sermon on the Mount.

miracles.name: miracles
miracles.desc: 'to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues.' (1Cor 12:10).

orgies.name: orgies
orgies.desc: 'and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like. I warn you, as I did before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.' (Gal 5:21).

other_gods.name: other gods
other_gods.desc: 'You shall have no other gods before Me.' (Exod 20:3).

pastors.name: pastors
pastors.desc: 'And it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers,' (Eph 4:11).

peace_offering.name: peace offering
peace_offering.desc: 'If one's offering is a peace offering and he offers an animal from the herd, whether male or female, he must present it without blemish before the LORD.' (Lev 3:1).

peacemakers.name: peacemakers
peacemakers.desc: 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God.' (Matt 5:9).

persecution.name: persecution
persecution.desc: 'Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.' (Matt 5:10).

poor_in_spirit.name: poor in spirit
poor_in_spirit.desc: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.' (Matt 5:3).

prophecy.name: prophecy
prophecy.desc: 'to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues.' (1Cor 12:10).

raised_with_him.name: raised with Him
raised_with_him.desc: 'And having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him through your faith in the power of God, who raised Him from the dead.' (Col 2:12).

rivalries.name: rivalries
rivalries.desc: 'idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions,' (Gal 5:20).

seven_bowls.name: the seven bowls
seven_bowls.desc: 'Then one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever.' (Rev 15:7).

seven_seals.name: the seven seals
seven_seals.desc: 'Then I saw a scroll in the right hand of the One seated on the throne. It had writing on both sides and was sealed with seven seals.' (Rev 5:1).

seven_spirits_of_god.name: the seven spirits of God
seven_spirits_of_god.desc: 'the seven spirits of God' (Rev 3:1). Revelation names them four times and does not list them: at 4:5 they are 'seven torches of fire' before the throne, at 5:6 the Lamb's 'seven horns and seven eyes'.

seven_trumpets.name: the seven trumpets
seven_trumpets.desc: 'And I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and they were given seven trumpets.' (Rev 8:2).

sevens_of_revelation.name: the sevens of Revelation
sevens_of_revelation.desc: Revelation counts in sevens: seven golden lampstands and seven stars (1:12, 16), seven seals (5:1), seven trumpets (8:2), seven golden bowls (15:7). A collection gathered here, not a list the text gives. Listed in the order the book gives them; the card does not say how the sevens relate to one another.

items.label: speaks of
items.name: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches

sexual_immorality.name: sexual immorality
sexual_immorality.desc: 'The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery;' (Gal 5:19).

sin_offering.name: sin offering
sin_offering.desc: 'If the anointed priest sins, bringing guilt on the people, he must bring to the LORD a young bull without blemish as a sin offering for the sin he has committed.' (Lev 4:3).

sorcery.name: sorcery
sorcery.desc: 'idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions,' (Gal 5:20).

tabernacle_curtains.name: the ten curtains
tabernacle_curtains.desc: 'You are to construct the tabernacle itself with ten curtains of finely spun linen, each with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and cherubim skillfully worked into them.' (Exod 26:1).

table_of_the_presence.name: the table of the Presence
table_of_the_presence.desc: 'You are also to make a table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high.' (Exod 25:23).

the_name_of_the_lord_in_vain.name: taking the name of the LORD in vain
the_name_of_the_lord_in_vain.desc: 'You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain.' (Exod 20:7).

the_veil.name: the veil
the_veil.desc: 'Make a veil of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it.' (Exod 26:31).

tongues.name: tongues
tongues.desc: 'to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues.' (1Cor 12:10).

walk_in_newness_of_life.name: walk in newness of life
walk_in_newness_of_life.desc: 'We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life.' (Rom 6:4).

items.label: told
items.name: They have moved on from here

items.label: asserts
items.name: They have moved on from here

a_chariot_of_fire_and_horses_of_fire.name: a chariot of fire with horses of fire
a_chariot_of_fire_and_horses_of_fire.desc:
'suddenly a chariot of fire with horses of fire appeared and separated the two of them, and Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind.' (2Kgs 2:11).

The chariot separates them and the whirlwind does the carrying — two things, and readers usually remember one. Elisha's cry names him as the thing lost: 'My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel' (2:12).

Scripture records only two people leaving without dying, and this is the one it describes.

a_coat_of_many_colors.name: a robe of many colors
a_coat_of_many_colors.desc:
'Now Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons, because Joseph had been born to him in his old age; so he made him a robe of many colors.' (Gen 37:3).

The garment is how the favouritism is made visible, and then how the lie is told. It is stripped off him (37:23), dipped in goat's blood (37:31) and shown to his father as evidence (37:32). The same object carries the love and the deception.

a_crown_of_thorns.name: a crown of thorns
a_crown_of_thorns.desc: Twisted together and put on his head with a staff in His right hand, as part of a mock coronation the text reports without comment.

a_dead_man.name: as good as dead
a_dead_man.desc: You are as good as dead

a_double_portion_of_your_spirit.name: a double portion of your spirit
a_double_portion_of_your_spirit.desc:
'Tell me, what can I do for you before I am taken away from you?” “Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit,” Elisha replied.' (2Kgs 2:9).

**The condition attached is seeing, not deserving**: 'if you see me as I am taken from you, it will be yours. But if not, then it will not be so' (2:10). It is the inheritance formula from Deuteronomy 21:17 -- the firstborn's double share -- asked for as a son would ask, by a man who was not his son.

an_eternal_weight_of_glory_that_is_far_b.name: an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison
an_eternal_weight_of_glory_that_is_far_b.desc:
'For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison.' (2Cor 4:17).

A comparison with both sides weighed. The affliction is light and momentary; the glory is weighty and eternal. Rom 8:18 makes the same comparison and declines to weigh it at all — 'not worthy to be compared' — so the text states the relation twice by the same writer and reaches it two different ways.

The affliction is not said to be followed by the glory. It is said to work it.

a_father_of_many_nations.name: a father of many nations
a_father_of_many_nations.desc:
'No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations.' (Gen 17:5).

**The name is changed to carry the claim, and the claim is in the past tense** -- *I have made you* -- said to a childless man of ninety-nine. Paul notices the tense and builds an argument on it: God 'calls into being what does not yet exist' (Rom 4:17).

a_great_multitude.name: a large crowd
a_great_multitude.desc: The crowd that followed Jesus to the sea, gathered out of Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond Jordan, and about Tyre and Sidon.

a_greater_than_solomon_is_here.name: One greater than Solomon is here
a_greater_than_solomon_is_here.desc:
'The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here.' (Matt 12:42).

The comparison is made by way of a foreigner who travelled. The argument is not that Solomon was small but that she came a long way for less, and it is one of the few places the text uses a Gentile as the standard by which Israel is judged.

a_grief_of_mind.name: a grief of mind
a_grief_of_mind.desc: The verdict on Esau's wives: they They brought grief to Isaac and Rebekah.

a_jealous_god.name: a jealous God
a_jealous_god.desc: the LORD your God, who is among you, is a jealous God (Deut 6:15).

a_righteous_man_blameless_in_his_generat.name: a righteous man, blameless in his generation
a_righteous_man_blameless_in_his_generat.desc:
'Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation; Noah walked with God.' (Gen 6:9).

**Ezekiel names him in a very short list**: 'even if these three men — Noah, Daniel, and Job— were in it, their righteousness could deliver only themselves' (14:14). Three names, chosen as the limit case of how much one person's righteousness can do for anybody else, and the answer given is nothing.

2 Peter 2:5 adds a description the flood narrative never gives him: 'a preacher of righteousness'.
aka: righteous man, blameless in his generation

a_keeper_of_sheep.name: a keeper of sheep
a_keeper_of_sheep.desc: Abel is identified by occupation: 'Abel was a keeper of sheep'.

a_king_ready_to_the_battle.name: a king poised to attack
a_king_ready_to_the_battle.desc: Simile: 'like a king poised to attack'.

items.label: is used as an image for
items.name: Distress and anguish

a_land_of_darkness_as_darkness_itself.name: to a land of utter darkness

a_lawgiver_from_between_his_feet.name: nor the staff from between his feet
a_lawgiver_from_between_his_feet.desc: nor the staff from between his feet

a_leathern_girdle_about_his_loins.name: a leather belt around his waist
a_leathern_girdle_about_his_loins.desc:
'John wore a garment of camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist' (Matt 3:4); 'He was a hairy man,” they answered, “with a leather belt around his waist.' (2Kgs 1:8).

**Near enough to be recognised and not close enough to be a quotation.** Matthew has a leather belt, Kings a leather belt, and both put it about the loins. Neither text remarks on the other.

It is corroboration rather than the claim. The identification is stated outright elsewhere -- 'he is the Elijah who was to come' (Matt 11:14) -- and Mal 4:5 is what that answers. The clothing is what a reader notices first and the weakest of the three grounds.

a_living_sacrifice.name: as living sacrifices
a_living_sacrifice.desc:
'Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God's mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.' (Rom 12:1).

Two words Scripture otherwise keeps apart. Every other sacrifice dies; this one is asked to live. The phrase holds both halves of the paradox that Gal 2:20 states as 'I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me'.

It opens the letter's turn from argument to conduct, on 'therefore' — the second of Romans' hinges, after Rom 8:1.

a_man_after_his_own_heart.name: a man after his own heart
a_man_after_his_own_heart.desc:
'the LORD has sought a man after His own heart' (1Sam 13:14), and Paul quotes it back a thousand years later: 'I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart; he will carry out My will in its entirety.' (Acts 13:22).

The verdict is delivered before he has done anything. 1 Samuel 13:14 comes while Saul is still king and David has not appeared in the narrative; he is not named in the verse at all. What the phrase is measuring is therefore not a record of conduct, which is the difficulty every reader of 2 Samuel 11 runs into.

Scripture keeps the verdict as well — 1 Kings 15:5 says he did right 'except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite', which names the exception and keeps the verdict.

a_mighty_hunter_before_the_lord.name: a mighty hunter before the Lord

a_mighty_one_in_the_earth.name: a mighty one on the earth

a_mother_in_israel.name: a mother in Israel
a_mother_in_israel.desc:
'Life in the villages ceased; it ended in Israel, until I, Deborah, arose, a mother in Israel.' (Judg 5:7).

She says it of herself, in a song, in the first person. Most verdicts in the text are the narrator's; this one is the subject's, and it is sung.

She is also the only judge the book describes holding court — sat under a named tree with people coming to her for judgment (4:5) — where the others are described delivering.

a_new_heart_will_i_give_you.name: I will give you a new heart
a_new_heart_will_i_give_you.desc:
'I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.' (Ezek 36:26).

**Every verb is first person and none of them is conditional.** Give, put, take away, give -- and nothing is asked of the hearer in the sentence, which is unusual for a passage about change.

items.label: is a core concept of the major theme
items.name: Covenant (major theme)

items.label: is a core concept of the major theme
items.name: Law / Wisdom (major theme)

a_new_heaven_and_a_new_earth.name: new Jerusalem, prepared as a bride
a_new_heaven_and_a_new_earth.desc:
'I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.' (Rev 21:2).

**A city described as a woman dressed for a wedding**, which is two figures at once and the book does not choose between them. The chapters that follow measure it like architecture and address it like a person.

The closing images are the opening ones returned: a river, and 'a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit' (22:2) -- the tree last seen in Genesis 3 with a guard on it.

a_peculiar_people.name: a people for His own possession
a_peculiar_people.desc: 'purify for Himself a people for His own possession'

a_plumbline_in_the_midst.name: a plumb line among My people
a_plumbline_in_the_midst.desc:
'Amos, what do you see?” asked the LORD. “A plumb line,” I replied. “Behold,” said the Lord, “I am setting a plumb line among My people Israel' (Amos 7:8).

**The figure is a measuring tool rather than a weapon**, and what it measures is whether a wall is upright. It is set *in the midst of* the people, not against them, and the judgment is what the measurement discloses.

a_prophet_like_unto_me.name: a prophet like me from among your brothers
a_prophet_like_unto_me.desc:
'The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him.' (Deut 18:15).

Moses is the only person in the text who describes a successor by comparison with himself, and Deuteronomy 34:10 then says it never happened: 'Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses'. The two verses are twenty-six chapters apart in one book.

Peter quotes it at Acts 3:22 and Stephen at 7:37, both applying it.

items.label: is a core concept of the major theme
items.name: Prophetic Word & Fulfillment (major theme)

items.label: asserts
items.name: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons

a_ransom_for_many.name: a ransom for many
a_ransom_for_many.desc: Kept as a saying rather than folded into `redemption`, because the two Gospels say 'for many' and 1 Timothy says 'for all', and that difference is the whole of a long argument. Recording it as one concept would settle by tidying what the verses leave open.

items.label: is a core concept of the major theme
items.name: Deliverance / Salvation (major theme)

a_solitary_place.name: a solitary place
a_solitary_place.desc: "Jesus got up and slipped out to a solitary place to pray".

a_stench_to_the_inhabitants_of_the_land.name: a stench to the inhabitants of the land
a_stench_to_the_inhabitants_of_the_land.desc: You have brought trouble upon me by making me a stench to the Canaanites and Perizzites, the people of this land

a_still_small_voice.name: a still small voice
a_still_small_voice.desc:
'After the earthquake there was a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire came a still, small voice.' (1Kgs 19:12).

The passage is built entirely out of denials. A great wind, an earthquake and a fire are each named and each followed by the LORD was not in it — three standard signs of presence, ruled out in three clauses. What is left is defined only by being none of them.

a_stone_laid_in_zion.name: I lay a stone in Zion
a_stone_laid_in_zion.desc:
'So this is what the Lord GOD says: See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken.' (Isa 28:16).

Held as a saying in its own right because the New Testament quotes it as one: 'it stands in Scripture: See, I lay in Zion a stone, a chosen and precious cornerstone' (1Pet 2:6). Rom 9:33 quotes it with 'As it is written' and fuses it with the stone of stumbling of Isa 8:14, so the two halves of that verse come from two places.

items.label: draws on the image of
items.name: the rejected stone and the cornerstone

a_stone_of_stumbling_and_a_rock_of_offen.name: a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense
a_stone_of_stumbling_and_a_rock_of_offen.desc:
'And He will be a sanctuary-but to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, to the dwellers of Jerusalem a trap and a snare.' (Isa 8:14).

Quoted at Rom 9:33, where it completes a sentence begun from Isa 28:16, and again at 1Pet 2:8 where it is set against the head of the corner in the verse before. In Isaiah the sanctuary and the snare are the same 'he', which is the shape the New Testament keeps.

a_stranger_and_a_sojourner.name: a foreigner and an outsider
a_stranger_and_a_sojourner.desc: I am a foreigner and an outsider among you

a_sword_shall_pierce_through_your_own_so.name: a sword will pierce your soul
a_sword_shall_pierce_through_your_own_so.desc:
'so that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed-and a sword will pierce your soul as well.' (Luke 2:35).

Said to her in the temple, eight days into the child's life, by an old man who had come to see the Lord's Christ before he died. It sits in brackets in the middle of a sentence about the child.

The text never says what the sword was, and never refers to the saying again.

a_thorn_in_the_flesh.name: a thorn in my flesh
a_thorn_in_the_flesh.desc: Never identified. The chapter says what it was for -- 'to keep me from becoming conceited' -- and not what it was.

items.label: is drawn on by
items.name: My power is perfected in weakness

a_tiller_of_the_ground.name: a tiller of the soil
a_tiller_of_the_ground.desc: Cain is identified by occupation: 'Cain was a tiller of the soil'.

a_tree_planted_by_the_waters.name: like a tree planted by the waters
a_tree_planted_by_the_waters.desc: Jeremiah 17:8 and Psalm 1:3 are the same figure with the same conclusion -- the tree does not fail because of where it is planted, not because of what it does.
aka: shall not cease from yielding fruit

items.label: is used as an image for
items.name: chaff driven off by the wind

a_virgin_shall_be_with_child.name: the virgin will be with child
a_virgin_shall_be_with_child.desc:
'Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will be with child and give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.' (Isa 7:14), quoted at Matt 1:23.

The first of Matthew's fulfilment citations and the one that sets the formula: 'All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet:' (Matt 1:22). Isaiah's setting is a sign offered to Ahaz in a war; Matthew does not mention the war, and quotes the sign.

a_well_of_water_springing_up.name: a fount of water springing up to eternal life

'whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.' (John 4:14).

**The longest recorded conversation Jesus has with anybody in the gospels is with a Samaritan woman at a well**, and she does most of the talking. Her reply to the figure is practical: 'give me this water so that I will not get thirsty and have to keep coming here to draw water' (4:15).

She then becomes the first person in John to bring a town to him, and the question she uses is a careful one: 'is not this the Christ?' (4:29).

a_white_horse_and_his_name_faithful_and_.name: a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True

'Then I saw heaven standing open, and there before me was a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True. With righteousness He judges and wages war.' (Rev 19:11).

This rider is named three times in six verses — Faithful and True, The Word of God (19:13), and KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS written on his thigh (19:16). The rider on the white horse at 6:2 is named nothing at all.

That difference is the whole of the argument about whether they are the same figure.

**Kept as a sign rather than a relic**: 'Put Aaron's staff back in front of the Testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebellious' (17:10). Hebrews 9:4 places it inside the ark with the manna and the tables.

abba.name: Abba
abba.desc:
'Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You.' (Mark 14:36).

Three occurrences in Scripture and no more: Jesus in Gethsemane, and twice in Paul — Rom 8:15 and Gal 4:6. Four things are true of all three, and together they are why this is held as a title rather than folded into the Father's names.

It never stands alone. Every occurrence is 'Abba, Father' — the Aramaic kept and translated in the same breath. A name used as an alias is usable by itself; this one is not.

All three are vocative. Nobody in Scripture says Abba did anything. They say it to him. It is what he is called when he is being called, not when he is being described.

All three are cries. Gethsemane; 'not a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear' (Rom 8:15); 'crying out, Abba, Father!' (Gal 4:6).

The address is transferred, and Galatians says how. Mark 14:36 is the Son's word. Rom 8:15 and Gal 4:6 put it in the mouths of believers, and Gal 4:6 gives the mechanism outright: 'God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, Abba, Father!.' What is claimed is not that they have found a name for God but that the Son's own address has been given them.

Is it a term of affection? Widely read that way, and the text does not say so. What it does say is what the cry is set against: 'you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption to sonship, by whom we cry, Abba! Father!' (Rom 8:15), and 'because you are sons' (Gal 4:6). Bondage and fear on one side, sonship on the other, with the word on the second side both times. That is the frame the text puts around it. Whether the Aramaic itself carried the warmth of a child's word for a father is a question about first-century Aramaic, not about this text.

'for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus' (Rom 3:23-24).

**The hinge, and it is one sentence.** v23 closes the case Paul has been building since Rom 1:18 -- and closes it against everybody, Jew and Gentile alike, with no exception offered. v24 begins with a participle, not a new sentence: the verdict and the remedy are grammatically joined.

Three verses earlier the alternative is ruled out: 'no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law' (Rom 3:20). What replaces it is named as free and as grace, and the same argument reaches its collision six chapters later at the stone laid in Zion (Rom 9:32-33).

angel_of_the_lord.name: the angel of the Lord
angel_of_the_lord.desc:
'Just then the angel of the LORD called out to him from heaven' (Gen 22:11), one of many appearances under this title; the first is to Hagar at the spring (Gen 16:7).

Scripture speaks of him in two ways and does not settle which is meant. At Genesis 22:15-16 he speaks in the first person: 'By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD'; at 2 Samuel 24:16 he is distinguished from the LORD, who speaks to him. Whether he is the LORD himself, a messenger who speaks for him, or a title used of more than one figure, the text does not say.

Where he is spoken of, or is answered, as the LORD or as God: Hagar gave a name 'to the LORD who had spoken to her': 'You are the God who sees me' (Gen 16:13); at the bush 'the angel of the LORD appeared', and then 'God called out to him from within the bush' (Exod 3:2, 4); in Judges 6 the narrator says 'the angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon' (6:12), then 'The LORD turned to him and said' (6:14), and Gideon cries 'Oh no, Lord GOD! I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!' (6:22); Manoah, who 'did not know that it was the angel of the LORD' (Judg 13:16) and realized it afterwards (13:21), says 'We have seen God!' (13:22). Where he is distinguished from the LORD: 'if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD' (Judg 13:16); the LORD says to the angel, 'Enough! Withdraw your hand now!' (2 Sam 24:16); the angel of the LORD asks, 'How long, O LORD of Hosts?' (Zech 1:12).

'There was also a prophetess named Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher' (Luke 2:36).

Luke gives her more identifying detail than he gives most men in the chapter — a father, a tribe, a marriage of seven years, eighty-four years of widowhood, and a practice: 'She never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying' (2:37).

Simeon in the same scene gets a speech the church has recited for centuries; Anna gets 'she gave thanks to God and spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem' (2:38), and what she said is not recorded. She is called a prophetess and none of her prophecy is preserved.

as_moses_lifted_up_the_serpent.name: Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness
as_moses_lifted_up_the_serpent.desc:
'Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,' (John 3:14).

The thing chosen is a brass copy of the animal that was killing them, and looking at it was the cure. Jesus makes it a figure of himself in one sentence, three verses before John 3:16.

Hezekiah 'demolished the bronze snake called Nehushtan that Moses had made, for up to that time the Israelites had burned incense to it' (2Kgs 18:4). The same object is a cure, a type and an idol in three different places.

as_the_clay_is_in_the_potters_hand.name: Just like clay in the potter's hand
as_the_clay_is_in_the_potters_hand.desc:
'Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel' (Jer 18:6).

The figure is about remaking rather than making. The vessel in 18:4 is marred in the potter's hand and he makes it again — the point of the sign is the second attempt, and the chapter goes on to make the outcome conditional on what the nation does (18:7-10).

Paul uses the same figure at Romans 9:21 to argue something the conditional clauses here do not obviously support.

as_the_days_of_noe_were.name: As it was in the days of Noah

**What the comparison rests on is ordinariness, not wickedness.** The next verse lists eating, drinking, marrying and giving in marriage -- nothing condemned -- and the point made is that they 'knew not until the flood came' (24:39).

atonement.desc:

baptized_with_the_holy_ghost.name: baptized with the Holy Spirit
baptized_with_the_holy_ghost.desc:
'He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.' (Matt 3:11), spoken by John the Baptist about someone not yet named.

Four writers use the phrase and it is always a contrast with water. John sets it against his own baptism; Acts 1:5 repeats him almost word for word — 'John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit' — and Acts 2:4 is the report that it happened. Paul takes it somewhere else entirely: 'in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body' (1Cor 12:13), where the thing entered is not water and not the Spirit but the church.

The fire of Matthew 3:11 is the only element the promise names besides the Spirit, and Acts 2:3 supplies it: 'tongues like flames of fire that separated'. Whether Matthew's fire is that fire or the judgement of the next verse is a real question and the text leaves it open.

'Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.' (Rom 12:2).

**Not X but Y, and the two halves are not symmetrical.** Conforming is something done to you and transforming is something done to you; what changes is the agent and the direction, not the voice. The instrument is named and it is the mind.

The verse before it asks for a body 'a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God' (12:1), which puts sacrifice, holiness and transformation in two consecutive sentences.

before_abraham_was_i_am.name: before Abraham was born, I am!
before_abraham_was_i_am.desc:
'Truly, truly, I tell you,” Jesus declared, “before Abraham was born, I am!' (John 8:58).

The next verse is the evidence for how it was heard: 'they picked up stones to throw at Him' (8:59). The text does not say what the offence was here, but it does at John 10:33 in the same pattern: 'We are not stoning You for any good work, said the Jews, but for blasphemy, because You, who are a man, declare Yourself to be God.'

Whether this reaches back to Exodus 3:14 is the question, and the text does not answer it. The two sayings are joined here because the words are the same words and readers have argued over them for centuries — not because Scripture states a connection. It does not. No verse quotes one at the other.

What can be said plainly: the Greek behind both is not held here, the Septuagint is not either, and the whole weight of the reading rests on wording in translation.

before_i_formed_you_in_the_belly.name: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you

'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I set you apart and appointed you as a prophet to the nations.' (Jer 1:5).

His answer is an objection: 'Ah, Lord GOD, I surely do not know how to speak, for I am only a child!' (1:6). It is the opposite response to Isaiah's, to a call that is stated more absolutely.

before_the_cock_crow.name: before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times
before_the_cock_crow.desc:
'before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times' (Matt 26:34), and the report of it: 'Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken ... and he went outside and wept bitterly' (26:75).

One of very few predictions in Scripture whose fulfilment is narrated in the same book, at the same length, with the same words. Luke adds the detail the others leave out: 'the Lord turned and looked at Peter' (22:61).

behold_my_servant.name: Here is My Servant
behold_my_servant.desc:
'Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him' (Isa 42:1), quoted at Matt 12:18 as 'Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him'.

The longest of Matthew's citations -- it runs to four verses (12:18-21) -- and it is quoted to explain why Jesus told those he healed not to make him known. The words about the soul being well pleased are the words of the voice at the baptism (Matt 3:17).

behold_the_handmaid_of_the_lord.name: I am the Lord's servant
behold_the_handmaid_of_the_lord.desc:
'I am the Lord's servant,” Mary answered. “May it happen to me according to your word.' (Luke 1:38).

It is an answer, and the text records the question it answers. Gabriel has just told her what will happen; she asks one practical question at 1:34 and then says this. The whole of her reply is eleven words and none of them is a condition.

The angel's greeting — 'Blessed are you among women' (1:28) — and her own reading of it — 'From now on all generations will call me blessed' (1:48) — are among the most contested sentences in Scripture, and the text records that they were said.

behold_the_lamb_of_god.name: Look, the Lamb of God
behold_the_lamb_of_god.desc:
'The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said, Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!' (John 1:29).

Said twice on consecutive days, and the second time it costs him two disciples, who leave him and follow Jesus (1:36-37). The text reports that without comment.

being_fruitful_in_every_good_work.name: bearing fruit in every good work
being_fruitful_in_every_good_work.desc:
'so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God,' (Col 1:10).

The one place the text puts the two words in a single phrase. Fruit and works run through the letters as separate vocabularies — Gal 5:22 calls the Spirit's output fruit and never works, and Eph 2:9-10 argues about works without once saying fruit. Reading the two as one thing is a step the reader takes, not a step Galatians or Ephesians takes.

Colossians takes it. So does Titus, from the other end: 'our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful.' (Titus 3:14). And Eph 5:11 gives the negative of the same pairing, 'the unfruitful works of darkness'.

Held as its own saying because it is the joint. Anyone tracing the Spirit's fruit toward the works believers were created for passes through here, and if they do not, they are supplying the link themselves.

**As a temple,** Paul to the church in Corinth: 'Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body' (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). The same words return a chapter later: 'You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men' (7:23).

book_of_the_law.name: the book of the law of Moses
book_of_the_law.desc:
'When Moses had finished writing in a book the words of this law from beginning to end,' (Deut 31:24), laid up beside the ark 'as a witness against you' (31:26).

The text keeps referring to it as a physical book that can be lost and found. Hilkiah finds it in the temple in Josiah's day and the king rends his clothes at what it says (2Kgs 22:8-11); Ezra reads it aloud from morning until midday and the people weep (Neh 8:1-9).

Held apart from [[ten_commandments]], which the text names separately and numbers.

born_again.name: you must be born again
born_again.desc:
'no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again' (John 3:3), restated at 3:5 as 'born of water and the Spirit' and pressed at 3:7: 'Do not be amazed that I said, “You must be born again.”'

The exchange is built on a misunderstanding the text keeps. Nicodemus takes it literally — 'How can a man be born when he is old ... Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time?' (3:4) — and Jesus does not correct the reading so much as go past it, drawing the line at 3:6 between what is born of the flesh and what is born of the Spirit.

The saying is recorded rather than a doctrine because that is what the text supplies: three statements of it, one objection, and a figure. What being born again consists of is not stated here.

The name is a translation choice. The ASV reads 'born anew' at 3:3 and 3:7 where older versions read 'born again', and the underlying word carries both senses — a second time, and from above. Nicodemus answers as though it meant the first, which is what makes the misunderstanding work, and a reader who knows only one of the two English renderings sees only half of why.

Two more differences in the same conversation. At 3:2 the older versions have 'miracles' and the ASV 'signs' — and signs is a structural word in this gospel, which numbers them. At 3:10 the older versions have 'a master' and the ASV 'the teacher of Israel', definite, which makes the rebuke sharper than it reads here.

brought_forth_bread_and_wine.name: brought out bread and wine
brought_forth_bread_and_wine.desc:
'Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine-since he was priest of God Most High-' (Gen 14:18).

Three verses in Genesis, one in the Psalms, and a chapter of Hebrews. He appears without introduction, blesses Abraham, receives a tenth, and leaves. The text never mentions him again until Psalm 110:4 — 'You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek' — a thousand years later.

Hebrews 7:3 argues from what Genesis does not say: 'Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life'. That is an argument from silence, made explicitly.

buried_with_him_by_baptism.name: buried with Him through baptism
buried_with_him_by_baptism.desc:
'Or aren’t you aware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life' (Rom 6:3-4).

This is the passage that joins the whole cluster, and it does the joining itself. A death, a burial, a raising, and a new life, in two verses, with the believer put through each in turn. Everything else in this area is a reader assembling pieces; here Scripture assembles them.

6:5 states the comparison outright — 'For if we have been united with Him like this in His death, we will certainly also be united with Him in His resurrection' — and its two terms are both events rather than things.

burning_bush.name: the burning bush
burning_bush.desc:
'the bush ablaze with fire, but it was not consumed' (Exod 3:2), and Moses turning aside to see 'Why is the bush not burning up' (3:3).

The sight is what gets his attention, and the voice waits for him to turn — 'When the LORD saw that he had gone over to look, God called out to him from within the bush' (3:4).

The text refers back to it as a place in the text rather than a place on the ground: Mark 12:26 says 'have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses, how God told him', naming a passage by its scene.

The text itself speaks of it as a place: 'the place where you are standing is holy ground' (Exod 3:5), and Deuteronomy 33:16 blesses by 'the goodwill of Him who dwelt in the burning bush'. That puts it with Mamre and Peniel — a named locale that is not a settlement — rather than with the rod and the tables.

but_if_not.name: But even if He does not, let it be known to you
but_if_not.desc:
'our God whom we serve is able to deliver us ... But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods' (Dan 3:17-18).

The whole weight of the sentence is on three words. The claim is that God can deliver, and then the refusal is detached from whether he does. It is one of very few places in Scripture where obedience is stated as independent of outcome.

Daniel is not in this episode. The three are Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego.

by_faith_the_elders.name: the ancients were commended
by_faith_the_elders.desc:
'Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. This is why the ancients were commended' (Heb 11:1-2).

Hebrews 11:1 is a definition of faith.

The chapter is a template repeated twenty times. Twenty of forty verses open "by faith" or "through faith", each attaching the same word to a different person and a different deed. The variable slot is the person; the constant is the claim about why they acted.

It ends by taking the reward away from all of them: 'These were all commended for their faith, yet they did not receive what was promised' (11:39). The chapter is a list of people commended for trusting something that did not arrive in their lifetimes.

Three things it does that the Old Testament does not. Genesis says Abel's offering was accepted and does not say why (Gen 4:4-5); Hebrews supplies faith as the reason. Genesis 18:12 has Sarah laugh at the promise; Hebrews names her among the faithful and does not mention it. Genesis 27 has Isaac's blessing obtained by deception; Hebrews records the blessing without it. This chapter is a reading of the older books, and a generous one.

by_grace_you_have_been_saved.name: it is by grace you have been saved through faith
by_grace_you_have_been_saved.desc:
'For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast' (Eph 2:8-9).

The verse that most of the faith-and-works argument is conducted on, and it is built from three negations — not of yourselves, not by works, so that no one can boast. What "that" refers to in 'that not of yourselves' has been read as the faith, the grace and the whole transaction.

by_hearing_you_shall_hear_and_shall_not_.name: You will be ever hearing but never understanding
by_hearing_you_shall_hear_and_shall_not_.desc:
'In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled: You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving.' (Matt 13:14), from Isa 6:9.

Isaiah's wording is an instruction -- 'Go and tell this people, Be ever hearing, but never understanding' -- and Matthew's is a description of what happens. It is quoted to explain why Jesus taught in parables, immediately before another fulfilment citation about parables at 13:35.

by_the_hearing_of_faith.name: by hearing with faith
by_the_hearing_of_faith.desc:
'I would like to learn just one thing from you: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?' (Gal 3:2), and again in the same form at v5.

**The letter's question, asked twice.** It puts the Spirit, the works of the law and faith into one sentence, which is why the argument of Galatians 5 is the argument of Galatians 3 continued: the flesh-and-Spirit contrast of chapter 5 is the law-and-faith contrast of chapters 2 and 3 carried into conduct.

The same opposition drives Rom 9:32 -- 'their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works' -- where what it collides with is the stone laid in Zion.

by_works_a_man_is_justified.name: a man is justified by his deeds
by_works_a_man_is_justified.desc:
'As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone.' (Jas 2:24), following 'faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead' (Jas 2:17).

Set beside Eph 2:8-9 without resolving it. Paul: saved by grace through faith, 'not by works, so that no one can boast'. James: 'by his deeds and not by faith alone'. Both use faith and works, and they are not obviously saying the same thing.

The two are placed where a reader meets both, and neither is decided between. Readings that reconcile them exist and are readings; the text states the two and does not state the reconciliation.

'So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, where David made a covenant with them before the LORD. And they anointed him king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD through Samuel.' (1Chr 11:3), told again at 2Sam 5:3.

**A king and a people, not a king and God** -- which makes it unlike the covenant with David at 2Sam 7, and the two should not be read as one. The anointing is the third David receives: Samuel's in private (1Sam 16:13), Judah's at Hebron (2Sam 2:4), and this one over all Israel.

(1Sam 18:3), enlarged at 20:16 to bind the house as well as the man -- 'So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David' -- and sealed at 20:42: 'the two of us have sworn in the name of the LORD ... between your descendants and mine forever'.

**It is cited back years later, by name, as the reason for an act.** David asks 'Is there anyone left from the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?' (2Sam 9:1), and settles Saul's land and a place at his table on Mephibosheth. The covenant and its keeping are seven chapters and one book apart.

Stands immediately after 'not by works, so that no one can boast.' (Eph 2:9), and is held as its own saying because the pair is routinely quoted apart. Read alone, v8-9 says works do not save; read alone, v10 says believers exist for works. Read together, the same writer says both in consecutive sentences and neither is qualified.

crucified_with_christ.name: crucified with Christ
crucified_with_christ.desc:
'I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me.' (Gal 2:20).

The figure is a death the believer undergoes, and the tense is the whole of it: 'I have been crucified' is a completed act, not an ongoing condition.

Romans 6:6 gives it a subject: 'our old self was crucified with Him so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless'. Colossians 3:3 states it flatly — 'For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God'.

Not the same claim as taking up a cross daily (Luke 9:23), which is a thing to do, where this is a thing said to have happened. The text holds both and does not reconcile them.

The judgment is a test rather than a ruling, and the text says what it was testing for: the mother is identified by refusing it. The verdict at 3:27 reverses the order given two verses earlier.

It is the episode the text itself offers as evidence of the wisdom: 'they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice' (3:28).

Within this sense the text is not of one mind: Paul treats division as a symptom of carnality and asks that there be none (1Cor 1:10, 3:3), while Luke 12:51 has Jesus say he came to give it rather than peace, and John reports it three times as what happens around him.

dream_of_pharaoh.name: Pharaoh's dream of the cows and the ears
dream_of_pharaoh.desc: seven well-fed cows eaten by seven lean, and seven full ears devoured by seven thin (Gen 41:1-7). Joseph keys it item by item: 'The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven ripe heads of grain are seven years. The dreams have the same meaning.' (Gen 41:26), and the lean seven are seven years of famine (41:27). **The closing clause is itself an interpretive claim** -- that two dreams are one -- and the text makes it rather than the reader.

dream_of_the_baker.name: the baker's dream
dream_of_the_baker.desc: 'There were three baskets of white bread on my head' (Gen 40:16), keyed at 40:18-19: 'The three baskets are three days. Within three days Pharaoh will lift off your head.' The same figure and the same number as the butler's, with the opposite outcome, and the pairing is the point.

dream_of_the_barley_cake.name: the dream of the barley cake
dream_of_the_barley_cake.desc: 'Behold, I had a dream,” he said, “and I saw a loaf of barley bread come tumbling into the Midianite camp. It struck the tent so hard that the tent overturned and collapsed.' (Judg 7:13). His fellow answers with the key: 'This is nothing less than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite. God has delivered Midian and the whole camp into his hand.' (Judg 7:14). Neither the dreamer nor the interpreter is named -- both are men of the Midianite host, overheard by Gideon.

dream_of_the_butler.name: the chief cupbearer's dream
dream_of_the_butler.desc: 'In my dream there was a vine before me, and on the vine were three branches' (Gen 40:9-10), and Joseph's key in the next breath: 'This is the interpretation: The three branches are three days. Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore your position' (Gen 40:12-13). One identification, and the rest of the reading follows from it.

dream_of_the_great_image.name: Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the great image
dream_of_the_great_image.desc: A great image of gold, silver, brass, iron and clay, broken by a stone cut without hands (Dan 2:31-35). Daniel keys it at 2:36-45: 'You are that head of gold' (2:38), and each metal a kingdom after it, and the stone a kingdom that will never be destroyed. The most fully keyed dream in Scripture — ten verses of explanation for five of vision.

dream_of_the_sheaves.name: the dream of the sheaves
dream_of_the_sheaves.desc:
'We were binding sheaves of grain in the field, and suddenly my sheaf rose and stood upright, while your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to mine.' (Gen 37:7).

**Nobody interprets it and nobody needs to.** The brothers supply the reading themselves, as a question and an accusation: 'Do you intend to reign over us?' (37:8). It is the only dream in the Joseph narrative whose meaning is arrived at by its hearers.

dream_of_the_sun_moon_and_stars.name: the dream of the sun and moon and eleven stars
dream_of_the_sun_moon_and_stars.desc:
'this time the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me' (Gen 37:9).

**His father supplies the key and rejects it in the same sentence**: 'Will your mother and brothers and I actually come and bow down to the ground before you?' (37:10). The reading is correct and the rebuke stands.

The verse after records the two responses side by side: 'And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept in mind what he had said' (37:11).

dream_of_the_tree.name: Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the tree

enmity_between_your_seed_and_her_seed.name: enmity between your seed and her seed
enmity_between_your_seed_and_her_seed.desc:
'I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.' (Gen 3:15).

Spoken to the serpent, and it is the only sentence in the judgment scene addressed to him rather than about him. The two woundings are not matched — a head and a heel — and the asymmetry is the whole of what the verse claims.

It is read by many as the first promise of a deliverer, and the verse itself records no other verse referring back to it.

'The axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.' (Matt 3:10).

**John draws on both halves of Psalm 1 in three verses.** The unfruitful tree at v10 answers the tree planted by the streams of water, that brings forth its fruit (Ps 1:3); the chaff burned at v12 answers the chaff the wind drives away (Ps 1:4). Psalm 1 is two pictures and John uses both, in order, without naming the psalm.

What he adds is fire. In the psalm the chaff simply blows away and the tree simply stands; here the tree will be cut down and thrown into the fire, and the chaff is burned with fire unquenchable.

faith_hope_charity_these_three.name: these three remain: faith, hope, and love
faith_hope_charity_these_three.desc:
'And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love.' (1Cor 13:13).

One verse, three concepts, and a ranking. The text rarely names its own terms as a set and almost never puts them in order, which is why this verse does more structural work than its length suggests: it is the reason faith, hope and love can be joined at all, and the join runs through this statement rather than between them.

faith_is_the_assurance_of_what_we_hope_f.name: faith is the assurance of what we hope for
faith_is_the_assurance_of_what_we_hope_f.desc:
'Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see.' (Heb 11:1).

The text's one definition of faith, and it defines it by what it is rather than by what it does. Both halves point at what is absent: things hoped for are not yet had, things not seen are not there to look at. What is claimed is that faith is the substance and the evidence of them anyway.

'Evidence' is the text's own word and it belongs to the vocabulary of testimony — the same field as the Spirit bearing witness (Rom 8:16, 1John 5:6) and the disciples witnessing from the beginning (John 15:27). Hebrews then spends the rest of the chapter calling witnesses.

fear_not_for_i_am_with_you.name: Do not be afraid, for I am with you
fear_not_for_i_am_with_you.desc:
A construction rather than a phrase. Two negated imperatives about fear, then a reason introduced by for, and the reason is presence.

Don’t be afraid        |  Don’t you be afraid
Don’t be dismayed      |  Don’t be dismayed
for the LORD your God  |  for I am with you
  is with you          |

Joshua 1:9 on the left, Isaiah 41:10 on the right. The phrase layer cannot join them: what they share is 'don’t' and 'for', which are function words, and nothing else.

Run as a shape, the text gives eleven. Beyond the two above: Genesis 26:24 to Isaac, Deuteronomy 20:1 before battle, Deuteronomy 31:6 from Moses to Israel, 1 Chronicles 28:20 from David to Solomon, 2 Chronicles 20:17, Isaiah 43:5, Jeremiah 1:8 at his call, Jeremiah 42:11 about the king of Babylon, and Jeremiah 46:28.

Two of them are the same charge handed down. Moses says it to Israel at Deuteronomy 31:6, Joshua is given it at Joshua 1:9, and David says it to Solomon at 1 Chronicles 28:20 in almost the same words — 'Be strong and courageous ... He will neither fail you nor forsake you'. A formula for handing over a task.

Philippians 4:6-7, 1 Peter 5:7 and John 14:27 are read by many as the same message, and this construction finds none of them. Philippians replaces the second negation with a positive instruction and moves the promise into the next verse; 1 Peter compresses the whole thing to a participle and a clause, keeping only the for; John 14:27 inverts the order and gives the promise first.

That is worth stating rather than fixing. A detector loosened until it caught all of them catches fifty-four verses, most of which are about something else entirely. The Old Testament repeats a form; the New Testament varies it.

'For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place ... And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?' (Esth 4:14).

**Mordecai's argument does not depend on her**: deliverance will come either way, and what is at stake is whether she is part of it. The famous half of the verse is a question, and it is the second half.

*The book of Esther never uses the name of God*, and this verse is the closest it comes -- 'from another place', with the agent left unstated. That is a fact about the book worth knowing before reading the sentence as a promise.

Verse 15 is the line that is easiest to read past: 'from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name'.

fourteen_generations.name: fourteen generations
fourteen_generations.desc:
'In all, then, there were fourteen generations from Abraham to David, fourteen from David to the exile to Babylon, and fourteen from the exile to the Christ.' (Matt 1:17).

The text divides its own history, explicitly, at named points. This is a text stating its own structure and giving the pivots — Abraham, David, the carrying away into Babylon, Christ. Three of the four are people and the fourth is a national catastrophe.

Matt 1:1 sets the same frame in one line before the list begins: 'Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.'

Two genealogies of the same line disagree, and the text carries both. Matt 1:8 reads 'Joram the father of Uzziah'; 1Chr 3:11-12 puts Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah between them. Three names are present in Chronicles and absent from Matthew, and the identification that makes this visible — Uzziah with Azariah — rests on 2Kgs 14:21 and 2Chr 26:1 describing one coronation twice, same age and same father, under two names.

Matthew states the count as fourteen and does not say how it was arrived at. The text offers no reading that accounts for the difference. Both lines are held with their own citations, and a reader who counts finds what a reader who counts finds.

fruit_of_the_spirit.name: the fruit of the Spirit
fruit_of_the_spirit.desc:
'But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law' (Gal 5:22-23).

A declared list — nine named, closed by a clause that comments on the whole set. The noun is singular, fruit and not fruits.

The same writer says "the fruit of the light" at Ephesians 5:9, a different phrase with a much shorter list: 'for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth'. Three, and only goodness is on both.

fruit_unto_death.name: bearing fruit for death
fruit_unto_death.desc:
'For when we lived according to the flesh, the sinful passions aroused by the law were at work in our bodies, bearing fruit for death.' (Rom 7:5).

Four of the argument's terms in one sentence -- flesh, the law, work, and fruit -- and the fruit is death. The figure is not reserved for good outcomes: Matt 7:17 has a corrupt tree bringing forth evil fruit, and Eph 5:11 has unfruitful works of darkness.

It stands in the chapter that Rom 8:1 points back at with 'therefore', and Rom 8:2 picks up 'the law of sin' from Rom 7:25 word for word.

gift.name: gift
gift.desc: Named as a gift in order to rule something else out. Ephesians 2:8 spells out the exclusion -- 'not of yourselves' -- and Romans 6:23 sets it against wages, which is the same move: what is earned against what is given. James 1:17 puts the source above and says it does not vary. Distinct from the Old Testament's gifts, which are mostly offerings brought or bribes refused (Exod 23:8, 'a bribe blinds those who see').

gifts_of_the_spirit.name: different gifts, the same Spirit
gifts_of_the_spirit.desc:
'There are different gifts, but the same Spirit.' (1Cor 12:4), and nine follow at 12:8-10: the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, faith, the gifts of healing, the working of miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, various tongues, the interpretation of tongues.

A third enumerated list attached to the Spirit, alongside the fruit and the works of the flesh, and the only one whose point is that the items differ. The refrain does the arguing: by the Spirit ... by the same Spirit ... by the same Spirit, four times in three verses, closed by 'All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines' (12:11).

That closing clause is where the passage becomes contested. It attributes the distribution to the Spirit's own will, and whether the list is a description of the first century or a standing provision is a question the verse does not answer.

glory.name: glory
glory.desc:
'our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us.' (Rom 8:18).

The word does two jobs in Scripture and the text does not separate them: a visible weight resting on a mountain or filling a tabernacle, and a future condition promised to people. Exodus 24:17 is the first and Romans 8:18 the second.

go.desc:

Nothing is claimed here about what the word means.

go_take_unto_you_a_wife_of_whoredoms.name: Go, take a prostitute as your wife
go_take_unto_you_a_wife_of_whoredoms.desc:
'He told him, Go, take a prostitute as your wife and have children of adultery, because this land is flagrantly prostituting itself' (Hos 1:2).

The longest enacted figure in Scripture, and the prophet is inside it. Most figurative language is spoken; this one is lived, for years, with named children whose names are also the message.

Chapter 3 sends him back a second time, and the verse states the comparison outright: 'show love to your wife again, though she is loved by another and is an adulteress. Love her as the LORD loves the Israelites' (3:1).

god.name: God
god.desc:
Scripture's most-named subject: God, the LORD (the divine name, יהוה), the Almighty, the Most High.

The Father has a card of his own, joined to this one on the verses that say "God the Father" and on Matthew 23:9, "you have one Father, who is in heaven". The two are kept apart so that what the text says to tell Jesus and the Father apart stays visible: folded into one card, those statements could not be told from statements about God.

god_is_a_spirit.name: God is Spirit
god_is_a_spirit.desc:
'God is Spirit, and His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth.' (John 4:24).

A predication offered as the reason for an instruction, not on its own account — it answers a question about which mountain to worship on, and the answer is that the question is the wrong shape.

The word Spirit here is doing something the text should not over-read. This is a statement about what God is, in a verse whose previous line is about the Father seeking worshippers; it is not the Holy Spirit as a person, and the text does not say it is.

god_is_love.name: God is love
god_is_love.desc:
'Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.' (1John 4:8), and again at 4:16 with a consequence attached: 'whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him'.

One of very few places Scripture makes a bare predication about God at all. The others are of the same kind and are worth reading beside it: 'God is Spirit' (John 4:24), 'God is light' (1John 1:5), 'For our God is a consuming fire' (Heb 12:29). Two of the four are in this one letter.

The letter does not leave it abstract. The verse between the two statements grounds it in an act: 'God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him' (4:9).

god_is_our_refuge_and_strength.name: God is our refuge and strength
god_is_our_refuge_and_strength.desc:
'God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble.' (Ps 46:1).

**Two figures and a qualifier, and the qualifier is doing the work.** *Very present* is the claim being made; refuge and strength are the terms it is made in.

Two letters carry the identical sentence and neither mentions the other. Both are quoting Proverbs 3:34.

It is also the only place Scripture makes grace conditional on anything, which is why it is cited on every side of arguments about grace.

god_so_loved_the_world.name: God so loved the world
god_so_loved_the_world.desc:
'For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.' (John 3:16).

The most quoted verse in Scripture, and structurally it is a single sentence with three clauses that each hand off to the next: a motive, an act, and a consequence with a condition inside it.

The next verse restates it as a negation — 'God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world' (3:17) — which is the not X, but Y construction that separates quoted verses from the rest.

grace_and_peace_from_god_our_father.name: Grace and peace to you from God our Father
grace_and_peace_from_god_our_father.desc:
'Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.' (Rom 1:7).

All thirteen letters attributed to Paul open with it, nine reading God our Father and four God the Father, and every one pairs it with the Lord Jesus Christ in the same breath.

It is reasonable to ask whether a greeting means anything, and the text answers it by containing the alternative. Three letters here use the ordinary opening word — 'The apostles and the elders, your brothers ... Greetings' (Acts 15:23), 'Claudius Lysias, To His Excellency, Governor Felix: Greetings.' (Acts 23:26), and 'James, a servant of God ... greeting' (Jas 1:1). One of the three is a Roman officer's dispatch about a prisoner. Paul never uses it, in thirteen letters, substituting grace and peace every time. The departure is visible without leaving the text.

And it does something to the rest of each letter. Paul names the Father in chapter 1 and then writes God for the remainder. Eleven of the thirteen put the formula in the first three verses. Romans contains 144 verses naming God and exactly two joint formulas — 1:7 and 15:6 — the greeting and the closing doxology, so the whole argument sits inside a bracket.

Whether the later, bare references carry that specification forward is a reading, and a common one. The text states the pattern, which is checkable, and stops there.

Genesis never says why one offering was accepted and the other was not, and Hebrews supplies a reason a reader could not have got from the narrative: faith. The text records the verse that supplies it and does not fold it back into Genesis.

He is the first person in Scripture to die and the first named in the roll of faith, and what he is credited with is still speaking.

'and he went and lived in a town called Nazareth. So was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophets: He will be called a Nazarene.' (Matt 2:23).

The one citation in the sweep with no source. Every other fulfilment in Matthew quotes a locatable verse. This one names no book, says 'the prophets' in the plural where the others say 'the prophet', and no sentence in the text reads 'He will be called a Nazarene'.

Held as it stands. The text records that Matthew claims a fulfilment and that the text does not contain what he claims to be fulfilling — which is a fact about the text, and a more useful one than any of the explanations for it.

The divergence is recorded rather than reconciled. It is visible in several of these citations and is worth a reader noticing: Matthew's quotations often do not match the Old Testament text as this corpus carries it.

holy_ghost.name: the Holy Spirit
holy_ghost.desc:
The Holy Spirit, in Greek πνεῦμα ἅγιον; older English translations say the Holy Ghost, for the same words. Often simply "the Spirit", and the text uses both names of one moment: "Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness" (Luke 4:1). John 14 gives two more names in the same discourse: "another Advocate ... the Spirit of truth" (14:16-17) and "the Advocate, the Holy Spirit" (14:26).

So "the Spirit" is kept with this card rather than as a card of its own. The "spirit of ..." construction is not taken with it -- a spirit of fear, of slavery, of stupor -- since most of those are not this.

The Old Testament's "Spirit of God" (Gen 1:2) and "Spirit of the LORD" (Judg 6:34, 1 Sam 16:13) are kept with this card because the New Testament makes the identification itself: "The Holy Spirit was right when He spoke to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet" (Acts 28:25); "as the Holy Spirit says", before Psalm 95 (Heb 3:7); Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1, "The Spirit of the Lord is on Me", of himself (Luke 4:18); and Peter gives Joel's "I will pour out My Spirit" as "what was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16-17). The Old Testament itself says "Your Holy Spirit" (Ps 51:11) and "His Holy Spirit" (Isa 63:10).

how_beautiful_are_the_feet.name: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet
how_beautiful_are_the_feet.desc:
'How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace, who bring good tidings, who proclaim salvation, who say to Zion, Your God reigns!' (Isa 52:7).

**Two prophets say it and one apostle quotes it.** Nah 1:15 has almost the same sentence -- 'Look to the mountains— the feet of one who brings good news, who proclaims peace' -- and neither prophet cites the other. Rom 10:15 quotes it as scripture: 'As it is written: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news.'

What the feet carry is named four times in one verse: good tidings, peace, good tidings of good, salvation. And the message itself is given at the end, addressed to a place -- 'who say to Zion, Your God reigns.'

Rom 10:15 sits two verses after 'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' (Rom 10:13) and in the same argument that collides with the stone laid in Zion at Rom 9:33. The good tidings and the stumbling stone are laid in the same place.

i_am.name: I AM
i_am.desc: Given at the bush as the answer to what Moses should say when they ask the name, and used as one in the next clause: 'I AM has sent me to you.' Held as a title on the same footing as the Alpha and Omega and the First and the Last, both of which are also names a speaker gives himself.

i_am_doing_a_great_work.name: I am doing a great work and cannot come down
i_am_doing_a_great_work.desc:
'I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?' (Neh 6:3).

**Sent four times and answered the same way each time** (6:4). The invitation is to a meeting in a village on a plain, and the text says plainly what it was for: 'they were planning to harm me' (6:2).

The wall is finished in fifty-two days (6:15).
aka: I am doing a great work

i_am_he.name: I am he
i_am_he.desc: Held apart from 'Before Abraham was, I am' for a reason that is about this translation and not about the doctrine: in every one of these verses the word 'he' is supplied, and printed editions italicise it to say so. Whether the underlying Greek differs from John 8:58 is a question no English translation settles. Isaiah 43:10 uses the same English construction of God — 'so that you may consider and believe Me ... that I am he' — which is why the verses are gathered rather than argued over. John 18:6 reports what happened when Jesus said it: the arresting party drew back and fell to the ground.

i_am_that_i_am.name: I AM WHO I AM
i_am_that_i_am.desc:
'God said to Moses, I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: I AM has sent me to you.' (Exod 3:14).

The most-quoted self-naming, and it is given as an answer to a practical question. Moses asks what to say when they ask the name, and this is what he is told to say.

Whether it declares being, or refuses the question, or promises presence, is argued in every direction and none of those readings is in the verse.

i_came_not_to_send_peace_but_a_sword.name: I have not come to bring peace, but a sword
i_came_not_to_send_peace_but_a_sword.desc: Luke has 'division' where Matthew has 'a sword'. The two are held on one record because they are the same saying reported twice; which word is the sharper is left to the reader.

i_desired_mercy_and_not_sacrifice.name: I desire mercy, not sacrifice
i_desired_mercy_and_not_sacrifice.desc:
'For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.' (Hos 6:6).

**Jesus quotes it twice in Matthew and both times against an argument from the law** -- once about eating with tax collectors ... and once about plucking corn on the sabbath (12:7). Each time the verse is offered as something the hearers should already have known.

i_have_learned_to_be_content.name: I have learned to be content regardless of my circumstances
i_have_learned_to_be_content.desc:
'I am not saying this out of need, for I have learned to be content regardless of my circumstances.' (Phil 4:11).

**Learned, not possessed.** v12 gives the curriculum -- 'I know how to live humbly, and I know how to abound ... to being filled and being hungry' -- so the contentment is trained by both halves and not by the comfortable one.

v13 is what it rests on, and is more often quoted without v11-12 than with them.

i_know_that_my_redeemer_lives.name: I know that my Redeemer lives
i_know_that_my_redeemer_lives.desc:
'But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth.' (Job 19:25).

The word is the kinsman-redeemer's, the legal one from Leviticus 25 and the book of Ruth — a relative with a right and a duty to buy back what was lost. Job uses it of God in the middle of an argument about having no advocate.

The two verses after it are among the most textually difficult in the text, and what they claim about seeing God in or without flesh is read several ways.

i_shall_not_want.name: I shall not want
i_shall_not_want.desc:

The consequence stated before anything it depends on. What follows -- the pastures, the waters, the table -- is the psalm showing what not wanting looks like rather than arguing for it.

if_i_perish_i_perish.name: if I perish, I perish
