'I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!' (Esth 4:16).

**She has just explained why it is fatal** -- anyone who approaches the king uncalled is put to death unless he holds out the sceptre, and she has not been called for thirty days (4:11). The decision is made with the risk stated in full and not minimised.

What she asks for first is a fast, by everybody, for three days.

if_i_speak_of_strength.name: If it is a matter of strength

if_my_people.name: if my people shall humble themselves
if_my_people.desc:
'and if My people who are called by My name humble themselves and pray and seek My face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.' (2Chr 7:14).

Four conditions and three consequences, in one sentence. Humbling comes first and praying second, which is the reverse of how the verse is usually quoted.

It is addressed to a named people at a named moment — Solomon's temple, after the dedication — because the verse names 'my people' and a land, and who those are today is the reader's question.

image_anchor.name: anchor
image_anchor.desc: 'We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain,' (Heb 6:19). One occurrence as a figure in the whole corpus, and the ground is stated in the same breath -- firm and secure -- which is what makes it worth a record at all.

image_anointing.name: anointing
image_anointing.desc:
'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power' (Acts 10:38). The verse states the identification outright — the oil is not mentioned and the Spirit stands in its place.

The figure works because the literal act is in the text first. Samuel takes a horn of oil and anoints David, 'and the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward' (1Sam 16:13) — the oil and the Spirit in one sentence, the first as act and the second as consequence.

Isaiah 61:1 puts them together again and Luke 4:18 has Jesus read it aloud: 'The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me'.

image_arm_that_has_no_strength.name: the arm that is feeble
image_arm_that_has_no_strength.desc: the arm 'that is feeble', a figure for weakness

image_armor.name: armor
image_armor.desc:
'Put on the full armor of God, so that you can make your stand against the devil's schemes.' (Eph 6:11).

The text builds the figure and then labels every part of it, which it does almost nowhere else. Six pieces across four verses, each named with the thing it stands for: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God.

The verbs are defensive. Stand, withstand, quench — and of the six only the sword could be used to attack. Whatever the passage is arguing, it is not arguing for advance.

items.name: the arrows of the Almighty have pierced me

image_balances.name: balances
image_balances.desc: A false balance is an abomination in four separate places, which makes the figure at Daniel 5:27 land the way it does: 'TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient' Isaiah 40:12 runs it the other way and weighs the mountains in them.

image_beast.name: beast
image_beast.desc: 'These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth.' (Dan 7:17), and again at 7:23, 'The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom that will appear on the earth'. The angel gives the key to Daniel when he asks for it. Four kings at 7:17 and a kingdom at 7:23 — the text itself moves between the ruler and the realm.

image_body.name: body, as a figure
image_body.desc: 'Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it.' (1Cor 12:27). The figure is worked at length before it is keyed -- foot, hand, ear, eye, each protesting its place -- and the key at 12:27 is an address rather than an equation.

image_bones.name: bones, as a figure
image_bones.desc: 'Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Look, they are saying, Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off.' (Ezek 37:11). The vision is keyed in the same breath it is explained, and the key names the despair as well as the referent.

image_bottles_of_heaven.desc: the phrase 'bottles of heaven' in Job 38:37, the containers of rain

image_branch.desc: 'I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit.' (John 15:5). The key is an address, like 'you are the salt of the earth', and the figure is worked through pruning and burning in the verses around it. Paul uses the same word for grafted Gentiles at Romans 11:17, on an olive rather than a vine.

image_bread.desc: Sometimes the figure and the thing are in the same hand: 'Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, Take and eat; this is My body.' (Matt 26:26). Elsewhere the distance is a generation -- the manna their fathers ate in the desert, answered with 'I am the bread of life' (John 6:31-35).

image_breastplate.name: breastplate
image_breastplate.desc: 'with the breastplate of righteousness arrayed' (Eph 6:14). **The figure is older than Paul** -- Isaiah 59:17 has God putting on 'righteousness as a breastplate', the same pairing, and 1 Thessalonians 5:8 pairs it instead with faith and love.

image_breath.name: breath, as a figure
image_breath.desc:
'He breathed on them and said, Receive the Holy Spirit.' (John 20:22). The act and the naming are one sentence, which is as close to a stated key as a gesture gets.

It reaches back a long way. God breathes into the man at Genesis 2:7 and he becomes a living soul; Ezekiel is told to prophesy to the breath so the slain may live (37:9); Job 33:4 has 'the breath of the Almighty gives me life'. The text does not connect John 20:22 to any of them, and a reader will.

image_bridegroom.name: the bridegroom
image_bridegroom.desc: The figure of the bridegroom whose presence forbids fasting and whose being taken away brings it (Mark 2:19-20).

image_bushel.name: basket
image_bushel.desc: 'Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a basket. Instead, they set it on a stand' (Matt 5:15). The absurd act carries the point; all three synoptics keep it.

image_camel.name: camel
image_camel.desc: Twice, and both times as the largest thing to hand. Through the eye of a needle, and swallowed whole by someone straining out a gnat.

image_candlestick.name: lampstand
image_candlestick.desc: 'the seven lampstands are the seven churches' (Rev 1:20). John is shown the vision and told what it means in the same verse. The word is also the golden lampstand of the tabernacle (Exod 25:31), which is a different thing and keeps its own verses.

image_chaff.name: chaff
image_chaff.desc:
'Not so the wicked! For they are like chaff driven off by the wind.' (Ps 1:4).

**Never used of anything but what is discarded, and always in motion or on fire.** The wind drives it (Ps 1:4, Ps 35:5, Isa 17:13), the whirlwind takes it (Hos 13:3), the fire burns it (Matt 3:12). It has no weight of its own in any of them.

It is the second half of a pair wherever Psalm 1 is in view: the tree planted by the waters stands and bears, the chaff blows away.

image_corner_stone.name: the rejected stone and the cornerstone
image_corner_stone.desc:
'The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.' (Ps 118:22); 'See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone' (Isa 28:16).

Two Old Testament sayings, not one. The text carries a rejected stone that becomes the chief one, and a stone God lays as a foundation. They are quoted separately — Ps 118:22 at Matt 21:42, Mark 12:10 and Acts 4:11; Isa 28:16 at 1Pet 2:6 — and 1Pet 2:6-7 sets them side by side. Held as one image because every quotation calls it the same thing: the head of the corner.

image_creation.name: creation
image_creation.desc:
Named for the word the text actually uses. 'Creature' is in 28 verses and 'creation' in six, and 2 Corinthians 5:17 and Galatians 6:15 both say creature — so the figure is filed under that and the verb 'created' runs alongside it.

A word the text starts with and then keeps using for people. 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.' (Gen 1:1) is the first line; by 2 Corinthians 5:17 the same verb is being applied to a person: 'if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation'.

It runs through the middle too, and not only in the New Testament. 'Create in me a clean heart, O God' (Ps 51:10) asks for it in the first person. Isaiah has it twice as promise — 'Behold, I am about to do something new' (43:19) and 'I will create new heavens and a new earth' (65:17).

And it closes the text: 'Behold, I make all things new' (Rev 21:5), which is the last of the figure and the only place a voice says it of everything at once.

The text does not claim these are one idea. They are one word, used by writers a thousand years apart, and a reader who sees a thread from Genesis to Revelation is doing something the text does not do on the page.

image_cross.name: cross
image_cross.desc:
The instrument, used as a figure. 'the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God' (1Cor 1:18).

The text turns it into something a reader carries. 'If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.' (Luke 9:23) — said before any crucifixion has happened in the narrative, to hearers for whom it was still only a Roman execution.

Paul makes it the one thing to boast in: 'But as for me, may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.' (Gal 6:14). Kept apart from the crucifixion itself, which is an event with a place and a date, the way every figure here is kept apart from the thing it is drawn from.

image_crown.name: crown, as a figure
image_crown.desc: Always qualified, and the qualifier is the meaning: 'the crown of righteousness' (2Tim 4:8), 'the crown of life' (Jas 1:12), 'the crown of glory that will never fade away' (1Pet 5:4). Beside the literal crowns of the kings, which are a different record.

image_cup.name: cup
image_cup.desc: Two figures under one word, and the verses keep them apart. The cup of the covenant: 'He took the cup, gave thanks ... This is My blood of the covenant' (Matt 26:27-28), stated outright at 1Cor 11:25 — 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood'. The cup of suffering and of wrath: 'let this cup pass from Me' (Matt 26:39), 'Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?' (Matt 20:22), and in the hand of the LORD at Ps 75:8 and Rev 14:10. The text does not join them.

items.label: is the image behind

image_darkness.name: darkness, as a figure
image_darkness.desc:
'God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.' (1John 1:5).

The text almost never uses it alone. It appears as the half of a pair — 'what fellowship does light have with darkness?' (2Cor 6:14), 'you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord' (Eph 5:8), 'Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.' (John 8:12).

John 3:19-20 gives it a motive rather than leaving it a condition: 'men loved the darkness rather than the Light because their deeds were evil. Everyone who does evil hates the Light, and does not come into the Light for fear that his deeds will be exposed.'

image_death.name: death, as a figure
image_death.desc:
A word the text uses for two different things and rarely marks which. There is dying, and there is a state a living person can already be in.

'The mind of the flesh is death' (Rom 8:6). 'the wages of sin is death' (Rom 6:23). 'The one who does not love remains in death.' (1John 3:14) — said of people who are demonstrably alive.

It begins in Genesis with a warning whose timing is disputed on the page: 'in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die' (Gen 2:17), and Adam lives 930 years, and it ends with a second one: 'Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death' (Rev 20:14), which implies the first was not final.

The same chapter runs the shepherd, the sheep, the fold and the gatekeeper, so the door here is a fold's door rather than a house's. Revelation 3:20 uses the word for a different figure entirely — 'Behold, I stand at the door, and knock' — and the text keeps them apart.

image_earnest.name: the Spirit as a pledge
image_earnest.desc:
'placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come.' (2Cor 1:22), repeated at 5:5 and again at Ephesians 1:14.

A down payment: money handed over that both proves the buyer means it and is itself part of the price. The figure claims the Spirit is not a token of something later but the first instalment of it.

One of the few figures in the New Testament drawn from commerce rather than from farming, weather or the household, and Paul is the only one who uses it.

image_fig_tree.name: fig tree
image_fig_tree.desc:
'Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, He went to see if there was any fruit on it. But when He reached it, He found nothing on it except leaves' (Mark 11:13), and the next morning 'they saw the fig tree withered from its roots' (11:20).

Mark wraps the temple inside it. The tree is cursed on the way in (11:12-14), the tables are overturned (11:15-19), and the withering is found on the way out (11:20-21) — one act split around another, a shape Mark uses elsewhere.

The text does not say the tree is the temple, so it is treated as a figure and not as a key.

image_fire.name: fire, as a figure
image_fire.desc: 'For our God is a consuming fire' (Heb 12:29), quoting Deuteronomy 4:24. Acts 2:3 has 'tongues like flames of fire' at Pentecost, and 1 Peter 1:7 the trial of faith 'refined by fire'. Presence, purging and judgment under one word, and each verse says which.

Job sets it beside the shadow -- 'Like a flower, he comes forth, then withers away; like a fleeting shadow, he does not endure.' (Job 14:2).

'You are my refuge and my fortress' (Ps 91:2).

One of a cluster David piles up in a single verse: 'The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer' (2Sam 22:2, repeated at Ps 18:2). **Six figures for the same claim in one sentence**, which is the psalms preferring accumulation to precision.

image_fruit.name: fruit, as a figure
image_fruit.desc:
What a thing produces, standing for what the thing is.

One of the most heavily worked figures in the New Testament and one of the few used as a test. 'by their fruit you will recognize them' (Matt 7:20) makes it evidential — the fruit is how the tree is identified, not merely what it yields. John the Baptist demands 'fruits meet for repentance' (Matt 3:8) on the same logic.

It attaches to whatever is claimed to be the source. Of the Spirit at Galatians 5:22 and Ephesians 5:9; of abiding in Christ at John 15:5, where the vine figure supplies it; of righteousness at Philippians 1:11, Hebrews 12:11 and James 3:18; of the tree at Matthew 7:17, good or corrupt.

The text uses the word for actual produce constantly, but no particular fruit is identified as the figure.

image_life.name: life, as a figure
image_life.desc:
Almost always set against death rather than defined on its own. 'I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life' (Deut 30:19) is the pattern, and the pairing does the work.

Scripture repeatedly describes a crossing between the two rather than a difference of degree: 'has crossed over from death to life' (John 5:24), 'We know that we have passed from death to life' (1John 3:14), 'walk in newness of life' (Rom 6:4).

'I am the resurrection and the life' (John 11:25) is the one place a person is identified with the word.

image_light.name: light, as a figure
image_light.desc: 'I am the light of the world' (John 8:12, repeated 9:5), and the same words turned on the hearers at Matthew 5:14 -- 'You are the light of the world'. Psalm 119:105 makes it the word: 'Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path'

image_narrow_gate.name: the narrow gate
image_narrow_gate.desc: 'Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction' (Matt 7:13), against the narrow gate and restricted way 'that leads to life'. Two roads and two ends, with the ends named in the verses themselves.

image_net.name: net
image_net.desc: Two settings and the same object. In the Psalms and prophets it is always laid for someone -- 'He will free my feet from the mesh' (Ps 25:15), 'But I will spread My net over him' (Ezek 12:13). In the Gospels it is work, and then a figure for the kingdom: 'like a net that was cast into the sea and caught all kinds of fish' (Matt 13:47). Luke 5:6 has the net break under the catch; John 21:11 makes a point of one that does not.

image_of_god.name: image of God
image_of_god.desc:
Said of humankind at creation: "So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them" (Gen 1:27), given with a task: "to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air ... and over all the earth" (1:26).

Genesis says it twice more: Adam "had a son in his own likeness, after his own image" (5:3), and the reason given against shedding blood is "for in His own image God has made mankind" (9:6). James still argues from it, of men "who have been made in God's likeness" (3:9).

In the New Testament the phrase is given to Christ, "who is the image of God" (2 Cor 4:4) and "the image of the invisible God" (Col 1:15). The same Greek word, εἰκών, describes what believers are becoming: "being transformed into His image" (2 Cor 3:18), "being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator" (Col 3:10), "conformed to the image of His Son" (Rom 8:29).

'He will make your paths straight' (Prov 3:6); 'He guides me in the paths of righteousness' (Ps 23:3); 'Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths.' (Ps 25:4).

Where paths appear, someone else is directing, leading, teaching or lighting it — and the one going is not the one choosing. Ps 119:105 makes the lamp the word; Isa 30:21 puts a voice behind rather than a map ahead.

Ps 23:3 joins paths and leading. That is what lets a reader go from being told to trust (Prov 3:5-6) to being led (Ps 23), without either verse mentioning the other.

image_stone_of_stumbling.name: stone of stumbling
image_stone_of_stumbling.desc:
'And He will be a sanctuary-but to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' (Isa 8:14).

**The same stone, received two ways.** 1Pet 2:7-8 puts it plainly: to those who believe the stone is precious and has become the cornerstone; to the disobedient the identical stone is one of stumbling. Nothing changes about the stone. What differs is who meets it.

Rom 9:33 is where this is easiest to miss. Paul writes 'Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' -- which reads as one quotation and is two: the opening is Isa 28:16, where God lays a sure foundation, and the ending is Isa 8:14, where the stone trips people. He joins a promise to a warning in a single sentence.

image_temple.name: temple
image_temple.desc:
The temple used as a figure for where God dwells. The building in Jerusalem has its own card: [[temple]].

**God himself as a sanctuary,** to the exiles far from the temple: 'yet for a little while I have been a sanctuary for them in the countries to which they have gone' (Ezekiel 11:16).

**Jesus's body:** 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again' (John 2:19). His hearers take him to mean the building, and the narrator explains, 'But Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body' (John 2:21).

**The community of believers,** to the church in Corinth: 'Do you not know that you yourselves are God's temple, and that God's Spirit dwells in you?' (1 Corinthians 3:16).

**The believer's body:** 'Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God?' (1 Corinthians 6:19).

**The new Jerusalem:** 'But I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple' (Revelation 21:22).

**Where readers differ.** Some passages are read in more than one way: the temple in them has been understood as the building that stood in Jerusalem when the passage was written, a temple yet to be built, a temple in heaven, the people of God, or a figure of something else. The site shows these verses and does not choose among the readings: 2 Thessalonians 2:4, of the one called 'the man of lawlessness' in verse 3, 'So he will seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God'; Matthew 24:15; Haggai 2:9; Ezekiel 40-48, the temple the prophet is shown 'in visions of God' (40:2); Revelation 11:1-2; and Zechariah 6:12-15.

'The Song of Solomon uses the same word for the opposite job. 'Your neck is like the tower of David, built with rows of stones; on it hang a thousand shields, all of them shields of warriors.' (Song 4:4) — a comparison, marked with 'like', and describing what a body looks like rather than what God is. The two uses share a word and nothing else.

image_wisdom.name: wisdom, as a figure
image_wisdom.desc:
A word the text personifies and then argues about. Proverbs makes her a person — 'Wisdom calls out in the street, she lifts her voice in the square' (1:20), 'Wisdom has built her house' (9:1).

What it is here to hold is the disagreement, and the disagreement has speakers. Not 'the text says' but these voices say:

  * Solomon, whose proverbs these are said to be (Prov 1:1, 10:1): 'She is more precious than rubies; nothing you desire compares with her' (3:15, again at 8:11); 'Wisdom is supreme; so acquire wisdom' (4:7).
  * the Preacher, who names himself at Eccl 1:1 and speaks in the first person at 1:12: 'For with much wisdom comes much sorrow, and as knowledge grows, grief increases' (1:18); 'The fate of the fool will also befall me. What then have I gained by being wise?' (2:15); 'there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool' (2:16).

And the Preacher contradicts himself, not only Solomon. The same voice says 'wisdom, like money, is a shelter ... wisdom preserves the life of its owner' (7:12) and 'Wisdom is better than strength' (9:16). Reading Ecclesiastes as simply contrarian is a reading the book does not support; the tension is inside one speaker.

Whether he holds both on purpose is a reading and is not recorded here. What is recorded is that he says both, and where.

image_wolf.name: wolves
image_wolf.desc: 'Beware of false prophets, They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves' (Matt 7:15). image_yoke.name: yoke
image_yoke.desc: One word, and every use turns on who does the putting. Imposed: Rehoboam adding to it (1Kgs 12:11), a yoke of iron on the neck (Deut 28:48), the law that neither fathers nor sons could bear (Acts 15:10), the yoke of bondage (Gal 5:1). Broken: Isaiah 9:4, Leviticus 26:13, and Isaiah 58:6, where breaking it is the fast God chose. Offered: 'Take my yoke upon you ... my yoke is easy' (Matt 11:29-30), which is the only place the wearer is asked. Jeremiah wears a literal one through two chapters as a sign, so the figure and the object are the same object there.

immanuel.name: Immanuel
immanuel.desc:
'Behold, the virgin will be with child and give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.' (Isa 7:14).

Matt 1:23 quotes Isaiah and then adds the gloss: 'they will call Him Immanuel (which means, God with us).' That is unusual — most names in Scripture are left to stand — and it means the meaning is the text's own and not a reader's.

Isaiah's Hebrew is ʿImmanuʾel (Immanuel); Matthew's Greek writes Emmanouēl (Emmanuel). The Berean uses Immanuel in both. It is never used as an address or a form of speech: it is given as a name he will be called, twice, and then not used again.

The only place Scripture gives the Father a house, and the figure is domestic rather than royal — rooms, and someone going ahead to make one ready. It opens the same discourse that gives the Comforter and 'No one comes to the Father'.

in_the_beginning_god_created.desc:

Scripture's first sentence, and John's gospel opens on its first three words. Nothing precedes it and nothing in it is argued for — the beginning, the actor and the act arrive together.

in_the_beginning_was_the_word.name: In the beginning was the Word
in_the_beginning_was_the_word.desc:
'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1).

The first three words are Genesis 1:1's first three words. The gospel does not say it is quoting and does not need to; it is Scripture's most recognisable opening and John puts something else in the sentence.

Three clauses, and the third is not the second. With God, and God — stated in one verse without reconciliation, and repeated at v2 rather than explained.

in_the_bush_god_spoke_unto_him.name: in the bush God spoke to him
in_the_bush_god_spoke_unto_him.desc:
'have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses, how God told him, 'I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'?' (Mark 12:26).

The bush is used as an argument for the resurrection, which is not what a reader expects it to be for. Jesus is answering the Sadducees, and the whole weight of the reply is on a tense: God says I am, not I was, of three men long dead.

It is also how Scripture itself refers to the episode — 'in the bush' as a way of naming a passage, the way one might say the burning bush today. Stephen tells it again at Acts 7:30 and Paul never mentions it.

in_the_spirit_and_power_of_elias.name: in the spirit and power of Elijah
in_the_spirit_and_power_of_elias.desc:
'And he will go on before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah' (Luke 1:17), said of John the Baptist before his birth.

Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah himself — 'behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD' — and the New Testament applies it to somebody else. Matthew 11:14 makes the application conditional in an odd way: 'if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come'.

John himself denies it. Asked directly whether he is Elijah, he says 'I am not' (John 1:21).

all_the_families_of_the_earth_will_be_bl.name: all the families of the earth will be blessed through you
all_the_families_of_the_earth_will_be_bl.desc:
'All the families of the earth will be blessed through you' (Gen 12:3). It is spoken five times in Genesis in the LORD's name: to Abraham (12:3), of Abraham (18:18, 'through him'), to Abraham again by 'the angel of the LORD' (22:15-18, 'through your offspring'), to Isaac (26:4) and to Jacob (28:14). The wording varies between 'families' and 'nations', and between 'through you', 'through him', 'through your offspring' or, in 28:14, both you and your offspring.

The Hebrew uses two forms of the verb: one in 12:3, 18:18 and 28:14, the other in 22:18 and 26:4. Translators differ on both, rendering either 'be blessed' or 'bless themselves'.

Acts 3:25 cites it as 'Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed', and Gal 3:8 as 'All nations will be blessed through you'. Both are passive in the Greek.

jacob_speech_30_25.name: Jacob asks to leave with wives and children
jacob_speech_30_25.desc: Send me on my way so I can return to my homeland ... Give me my wives and children for whom I have served you, that I may go on my way. You know how hard I have worked for you.

jacob_speech_30_29.name: Jacob reminds Laban of his service
jacob_speech_30_29.desc: Then Jacob answered, You know how I have served you and how your livestock have thrived under my care. Indeed, you had very little before my arrival, but now your wealth has increased many times over. The LORD has blessed you wherever I set foot. But now, when may I also provide for my own household?

jacob_speech_30_31_33.name: Jacob proposes the marked animals as his hire
jacob_speech_30_31_33.desc: What can I give you? Laban asked. You do not need to give me anything, Jacob replied. If you do this one thing for me, I will keep on shepherding and keeping your flocks. Let me go through all your flocks today and remove from them every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-colored lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat. These will be my wages. So my honesty will testify for me when you come to check on my wages in the future. If I have any goats that are not speckled or spotted, or any lambs that are not dark-colored, they will be considered stolen.

jacobs_ladder.name: a ladder that rested on the earth
jacobs_ladder.desc:
'And Jacob had a dream about a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven, and God's angels were going up and down the ladder.' (Gen 28:12).

Jesus refers to it and changes what the angels climb. 'you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man' (John 1:51) — the same two verbs in the same order, with a person where the ladder was.

Jacob's own reading is the sentence after he wakes: 'Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it' (28:16).

jehoiachin.name: Jehoiachin
jehoiachin.desc: Four spellings, one king: Jehoiachin in Kings, Jeconiah in Chronicles and Jeremiah 27, Coniah in Jeremiah 22, Jeconiah in Matthew. Jeremiah 27:20 joins two of them in a clause — 'Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah'. He therefore has two recorded fathers, Jehoiakim in Kings and Josiah in Matthew, and both accounts stand; the scribes who carried both lines for a thousand years did not reconcile them, and the disagreement is evidence rather than damage.

jephthah_vowed_a_vow.desc:
'Jephthah made this vow to the LORD: If indeed You will deliver the Ammonites into my hand,' (Judg 11:30).

The Spirit had already come upon him two verses earlier (11:29), and he vows anyway.

The text reports his words at 11:35 — 'I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back' — and it does not say whether he was right, whether the vow was binding, or what was finally done.

jesus_says_unto_her_mary.name: Jesus said to her, “Mary.”
jesus_says_unto_her_mary.desc:
'Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to Him in Hebrew, “Rabboni!” (which means “Teacher”).' (John 20:16).

She has already seen him and taken him for the gardener (20:15). What identifies him is one word, and the word is her name.

She is then sent to tell the others (20:18), the first person reported as commissioned to tell of the resurrection.

jesus_wept.name: Jesus wept
jesus_wept.desc:
'Jesus wept' (John 11:35).

He has already said the sickness is not unto death, already waited two days deliberately, and is four verses from calling the man out of the tomb. The weeping is not because it cannot be fixed.

The bystanders read it one way — 'behold how he loved him' (11:36) — and the text reports their reading without endorsing it.

jews.name: the Jewish people
jews.desc: The Bible uses "Jews" for the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem (Ezra 5:1) and for Israelites of other tribes: Mordecai is "a Jewish man from the tribe of Benjamin" (Esth 2:5), and Paul says both "I am a Jew" (Acts 22:3) and "I am an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin" (Rom 11:1). God says to Israel, "Jacob, whom I have chosen, descendant of Abraham My friend" (Isa 41:8). Paul asks, "did God reject His people?" and answers, "Certainly not!" (Rom 11:1); of Israel (11:26) he writes, "Regarding the gospel, they are enemies on your account; but regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs" (11:28), the "you" being the Gentiles he addresses (11:13), and "God's gifts and His call are irrevocable" (11:29).

job_12_14_speech.desc: What He tears down cannot be rebuilt; the man He imprisons cannot be released.

job_12_15_speech.name: Job 12:15 speech
job_12_15_speech.desc: If He holds back the waters, they dry up, and if He releases them, they overwhelm the land.

job_12_16_speech.name: Job 12:16 speech
job_12_16_speech.desc: True wisdom and power belong to Him. The deceived and the deceiver are His.

job_12_17_speech.name: Job 12:17 speech
job_12_17_speech.desc: He leads counselors away barefoot and makes fools of judges.

job_12_18_speech.name: Job 12:18 speech
job_12_18_speech.desc: He loosens the bonds placed by kings and fastens a belt around their waists.

job_12_19_speech.name: Job 12:19 speech
job_12_19_speech.desc: He leads priests away barefoot and overthrows the established.

job_12_1_1.name: Job's reply begins
job_12_1_1.desc: Speech formula opens the chapter: "Then Job answered:"

job_12_20_speech.name: Job 12:20 speech
job_12_20_speech.desc: He deprives the trusted of speech and takes away the discernment of elders.

job_12_21_speech.name: Job 12:21 speech
job_12_21_speech.desc: He pours out contempt on nobles and disarms the mighty.

job_12_22_speech.name: Job 12:22 speech
job_12_22_speech.desc: He reveals the deep things of darkness and brings deep shadows into light.

job_12_23_speech.name: Job 12:23 speech
job_12_23_speech.desc: He makes nations great and destroys them; He enlarges nations, then disperses them.

job_12_24_speech.name: Job 12:24 speech
job_12_24_speech.desc: He deprives the earth’s leaders of reason and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland.

job_12_2_6.name: Sarcasm: wisdom shall die with you
job_12_2_6.desc: Second-person mockery of the friends, "Truly then you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die... I am not inferior to you", ending with the complaint that "The tents of robbers are safe"

job_12_2_speech.name: Job at Job 12:2
job_12_2_speech.desc: Job's words: Truly then you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die!.

job_12_3_speech.name: Job at Job 12:3
job_12_3_speech.desc: Job's words: But I also have a mind; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these??

job_12_4_speech.name: Job at Job 12:4
job_12_4_speech.desc: Job's words: I am a laughingstock to my friends, though I called on God, and He answered. The righteous and upright man is a laughingstock.

job_12_5_speech.name: Job at Job 12:5
job_12_5_speech.desc: Job's words: The one at ease scorns misfortune as the fate of those whose feet are slipping.

job_12_6_speech.name: Job at Job 12:6
job_12_6_speech.desc: Job's words: The tents of robbers are safe, and those who provoke God are secure— those who carry their god in their hands.

job_12_7_12.name: Ask the beasts: even they know
job_12_7_12.desc: Turns with "But ask the animals, and they will instruct you" -- singular "you" and a new appeal to creation and to the wisdom of "the elderly"

job_12_7_speech.name: Job at Job 12:7
job_12_7_speech.desc: Job's words: But ask the animals, and they will instruct you; ask the birds of the air, and they will tell you:

job_12_8_speech.name: Job at Job 12:8
job_12_8_speech.desc: Job's words: Or speak to the earth, and it will teach you; let the fish of the sea inform you.

job_12_9_speech.name: Job at Job 12:9
job_12_9_speech.desc: Job's words: Which of all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this?

job_13_10_speech.name: Surely He would rebuke you
job_13_10_speech.desc: Job's words: Surely He would rebuke you if you secretly showed partiality.

job_13_11_speech.name: Would His majesty not terrify you?
job_13_11_speech.desc: Job's words: Would His majesty not terrify you? Would the dread of Him not fall upon you??

job_13_12_speech.name: Your maxims are proverbs of ashes
job_13_12_speech.desc: Job's words: Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.

job_13_13_19.name: Let me alone, I will plead my own cause
job_13_13_19.desc: "Be silent, and I will speak" turns from accusing them to staking his own case: "I have prepared my case, I know that I will be vindicated"

job_13_1_5.name: I know as much as you do
job_13_1_5.desc: Opens "Indeed, my eyes have seen all this ... I am not inferior to you" and closes with the wish "If only you would remain silent!"

job_13_1_speech.name: Indeed, my eyes have seen all this
job_13_1_speech.desc: Job's words: Indeed, my eyes have seen all this; my ears have heard and understood.

job_13_20_28.name: Job's plea turned to God
job_13_20_28.desc: The address turns to second person singular of God: "Only grant these two things to me, so that I need not hide from You... Why do You hide Your face"

job_13_25_speech.name: Job at Job 13:25
job_13_25_speech.desc: The verse as Job speaks it: 'Would You frighten a windblown leaf? Would You chase after dry chaff?'

job_13_26_speech.name: Job at Job 13:26
job_13_26_speech.desc: The verse: 'For You record bitter accusations against me and bequeath to me the iniquities of my youth'

job_13_27_speech.name: Job at Job 13:27
job_13_27_speech.desc: The verse: 'You put my feet in the stocks and stand watch over all my paths; You set a limit for the soles of my feet'

job_13_28_speech.name: Job's words: he, as a rotten thing, consumes
job_13_28_speech.desc: The verse: 'So man wastes away like something rotten, like a moth-eaten garment'

job_13_2_speech.name: What you know, I also know
job_13_2_speech.desc: Job's words: What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you.

job_13_3_speech.name: Yet I desire to speak to the Almighty
job_13_3_speech.desc: Job's words: Yet I desire to speak to the Almighty and argue my case before God.

job_13_4_speech.name: You, however, smear with lies
job_13_4_speech.desc: Job's words: You, however, smear with lies; you are all worthless physicians.

job_13_5_speech.name: If only you would remain silent
job_13_5_speech.desc: Job's words: If only you would remain silent; for that would be your wisdom!.

job_13_6_12.name: Warning to the friends who plead God's case
job_13_6_12.desc: "Hear now my reasoning" opens a fresh appeal; the subject turns to their partiality, "Will you speak wickedly on God's behalf or speak deceitfully for Him?" ... "He will surely reprove you"

job_13_6_speech.name: Hear now my argument
job_13_6_speech.desc: Job's words: Hear now my argument, and listen to the plea of my lips.

job_13_7_speech.name: Will you speak wickedly on God's behalf
job_13_7_speech.desc: Job's words: Will you speak wickedly on God’s behalf or speak deceitfully for Him??

job_13_8_speech.name: Would you show Him partiality
job_13_8_speech.desc: Job's words: Would you show Him partiality or argue in His defense??

job_13_9_speech.name: Would it be well when He examined you?
job_13_9_speech.desc: Job's words: Would it be well when He examined you? Could you deceive Him like a man??

job_14_10_speech.name: Job at Job 14:10
job_14_10_speech.desc: Job's words: "But a man dies and is laid low; he breathes his last, and where is he?"

job_14_11_speech.name: Job at Job 14:11
job_14_11_speech.desc: Job's words: "As water disappears from the sea and a river becomes parched and dry"

job_14_12_speech.name: Job at Job 14:12
job_14_12_speech.desc: Job's words: "so a man lies down and does not rise. Until the heavens are no more, he will not be awakened or roused from sleep"

job_14_13_17.name: If only You would hide me in Sheol
job_14_13_17.desc: The vocative wish "If only You would hide me in Sheol" turns the address back to God, and the hope holds through "You will call, and I will answer" until "For then You would count my steps" recalls the present watching.

job_14_13_speech.name: Job at Job 14:13
job_14_13_speech.desc: Job's entreaty that God hide him in the grave until his wrath passes, then appoint a set time and remember him.

job_14_14_speech.name: Job at Job 14:14
job_14_14_speech.desc: Job asks whether a man will live again and says he will wait the days of his appointed time until his change.

job_14_15_speech.name: Job at Job 14:15
job_14_15_speech.desc: Job promises that when God calls he will answer, and says God desires the work of his hands.

job_14_16_speech.name: Job at Job 14:16
job_14_16_speech.desc: Job says God numbers his steps and asks whether God watches over his sin.

job_14_17_speech.name: Job at Job 14:17
job_14_17_speech.desc: Job says his transgression is sealed in a bag and his iniquity sewed up.

job_14_18_22.name: You Destroy the Hope of Man
job_14_18_22.desc: "But as a mountain erodes and crumbles" opens a new set of images of erosion, applied in "You destroy a man's hope", and ends with the dead man's ignorance of his sons and "He feels only the pain of his own body".

job_14_18_speech.name: Job at Job 14:18
job_14_18_speech.desc: Job observes that a falling mountain comes to nothing and a rock is removed from its place.

job_14_19_speech.name: Job at Job 14:19
job_14_19_speech.desc: Job says waters wear stones, God washes away plants, and God destroys man's hope.

job_14_1_6.name: Man's Few Days: Turn From Him
job_14_1_6.desc: Opens with a general maxim, "Man, who is born of woman, is short of days", then turns to God in the second person ("Do You open Your eyes to one like this") and ends with a petition, "look away from him and let him rest".

job_14_1_speech.name: Job at Job 14:1
job_14_1_speech.desc: Job's words: "Man, who is born of woman, is short of days and full of trouble"

job_14_20_speech.name: Job at Job 14:20
job_14_20_speech.desc: Job says God prevails forever against man, changes his countenance and sends him away.

job_14_21_speech.name: Job at Job 14:21
job_14_21_speech.desc: Job says a man's sons receive honor or are brought low, but he neither knows nor perceives it.

job_14_22_speech.name: Job at Job 14:22
job_14_22_speech.desc: Job says the man's flesh will have pain and his soul will mourn.

job_14_2_speech.name: Job at Job 14:2
job_14_2_speech.desc: Job's words: "Like a flower, he comes forth, then withers away; like a fleeting shadow, he does not endure"

job_14_3_speech.name: Job at Job 14:3
job_14_3_speech.desc: Job's words: "Do You open Your eyes to one like this? Will You bring him into judgment before You?"

job_14_4_speech.name: Job at Job 14:4
job_14_4_speech.desc: Job's words: "Who can bring out clean from unclean? No one!"

job_14_5_speech.name: Job at Job 14:5
job_14_5_speech.desc: Job's words: "Since his days are determined and the number of his months is with You, and since You have set limits that he cannot exceed"

job_14_6_speech.name: Job at Job 14:6
job_14_6_speech.desc: Job's words: "look away from him and let him rest, so he can enjoy his day as a hired hand"

job_14_7_12.name: A Tree Sprouts Again, But Man Does Not
job_14_7_12.desc: "For there is hope for a tree" begins a sustained comparison, answered by "a man dies and is laid low" and closed with "so a man lies down and does not rise. Until the heavens are no more". Speaks about God's creatures, not to God.

job_14_7_speech.name: Job at Job 14:7
job_14_7_speech.desc: Job's words: "For there is hope for a tree: If it is cut down, it will sprout again, and its tender shoots will not fail"

job_14_8_speech.name: Job at Job 14:8
job_14_8_speech.desc: Job's words: "If its roots grow old in the ground and its stump dies in the soil"

job_14_9_speech.name: Job at Job 14:9
job_14_9_speech.desc: Job's words: "at the scent of water it will bud and put forth twigs like a sapling"

job_15_10_speech.name: Both the gray-haired and the aged are on our side-men much older than your father.
job_15_10_speech.desc: Eliphaz says, 'Both the gray-haired and the aged are on our side— men much older than your father'

job_15_13_speech.desc: The verse: 'as you turn your spirit against God and pour such words from your mouth?'

job_15_14_16.name: No man is clean before God
job_15_14_16.desc: Turns from Job to man in general: "What is man, that he should be clean?" with "If God puts no trust in His holy ones" and "How much less man, who is vile and corrupt"

job_15_14_speech.name: What is man, that he should be pure,
job_15_14_speech.desc: The verse: 'What is man, that he should be pure, or one born of woman, that he should be righteous?'

job_15_15_speech.name: If God puts no trust in His holy ones
job_15_15_speech.desc: The verse: 'If God puts no trust in His holy ones, if even the heavens are not pure in His eyes'

job_15_16_speech.name: how much less man, who is vile and corrupt
job_15_16_speech.desc: The verse: 'how much less man, who is vile and corrupt, who drinks injustice like water?'

job_15_17_19.name: Hear the tradition of the fathers
job_15_17_19.desc: Announcement formula: "Listen to me and I will inform you. I will describe what I have seen, what was declared by wise men"

job_15_17_speech.name: Listen to me and I will inform you.
job_15_17_speech.desc: The verse: 'Listen to me and I will inform you. I will describe what I have seen'

job_15_18_speech.name: Eliphaz at Job 15:18
job_15_18_speech.desc: The verse: 'what was declared by wise men and was not concealed from their fathers'

job_15_19_speech.name: to whom alone the land was given
job_15_19_speech.desc: The verse: 'to whom alone the land was given when no foreigner passed among them'

job_15_1_1.name: Eliphaz answers again
job_15_1_1.desc: Speech formula opens the chapter: "Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied"

job_15_20_35.name: The fate of the wicked man
job_15_20_35.desc: Third-person doctrine begins "A wicked man writhes in pain all his days" and runs to the summarising "For the company of the godless will be barren"

job_15_20_speech.name: Eliphaz at Job 15:20
job_15_20_speech.desc: The verse: 'A wicked man writhes in pain all his days; only a few years are reserved for the ruthless'

job_15_21_speech.name: Sounds of terror fill his ears
job_15_21_speech.desc: The verse: 'Sounds of terror fill his ears; in his prosperity the destroyer attacks him'

job_15_22_speech.name: Eliphaz at Job 15:22
job_15_22_speech.desc: The verse: 'He despairs of his return from darkness; he is marked for the sword'

job_15_23_speech.name: He wanders about as food for vultures
job_15_23_speech.desc: The verse: 'He wanders about as food for vultures; he knows the day of darkness is at hand'

job_15_24_speech.name: Distress and anguish terrify him
job_15_24_speech.desc: The verse: 'Distress and anguish terrify him, overwhelming him like a king poised to attack'

job_15_25_speech.name: Eliphaz at Job 15:25
job_15_25_speech.desc: For he has stretched out his hand against God and has vaunted himself against the Almighty.

job_15_26_speech.name: Eliphaz: he runs upon God
job_15_26_speech.desc: Rushing headlong at Him with a thick, studded shield:

job_15_27_speech.name: Eliphaz at Job 15:27
job_15_27_speech.desc: Though his face is covered with fat and his waistline bulges with flesh.

job_15_28_speech.name: Eliphaz: he dwells in desolate cities
job_15_28_speech.desc: He will dwell in ruined cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble.

job_15_29_speech.name: Eliphaz: the wicked shall not be rich
job_15_29_speech.desc: He will no longer be rich; his wealth will not endure. His possessions will not overspread the land.

job_15_2_35.name: Eliphaz's second speech
job_15_2_35.desc: All that follows "Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied" to the chapter's end is one continuous speech

job_15_31_speech.name: Eliphaz: let not the deceived trust in vanity

job_15_32_speech.name: Eliphaz: his branch will not flourish

job_15_34_speech.desc: For the company of the godless will be barren, and fire will consume the tents of bribery.

job_15_35_speech.name: Eliphaz at Job 15:35
job_15_35_speech.desc: They conceive trouble and give birth to evil; their womb is pregnant with deceit.

job_16_13_speech.name: Job's words in Job 16:13
job_16_13_speech.desc: His archers surround me. He pierces my kidneys without mercy and spills my gall on the ground.

job_16_14_speech.name: Job's words in Job 16:14
job_16_14_speech.desc: He breaks me with wound upon wound; He rushes me like a mighty warrior.

job_16_15_17.name: Sackcloth and Pure Prayer
job_16_15_17.desc: Subject shifts to Job's own mourning and innocence: "I have sewn sackcloth over my skin"... "yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure"

job_16_15_speech.name: Job's words in Job 16:15
job_16_15_speech.desc: I have sewn sackcloth over my skin; I have buried my horn in the dust.

job_16_16_speech.name: Job's words in Job 16:16
job_16_16_speech.desc: My face is red with weeping, and deep shadows ring my eyes;

job_16_17_speech.name: Job's words in Job 16:17
job_16_17_speech.desc: Yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure.

job_16_18_22.name: My Witness Is in Heaven
job_16_18_22.desc: Vocative address turns to the earth and a new appeal: "O earth, do not cover my blood"; "my witness is in heaven"; "Oh, that a man might plead with God"

job_16_18_speech.name: Job's words in Job 16:18
job_16_18_speech.desc: O earth, do not cover my blood; may my cry for help never be laid to rest.

job_16_19_speech.name: Job's words in Job 16:19
job_16_19_speech.desc: Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high.

job_16_1_22.name: Job's Reply to Eliphaz
job_16_1_22.desc: Whole chapter is one speech framed by "Then Job answered and said" with no other speaker introduced

job_16_1_5.name: Miserable Comforters
job_16_1_5.desc: Speech opens with "Then Job answered" and addresses the friends in second person: "miserable comforters are you all"... "if you were in my place"

job_16_20_speech.name: Job's words in Job 16:20
job_16_20_speech.desc: My friends are my scoffers as my eyes pour out tears to God.

job_16_21_speech.name: Job's words in Job 16:21
job_16_21_speech.desc: Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his neighbor!!

job_16_22_speech.name: Job's words in Job 16:22
job_16_22_speech.desc: For when only a few years are past I will go the way of no return.

job_16_2_12_speech.name: Job's answer: miserable comforters are you all

job_16_6_14.name: God Has Torn Me Like an Enemy
job_16_6_14.desc: Turn from the friends to God's attack: "Surely He has now exhausted me; You have devastated all my family"; sustained "His anger has torn me... He breaks me with wound upon wound"

job_17_10_speech.name: I will not find a wise man among you
job_17_10_speech.desc: Job tells his friends to return, for he finds no wise man among them.

job_17_11_16.name: My hope goes down to the pit
job_17_11_16.desc: Returns to first-person lament with a fresh opening, "my plans are broken off," and runs to the close: "where is now my hope?" ... "Will we go down together into the dust."

job_17_11_speech.name: My days have passed; my plans are broken off
job_17_11_speech.desc: Job says his days are past and his purposes, the thoughts of his heart, are broken off.

job_17_12_speech.name: They have turned night into day
job_17_12_speech.desc: Job says they change night into day, and making light seem near in the face of darkness.

job_17_13_speech.name: Job at Job 17:13
job_17_13_speech.desc: Job's words: 'If I look for Sheol as my home, if I spread out my bed in darkness'

job_17_14_speech.name: Job at Job 17:14
job_17_14_speech.desc: Job's words: 'and say to corruption, ‘ You are my father,’ and to the worm, ‘ My mother,’ or ‘ My sister,’'

job_17_15_speech.name: Job at Job 17:15
job_17_15_speech.desc: Job's words: 'where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?'

job_17_16_speech.name: Job at Job 17:16
job_17_16_speech.desc: Job's words: 'Will it go down to the gates of Sheol? Will we go down together into the dust?'

job_17_1_2.name: My days are extinct, and mockers surround me
job_17_1_2.desc: Opens with self-description of ruin, "My spirit is broken; my days are extinguished; the grave awaits me" and the complaint of "mockers with me" — spoken about his state, not yet to God.

job_17_1_speech.name: My spirit is broken; my days are extinguished
job_17_1_speech.desc: Job's lament: his breath is corrupt, his days are extinguished; the grave awaits him.

job_17_2_speech.name: Surely mockers surround me
job_17_2_speech.desc: Job asks whether mockers are not with him and his eye continues in their provocation.

job_17_3_5.name: the pledge You demand
job_17_3_5.desc: The address turns to God in the second person: "Give me, I pray, the pledge You demand"; bound on by "You have closed their minds to understanding; therefore You will not exalt them"

job_17_3_speech.name: the pledge You demand
job_17_3_speech.desc: Job asks God to lay down a pledge and be his surety.

job_17_4_speech.name: You have closed their minds to understanding
job_17_4_speech.desc: Job says God has hidden their heart from understanding and will not exalt them.

job_17_5_speech.name: If a man denounces his friends for a price
job_17_5_speech.desc: Job says one who flatters his friends will see his children's eyes fail.

job_17_6_9.name: Made a byword, yet the righteous hold on
job_17_6_9.desc: Third person of God resumes — "He has made me a byword among the people" — and widens to what "Upright men" and "the righteous" shall do.

job_17_6_speech.name: He has made me a byword of the people
job_17_6_speech.desc: Job says God has made him a byword, 'a man in whose face they spit' (Job 17:6).

job_17_7_speech.name: My eyes have grown dim with grief
job_17_7_speech.desc: Job says his eye is dim from sorrow and all his members are as a shadow.

job_17_8_speech.name: The upright are appalled
job_17_8_speech.desc: Job says upright men will be astonished and the innocent will stir up against the hypocrite.

job_17_9_speech.name: The righteous shall hold on his way
job_17_9_speech.desc: Job says the righteous will hold on his way and clean hands shall grow stronger.

job_17_death_nearness.name: The grave named as his dwelling
job_17_death_nearness.desc: The same figure frames the chapter: "the graves are for me" (v.1) and "Sheol is my house: I have spread my couch in the darkness" (v.13).

job_18_10_speech.name: Bildad's speech (Job 18:10)
job_18_10_speech.desc: A noose is hidden in the ground, and a trap lies in his path.

job_18_11_speech.name: Bildad's speech (Job 18:11)
job_18_11_speech.desc: Terrors frighten him on every side and harass his every step.

job_18_12_21.name: Destruction, extinction of name and seed
job_18_12_21.desc: Subject shifts from traps to consuming death and erasure: "calamity is ready at his side", "the king of terrors", "The memory of him perishes from the earth", closing with the summary formula "Surely such is the dwelling of the wicked"

job_18_12_speech.name: Bildad's speech (Job 18:12)
job_18_12_speech.desc: His strength is depleted, and calamity is ready at his side.

job_18_13_speech.desc: Bildad's speech on the fate of the wicked.

job_18_14_speech.name: Bildad at Job 18:14
job_18_14_speech.desc: Bildad's speech on the fate of the wicked.

job_18_15_speech.desc: Bildad's speech on the fate of the wicked.

job_18_16_speech.desc: Bildad's speech on the fate of the wicked.

job_18_17_speech.desc: Bildad's speech on the fate of the wicked.

job_18_18_speech.desc: Bildad's speech on the fate of the wicked.

job_18_19_speech.desc: Bildad's speech on the fate of the wicked.

job_18_1_21.desc: One speech bounded by the opening formula "Then Bildad the Shuhite replied" and the closing summary "the place of one who does not know God"

job_18_1_4.name: Bildad's rebuke of Job's words
job_18_1_4.desc: Speaker formula opens: "Then Bildad the Shuhite replied"; addressed to Job in second person plural, "How long until you end these speeches?" and "should the earth be forsaken on your account?"

job_18_20_speech.name: Bildad at Job 18:20
job_18_20_speech.desc: Bildad's speech on the fate of the wicked.

job_18_21_speech.name: Bildad at Job 18:21
job_18_21_speech.desc: Bildad's speech on the fate of the wicked.

job_18_3_speech.name: Bildad's speech (Job 18:3)
job_18_3_speech.desc: Why are we regarded as cattle, as stupid in your sight??

job_18_4_speech.name: Bildad's speech (Job 18:4)
job_18_4_speech.desc: You who tear yourself in anger— should the earth be forsaken on your account, or the rocks be moved from their place??

job_18_5_11.name: The wicked man's light put out and snares laid
job_18_5_11.desc: Turn from second-person rebuke to third-person doctrine, marked by "Indeed, the lamp of the wicked is extinguished"; the unit runs on images of net, noose, snare and trap to "Terrors frighten him on every side"

items.label: is an instance of
items.name: The lamp of the wicked put out

job_18_5_speech.name: Bildad's speech (Job 18:5)
job_18_5_speech.desc: Indeed, the lamp of the wicked is extinguished; the flame of his fire does not glow.

job_18_6_speech.name: Bildad's speech (Job 18:6)
job_18_6_speech.desc: The light in his tent grows dark, and the lamp beside him goes out.

job_18_7_speech.name: Bildad's speech (Job 18:7)
job_18_7_speech.desc: His vigorous stride is shortened, and his own schemes trip him up.

job_18_8_speech.name: Bildad's speech (Job 18:8)
job_18_8_speech.desc: For his own feet lead him into a net, and he wanders into its mesh.

job_18_9_speech.name: Bildad's speech (Job 18:9)
job_18_9_speech.desc: A trap seizes his heel; a snare grips him.

job_18_bildad_speech.name: “How long until you end these speeches?

job_19_10_speech.name: Job at Job 19:10
job_19_10_speech.desc: Job says God has destroyed him completely, removed his hope like a tree.

job_19_11_speech.name: Job at Job 19:11
job_19_11_speech.desc: Job says God has kindled his wrath against him and counts him as an enemy.

job_19_12_speech.name: Job at Job 19:12
job_19_12_speech.desc: Job says God's troops come together and encamp around his dwelling.

job_19_13_20.name: Abandoned by Kin and Household
job_19_13_20.desc: subject changes to human estrangement: "He has removed my brothers from me", "My kinsmen have failed me", down to the body itself, "My skin and flesh cling to my bones"

job_19_1_29.name: Job's Answer to Bildad
job_19_1_29.desc: the whole chapter is one speech bounded by "Then Job answered and said" and closed by the warning "so that you may know there is a judgment"

items.label: contains
items.name: I Know That My Redeemer Lives

items.label: contains
items.name: Warning of Judgment on the Friends

job_19_1_6.name: Job Rebukes His Friends' Words
job_19_1_6.desc: "Then Job answered and said" opens the speech; "How long will you torment me" and "Ten times now you have reproached me" address the friends, closing with the turn "God who has wronged me and drawn His net around me"

job_19_21_22.name: Have pity on me
job_19_21_22.desc: the address turns back to the friends in direct appeal: "Have pity on me, my friends, have pity"; "Why do you persecute me as God does"

job_19_23_27.name: I Know That My Redeemer Lives
job_19_23_27.desc: new wish-formula "I wish that my words were recorded!" and the bound confession "But I know that my Redeemer lives", ending "How my heart yearns within me"

job_19_25_speech.name: Job at Job 19:25
job_19_25_speech.desc: Job's declaration that his redeemer lives and will stand on the earth at the latter day.

job_19_26_speech.name: Job at Job 19:26
job_19_26_speech.desc: Job's confidence that in his flesh he will see God though worms destroy his body.

job_19_27_speech.name: Job at Job 19:27
job_19_27_speech.desc: Job's assertion that he himself will see God, his eyes beholding, even as his heart yearns within him.

job_19_28_29.name: Warning of Judgment on the Friends
job_19_28_29.desc: "If you say" turns back to the friends with a threat, "then you should fear the sword yourselves, because wrath brings punishment by the sword"

job_19_28_speech.name: Job at Job 19:28
job_19_28_speech.desc: Job's words telling his friends what they should say: that they persecute him because the root of the matter lies in him.

job_19_29_speech.name: Job at Job 19:29
job_19_29_speech.desc: Job's warning to his friends to fear the sword because wrath brings its punishments and there is a judgment.

job_19_2_12_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 19:2-12
job_19_2_12_speech.desc: Job's answer to his friends in Job 19:2-12.

items.label: contains
items.name: If indeed you would exalt yourselves above me

items.label: contains
items.name: then understand that it is God who has wronged me

job_19_2_speech.name: Job at Job 19:2
job_19_2_speech.desc: Job asks how long his friends will afflict him and crush him with words.

job_19_3_speech.name: Job at Job 19:3
job_19_3_speech.desc: Job says his friends have reproached him ten times and are not ashamed to estrange themselves from him.

job_19_4_speech.name: Job at Job 19:4
job_19_4_speech.desc: Job allows that if he has erred, the error stays with him alone.

job_19_5_condition.name: If indeed you would exalt yourselves above me
job_19_5_condition.desc: The conditional clause: 'If indeed you would exalt yourselves above me and use my disgrace against me'

items.label: is the condition for
items.name: then understand that it is God who has wronged me

job_19_5_speech.name: Job at Job 19:5
job_19_5_speech.desc: Job says his friends exalt themselves over him and use his reproach against him.

job_19_6_apodosis.name: then understand that it is God who has wronged me
job_19_6_apodosis.desc: The conclusion: 'then understand that it is God who has wronged me and drawn His net around me'

items.label: is conditional on
items.name: If indeed you would exalt yourselves above me

job_19_6_speech.name: Job at Job 19:6
job_19_6_speech.desc: Job declares that God has overturned him and surrounded him with a net.

job_19_7_12.name: God Has Besieged Me
job_19_7_12.desc: "Though I cry out, Violence!" begins a chain of third-person accusations: "He has blocked my way", "He has stripped me", "He tears me down", ending with "His troops... encamp around my tent"

job_19_7_speech.name: Job at Job 19:7
job_19_7_speech.desc: Job cries out of injustice but is not heard; there is no judgement.

job_19_8_speech.name: Job at Job 19:8
job_19_8_speech.desc: Job says God has blocked his way and made his paths dark.

job_19_9_speech.name: Job at Job 19:9
job_19_9_speech.desc: Job says God has stripped him of his glory and taken the crown from his head.

job_1_13_19.name: The Four Messengers of Disaster
job_1_13_19.desc: Returns to earth with "One day, while Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house"; four reports each linked by "While he was still speaking, another messenger came" and closed by "I alone have escaped to tell you."

job_1_14_message.name: a messenger at Job 1:14
job_1_14_message.desc: While the oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing nearby:

job_1_14_messenger.name: a messenger
job_1_14_messenger.desc: The first messenger, who came to Job and said, 'the oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing nearby, and the Sabeans swooped down and took them away ... They put the servants to the sword' (Job 1:14-15).

job_1_15_message.name: a messenger at Job 1:15
job_1_15_message.desc: The Sabeans swooped down and took them away. They put the servants to the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you!.

job_1_16_message.name: a messenger at Job 1:16
job_1_16_message.desc: The fire of God fell from heaven. It burned and consumed the sheep and the servants, and I alone have escaped to tell you.

job_1_16_messenger.name: a messenger
job_1_16_messenger.desc: The second messenger, who said, 'The fire of God fell from heaven. It burned and consumed the sheep and the servants.'

job_1_17_message.name: a messenger at Job 1:17
job_1_17_message.desc: The Chaldeans formed three bands, raided the camels, and took them away. They put the servants to the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you.

job_1_17_messenger.name: a messenger
job_1_17_messenger.desc: The third messenger, who said, 'The Chaldeans formed three bands, raided the camels, and took them away.'

job_1_18_message.name: a messenger at Job 1:18
job_1_18_message.desc: Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house:

job_1_18_messenger.name: a messenger
job_1_18_messenger.desc: The fourth messenger, whose speech begins in Job 1:18 and continues in Job 1:19: 'Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine... when suddenly a mighty wind swept in from the desert and struck the four corners of the house.'

job_1_19_message.name: a messenger at Job 1:19
job_1_19_message.desc: When suddenly a mighty wind swept in from the desert and struck the four corners of the house. It collapsed on the young people and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you!.

job_1_1_5.name: Job's Character, Family and Wealth
job_1_1_5.desc: Opens the narrative frame: "There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job"; closes with the summary formula "Thus did Job continually."

items.label: is an instance of
items.name: Perfect and Upright, Feared God, Shunned Evil

job_1_20_22.name: Job Worships and Does Not Sin
job_1_20_22.desc: Speaker changes to Job with the mourning action "Then Job stood up, tore his robe"; ends with the narrator's verdict "In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing"

job_1_21_speech.name: Job at Job 1:21
job_1_21_speech.desc: Saying: Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD.

job_1_5_quote.name: Job at Job 1:5
job_1_5_quote.desc: Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts.

job_1_6_12.name: The LORD and Satan in the Heavenly Court
job_1_6_12.desc: Scene shifts to heaven with "One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD"; ends when the scene breaks off: "Then Satan went out from the presence of the Lord."

items.label: is an instance of
items.name: Perfect and Upright, Feared God, Shunned Evil

job_20_10_speech.name: Zophar's words in Job 20:10
job_20_10_speech.desc: Zophar says: "His sons will seek the favor of the poor, for his own hands must return his wealth"

job_20_11_speech.name: Zophar's words in Job 20:11
job_20_11_speech.desc: Zophar says: "The youthful vigor that fills his bones will lie down with him in the dust"

job_20_12_18.name: Sweet sin turned to poison in the belly
job_20_12_18.desc: New "Though evil is sweet in his mouth... yet in his stomach his food sours" pair; sustained swallowing/vomiting imagery ends with "He must return the fruit of his labor without consuming it"

items.label: is an instance of
items.name: Though he rises high, yet he perishes

job_20_12_speech.name: Zophar's words in Job 20:12
job_20_12_speech.desc: Zophar says: "Though evil is sweet in his mouth and he conceals it under his tongue"

job_20_13_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:13
job_20_13_speech.desc: Though he cannot bear to let it go and keeps it in his mouth

job_20_14_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:14
job_20_14_speech.desc: Yet in his stomach his food sours into the venom of cobras within him

job_20_15_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:15
job_20_15_speech.desc: He swallows wealth but vomits it out; God will force it from his stomach

job_20_16_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:16
job_20_16_speech.desc: He will suck the poison of cobras; the fangs of a viper will kill him

job_20_17_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:17
job_20_17_speech.desc: He will not enjoy the streams, the rivers flowing with honey and cream

job_20_18_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:18
job_20_18_speech.desc: He must return the fruit of his labor without consuming it; he cannot enjoy the profits of his trading

job_20_19_28.name: God's wrath hunts him down
job_20_19_28.desc: "For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor... Because his appetite is never satisfied" states the ground and sentence; shifts from digestion to God's assault, "God will vent His fury upon him", weapon, fire, heaven and earth as witnesses

job_20_19_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:19
job_20_19_speech.desc: For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor; he has seized houses he did not build

job_20_1_29.name: Zophar's second speech
job_20_1_29.desc: Bounded by the speaker formula in v.1 and the closing summary in v.29; one continuous discourse on the fate of the wicked

job_20_1_3.name: Zophar takes up his reply
job_20_1_3.desc: Speaker formula "Then Zophar the Naamathite replied" plus his stated motive, "So my anxious thoughts compel me to answer... I have heard a rebuke that insults me"

job_20_20_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:20
job_20_20_speech.desc: Because his appetite is never satisfied, he cannot escape with his treasure

job_20_21_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:21
job_20_21_speech.desc: Nothing is left for him to consume; thus his prosperity will not endure

job_20_22_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:22
job_20_22_speech.desc: In the midst of his plenty, he will be distressed; the full force of misery will come upon him

job_20_23_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:23
job_20_23_speech.desc: When he has filled his stomach, God will vent His fury upon him, raining it down on him as he eats

job_20_24_speech.name: Zophar's speech in Job 20:24
job_20_24_speech.desc: Though he flees from an iron weapon, a bronze-tipped arrow will pierce him

job_20_25_speech.name: Zophar at Job 20:25
job_20_25_speech.desc: It is drawn out of his back, the gleaming point from his liver. Terrors come over him.

job_20_26_speech.name: Zophar at Job 20:26
job_20_26_speech.desc: Total darkness is reserved for his treasures. A fire unfanned will consume him and devour what is left in his tent.

job_20_27_speech.name: Zophar at Job 20:27
job_20_27_speech.desc: The heavens will expose his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.

job_20_28_speech.name: Zophar at Job 20:28
job_20_28_speech.desc: The possessions of his house will be removed, flowing away on the day of God’s wrath.

job_20_29_29.name: This is the wicked man's portion
job_20_29_29.desc: Summing formula closes the speech: "This is the wicked man's portion from God"

job_20_29_speech.name: Zophar at Job 20:29
job_20_29_speech.desc: This is the wicked man’s portion from God, the inheritance God has appointed him.

job_20_2_speech.name: Zophar's words in Job 20:2
job_20_2_speech.desc: Zophar says: "So my anxious thoughts compel me to answer, because of the turmoil within me"

job_20_3_speech.name: Zophar's words in Job 20:3
job_20_3_speech.desc: Zophar says: "I have heard a rebuke that insults me, and my understanding prompts a reply"

job_20_4_11.name: The wicked man's triumph is brief
job_20_4_11.desc: Turns to Job with a question, "Do you not know that from antiquity", stating the thesis "the triumph of the wicked has been brief"; the "Though his excellency mount up... Yet he shall perish" pair runs to "lie down with him in the dust"

items.label: is an instance of
items.name: Though he rises high, yet he perishes

job_20_4_speech.name: Zophar's words in Job 20:4
job_20_4_speech.desc: Zophar says: "Do you not know that from antiquity, since man was placed on the earth"

job_20_5_speech.name: Zophar's words in Job 20:5
job_20_5_speech.desc: Zophar says: "the triumph of the wicked has been brief and the joy of the godless momentary?"

job_20_6_speech.name: Zophar's words in Job 20:6
job_20_6_speech.desc: Zophar says: "Though his arrogance reaches the heavens, and his head touches the clouds"

job_20_7_speech.name: Zophar's words in Job 20:7
job_20_7_speech.desc: Zophar says: "he will perish forever, like his own dung; those who had seen him will ask, ‘Where is he?’"

job_20_8_speech.name: Zophar's words in Job 20:8
job_20_8_speech.desc: Zophar says: "He will fly away like a dream, never to be found; he will be chased away like a vision in the night"

job_20_9_speech.name: Zophar's words in Job 20:9
job_20_9_speech.desc: Zophar says: "The eye that saw him will see him no more, and his place will no longer behold him"

job_20_though_yet.name: Though he rises high, yet he perishes
job_20_though_yet.desc: Twice the concession-reversal shape: "Though his arrogance reaches the heavens... he will perish forever" and "Though evil is sweet in his mouth... yet in his stomach his food sours"

items.label: occurs as
items.name: Sweet sin turned to poison in the belly

items.label: occurs as
items.name: The wicked man's triumph is brief

job_21_13_speech.name: They spend their days in prosperity
job_21_13_speech.desc: Job's words: 'They spend their days in prosperity and go down to Sheol in peace'

job_21_14_speech.name: Job at Job 21:14
job_21_14_speech.desc: Leave us alone! For we have no desire to know Your ways.

job_21_14_wicked_speech.name: Leave us alone!
job_21_14_wicked_speech.desc: The wicked say unto God: 'Leave us alone! For we have no desire to know Your ways.'

job_21_15_speech.name: Job at Job 21:15
job_21_15_speech.desc: Who is the Almighty, that we should serve Him, and what would we gain if we pray to Him??

job_21_15_wicked_speech.name: Who is the Almighty
job_21_15_wicked_speech.desc: The wicked ask: 'Who is the Almighty, that we should serve Him, and what would we gain if we pray to Him?’'

job_21_16_speech.name: Still, their prosperity is not in their own hands
job_21_16_speech.desc: Job's words: 'Still, their prosperity is not in their own hands, so I stay far from the counsel of the wicked'

job_21_17_26.name: How Often is the lamp Put Out?
job_21_17_26.desc: New rhetorical opening "How often is the lamp of the wicked put out!" mocking the doctrine of punishment, and ends with the levelling of both kinds of death: "But together they lie down in the dust."

job_21_17_speech.name: Job at Job 21:17
job_21_17_speech.desc: Job's words: 'How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out ... God distributes sorrows in his anger.'

job_21_18_speech.name: Are they like straw before the wind
job_21_18_speech.desc: Job's words: 'Are they like straw before the wind, like chaff swept away by a storm?'

job_21_19_speech.name: Job at Job 21:19
job_21_19_speech.desc: Job's words: 'It is said that God lays up one’s punishment for his children. Let God repay the man himself, so he will know it'

job_21_1_6.name: Job Demands a Hearing
job_21_1_6.desc: Speech opens with "Then Job answered:" and the imperatives to the friends: "Hear diligently my speech", "Bear with me while I speak", "Mark me, and be astonished"; subject is Job's own right to speak, not yet the wicked.

items.label: is an instance of
items.name: Turning on the Friends with Second-Person Imperative or Accusation

job_21_20_speech.name: Let his eyes see his own destruction
job_21_20_speech.desc: Job's words: 'Let his eyes see his own destruction; let him drink for himself the wrath of the Almighty'

job_21_21_speech.name: For what does he care about his household
job_21_21_speech.desc: Job's words: 'For what does he care about his household after him, when the number of his months has run out?'

job_21_22_speech.name: Can anyone teach knowledge to God,

job_24_15_speech.desc: The eye of the adulterer watches for twilight. Thinking, No eye will see me, he covers his face.

job_24_16_speech.name: Job's words in Job 24:16
job_24_16_speech.desc: In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves in, never to experience the light.

job_24_17_speech.desc: For to them, deep darkness is their morning; surely they are friends with the terrors of darkness!.

job_24_1_speech.name: Job's words in Job 24:1

job_24_21_speech.desc: They prey on the barren and childless, and show no kindness to the widow.

job_24_22_speech.desc: Yet by His power, God drags away the mighty; though rising up, they have no assurance of life.

job_24_23_speech.desc: He gives them a sense of security, but His eyes are on their ways.

job_24_24_speech.name: Job's words in Job 24:24
job_24_24_speech.desc: They are exalted for a moment, then they are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they are cut off like heads of grain.

job_24_3_speech.desc: They drive away the donkey of the fatherless and take the widow’s ox in pledge.

job_24_4_speech.desc: They push the needy off the road and force all the poor of the land into hiding.

job_24_5_speech.name: Job's words in Job 24:5
job_24_5_speech.desc: Indeed, like wild donkeys in the desert, the poor go to work foraging for food; the wasteland is food for their children.

job_24_6_speech.name: Job's words in Job 24:6
job_24_6_speech.desc: They gather fodder in the fields and glean the vineyards of the wicked.

job_24_7_speech.name: Job's words in Job 24:7
job_24_7_speech.desc: Without clothing, they spend the night naked; they have no covering against the cold.

job_24_8_speech.name: Job's words in Job 24:8
job_24_8_speech.desc: Drenched by mountain rains, they huddle against the rocks for want of shelter.

job_24_9_speech.name: Job's words in Job 24:9
job_24_9_speech.desc: The fatherless infant is snatched from the breast; the nursing child of the poor is seized for a debt.

job_32_10_speech.name: Elihu at Job 32:10
job_32_10_speech.desc: Elihu asks the friends to hear his opinion.

job_32_11_14.name: None of You Answered Job
job_32_11_14.desc: Turn to what he observed of them: "Indeed, I waited while you spoke" ... "no one proved Job wrong", ending "I will not answer him with your arguments"; v.15 reverts to third person "They were amazed".

job_32_11_speech.name: Elihu at Job 32:11
job_32_11_speech.desc: Elihu on waiting for their words and hearing their reasons.

job_32_12_speech.name: Elihu at Job 32:12
job_32_12_speech.desc: Elihu on their failure to answer Job.

job_32_15_22.name: I Am Full of Matter and Must Speak
job_32_15_22.desc: Subject changes to his own compulsion after the friends' silence: "words have escaped them" ... "For I am full of words, and my spirit within me compels me", closing with the oath-like "or my Maker would remove me in an instant."

job_32_1_5.name: Elihu's Anger Kindled (narrator)
job_32_1_5.desc: Prose narration in the third person: "So these three men stopped answering Job"; "This kindled the anger of Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite" -- ends with the repeated "his anger was kindled" (v.5) before the speech formula in v.6.

job_32_6_10.name: Youth May Speak: Wisdom Is Not From Age
job_32_6_10.desc: Speech formula opens: "Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite declared: I am young in years, while you are old"; the argument closes with the connective conclusion "Therefore I say, ‘ Listen to me; I too will declare what I know.’"

job_32_6_22.name: Elihu's Preface
job_32_6_22.desc: One continuous speech introduced by "And Elihu ... answered and said" and unified by the thrice-repeated intention "I too will declare what I know".

job_33_19_speech.desc: Elihu's words: "A man is also chastened on his bed with pain and constant distress in his bones"

job_34_26_speech.desc: He strikes them for their wickedness in full view;

job_39_6_speech.name: God at Job 39:6
job_39_6_speech.desc: I made the wilderness his home and the salt flats his dwelling.

job_40_1_2.desc: "The LORD said to Job" opens a fresh speech formula; "Will the faultfinder contend with the Almighty?"

job_40_2_speech.desc: God's words in Job 40:2: 'Will the faultfinder contend with the Almighty? Let him who argues with God give an answer'

job_40_3_5.desc: Speaker changes: "Then Job answered the LORD"; Job speaks to God, "How can I reply to You?"

job_40_4_5_speech.desc: Job's words in Job 40:4-5: 'Behold, I am insignificant. How can I reply to You? I place my hand over my mouth. I have spoken once, but I have no answer — twice, but I have nothing to add'
