job_40_7_12_speech.name: God at Job 40:7
job_40_7_12_speech.desc: God's words in Job 40:7-12: 'Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me. Would you really annul My justice? Would you condemn Me to justify yourself? Do you have an arm like God’s? Can you thunder with a voice like His? Then adorn yourself with majesty and splendor, and clothe yourself with honor and glory. Unleash the fury of your wrath; look on every proud man and bring him low. Look on every proud man and humble him; trample the wicked where they stand'

job_41_10_speech.name: God at Job 41:10
job_41_10_speech.desc: God's rhetorical question about standing before him.

job_41_11_speech.name: God at Job 41:11
job_41_11_speech.desc: God's declaration of ownership over all under heaven.

job_41_12_24.name: The Parts and Armour of Leviathan
job_41_12_24.desc: Announced by "I cannot keep silent about his limbs, his power and graceful form" then an anatomy in third person: face, teeth, scales, eyes, mouth, neck, flesh, heart.

job_41_12_speech.name: God at Job 41:12
job_41_12_speech.desc: God's promise to declare leviathan's parts.

job_41_13_speech.name: God at Job 41:13
job_41_13_speech.desc: The LORD's rhetorical question about Leviathan's garment and double bridle.

job_41_14_speech.name: God at Job 41:14
job_41_14_speech.desc: The LORD asks who can open Leviathan's jaws and describes his teeth as terrible.

job_41_15_speech.name: God at Job 41:15
job_41_15_speech.desc: The LORD describes Leviathan's scales as his pride, tightly sealed.

job_41_16_speech.name: God at Job 41:16
job_41_16_speech.desc: The LORD describes the closeness of Leviathan's scales.

job_41_17_speech.name: God at Job 41:17
job_41_17_speech.desc: The LORD describes how Leviathan's scales are inseparably joined.

job_41_18_speech.name: God at Job 41:18
job_41_18_speech.desc: The LORD describes Leviathan's sneezings producing light and eyes like the morning eyelids.

job_41_19_speech.name: God at Job 41:19
job_41_19_speech.desc: The LORD describes fire and sparks coming from Leviathan's mouth.

job_41_1_8.name: Can You Catch Leviathan?
job_41_1_8.desc: A chain of second-person taunts opening "Can you pull in Leviathan with a hook?" and closing with the imperative "If you lay a hand on him, you will remember the battle and never repeat it!"

job_41_1_speech.name: God at Job 41:1
job_41_1_speech.desc: God's question to Job about drawing out leviathan.

job_41_20_speech.name: God at Job 41:20
job_41_20_speech.desc: The LORD describes smoke from Leviathan's nostrils like a boiling pot.

job_41_21_speech.name: God at Job 41:21
job_41_21_speech.desc: The LORD describes Leviathan's breath kindling coals and a flame from his mouth.

job_41_22_speech.name: God at Job 41:22
job_41_22_speech.desc: The LORD describes strength in Leviathan's neck and the transformation of sorrow to joy.

job_41_23_speech.name: God at Job 41:23
job_41_23_speech.desc: The LORD describes the firm and immovable flakes of Leviathan's flesh.

job_41_24_speech.name: God at Job 41:24
job_41_24_speech.desc: The LORD describes Leviathan's heart as firm as a stone and hard as a lower millstone.

job_41_25_32.name: No Weapon Can Touch Him
job_41_25_32.desc: Shifts from anatomy to battle: "When Leviathan rises up, the mighty are terrified"; "The sword that reaches him has no effect"; "he laughs at the sound of the lance."

job_41_25_speech.name: Job 41:25
job_41_25_speech.desc: When Leviathan rises up, the mighty are terrified; they withdraw before his thrashing.

job_41_26_speech.name: Job 41:26
job_41_26_speech.desc: The sword that reaches him has no effect, nor does the spear or dart or arrow.

job_41_27_speech.name: Job 41:27
job_41_27_speech.desc: He regards iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood.

job_41_28_speech.name: Job 41:28
job_41_28_speech.desc: No arrow can make him flee; slingstones become like chaff to him.

job_41_29_speech.name: Job 41:29
job_41_29_speech.desc: A club is regarded as straw, and he laughs at the sound of the lance.

job_41_2_speech.name: God at Job 41:2
job_41_2_speech.desc: God's question about hooking leviathan's nose and jaw.

job_41_30_speech.name: Job 41:30
job_41_30_speech.desc: His undersides are jagged potsherds, spreading out the mud like a threshing sledge.

job_41_31_speech.name: Job 41:31
job_41_31_speech.desc: He makes the depths seethe like a cauldron; he makes the sea like a jar of ointment.

job_41_32_speech.name: Job 41:32
job_41_32_speech.desc: He leaves a glistening wake behind him; one would think the deep had white hair!.

job_41_33_34.name: king over all the proud
job_41_33_34.desc: Summary verdict: "Nothing on earth is his equal" ... "he is king over all the proud" closes the poem.

job_41_33_speech.name: Job 41:33
job_41_33_speech.desc: Nothing on earth is his equal— a creature devoid of fear!.

job_41_34_speech.name: Job 41:34
job_41_34_speech.desc: He looks down on all the haughty; he is king over all the proud.

job_41_3_speech.name: God at Job 41:3
job_41_3_speech.desc: God's question about whether leviathan will plead.

job_41_4_speech.name: God at Job 41:4
job_41_4_speech.desc: God's question about covenant and servanthood.

job_41_5_speech.name: God at Job 41:5
job_41_5_speech.desc: God's question about playing with leviathan.

job_41_6_speech.name: God at Job 41:6
job_41_6_speech.desc: God's question about feasting and trading leviathan.

job_41_7_speech.name: God at Job 41:7
job_41_7_speech.desc: God's question about piercing leviathan's hide.

job_41_8_speech.name: God at Job 41:8
job_41_8_speech.desc: God's command to remember the battle.

job_41_9_11.name: None Can Stand Before Me
job_41_9_11.desc: "Behold" opens a turn from Job's inability to God's own claim: "Then who is able to stand against Me?" and "Everything under heaven is Mine" — the first person replaces the beast as subject.

job_41_9_speech.name: God at Job 41:9
job_41_9_speech.desc: God's statement about the vain hope of capturing leviathan.

job_42_10_17.desc: New subject, blessing rather than rebuke: "the LORD restored his prosperity"... "So the LORD blessed Job’s latter days more than his first", ending with the death formula "And so Job died, old and full of years"

job_42_1_6.desc: Speech formula opens: "Then Job replied to the LORD"; second person throughout ("I know that You can do all things") and closes with "Therefore I retract my words, and I repent in dust and ashes."

job_42_2_6_speech.name: Job's final answer to the LORD
job_42_2_6_speech.desc: Job's reply to the LORD: 'I know that You can do all things... Therefore I retract my words, and I repent in dust and ashes.'

job_42_7_8_lord_speech.name: God at Job 42:7
job_42_7_8_lord_speech.desc: The LORD's rebuke and command: 'My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends... take seven bulls and seven rams...'

job_42_7_9.desc: Narrative resumes and the speaker changes: "After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite"; closes when the command is carried out, "did as the LORD had told them."

job_4_10_speech.desc: Eliphaz describes the breaking of the lion's might.

job_4_11_speech.name: Eliphaz at Job 4:11
job_4_11_speech.desc: Eliphaz notes the perishing and scattering of the lion and its cubs.

job_4_12_speech.desc: Eliphaz mentions a secret thing brought to him.

job_4_13_16_speech.desc: Eliphaz's narrative of his night vision, beginning 'In disquieting visions in the night'.

job_4_17_21_voice_speech.name: a spirit at Job 4:16
job_4_17_21_voice_speech.desc: Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker? If God puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with error, how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundations are in the dust, who can be crushed like a moth! They are smashed to pieces from dawn to dusk; unnoticed, they perish forever. Are not their tent cords pulled up, so that they die without wisdom?.

job_4_4_speech.desc: Eliphaz continues about Job's supportive words.

job_4_9_speech.desc: Eliphaz says the wicked are destroyed by God's blast and breath.

job_5_11_speech.name: The low exalted to safety

job_5_12_speech.name: God disappoints the crafty
job_5_12_speech.desc: He thwarts the schemes of the crafty, so that their hands find no success.

job_5_13_speech.desc: He catches the wise in their craftiness, and sweeps away the plans of the cunning.

job_5_16_speech.name: the poor have hope

job_5_17_speech.name: Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects
job_5_17_speech.desc: Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects; so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty:

job_5_18_speech.name: He wounds, but He also binds
job_5_18_speech.desc: For He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal.

job_5_19_speech.name: He will rescue you from six calamities
job_5_19_speech.desc: He will rescue you from six calamities; no harm will touch you in seven.

job_5_1_speech.desc: Call out if you please, but who will answer? To which of the holy ones will you turn??

job_5_20_speech.desc: In famine He will redeem you from death, and in battle from the stroke of the sword.

job_5_21_speech.desc: You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and will not fear havoc when it comes.

job_5_22_speech.name: You will laugh at destruction and famine
job_5_22_speech.desc: You will laugh at destruction and famine, and need not fear the beasts of the earth.

job_5_23_speech.name: a covenant with the stones of the field
job_5_23_speech.desc: For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field, and the wild animals will be at peace with you.

job_5_24_speech.name: your tent is secure
job_5_24_speech.desc: You will know that your tent is secure, and find nothing amiss when inspecting your home.

job_5_25_speech.name: Eliphaz promises Job great seed and offspring
job_5_25_speech.desc: You will know that your offspring will be many, your descendants like the grass of the earth.

job_5_26_speech.name: Eliphaz promises Job a full age in the grave
job_5_26_speech.desc: You will come to the grave in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season.

job_5_27_27.name: Closing appeal: we have searched it out
job_5_27_27.desc: A closing formula in the first person plural breaks the run of promises: "Indeed, we have investigated, and it is true! So hear it and know for yourself"

job_5_27_speech.name: Eliphaz at Job 5:27
job_5_27_speech.desc: Indeed, we have investigated, and it is true! So hear it and know for yourself.

job_5_2_speech.name: Wrath kills the foolish man
job_5_2_speech.desc: For resentment kills a fool, and envy slays the simple.

job_5_3_speech.name: a fool taking root
job_5_3_speech.desc: I have seen a fool taking root, but suddenly his house was cursed.

job_5_4_speech.name: Children far from safety
job_5_4_speech.desc: His sons are far from safety, crushed in court without a defender.

job_5_5_speech.name: The hungry eat his harvest
job_5_5_speech.desc: The hungry consume his harvest, taking it even from the thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.

job_5_6_speech.name: Affliction comes not from dust
job_5_6_speech.desc: For distress does not spring from the dust, and trouble does not sprout from the ground;

job_5_7_speech.name: Man is born to trouble
job_5_7_speech.desc: Yet man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward.

job_5_8_16.name: Eliphaz would commit his cause to God
job_5_8_16.desc: Turn to first person resolve, "However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him —", then a chain of participial praise "who does great things", "He gives rain", ending in the summary "So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth"

job_5_8_speech.name: I would appeal to God
job_5_8_speech.desc: However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him —:

job_5_9_speech.name: God does great things
job_5_9_speech.desc: The One who does great and unsearchable things, wonders without number:

job_6_10_speech.name: It still brings me comfort
job_6_10_speech.desc: It still brings me comfort, and joy through unrelenting pain, that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.

job_6_11_speech.name: What strength do I have, that I should still hope?
job_6_11_speech.desc: What strength do I have, that I should still hope? What is my future, that I should be patient??

job_6_12_speech.name: Is my strength like that of stone
job_6_12_speech.desc: Is my strength like that of stone, or my flesh made of bronze??

job_6_13_speech.name: Job at Job 6:13
job_6_13_speech.desc: Job's rhetorical question: 'Is there any help within me now that success is driven from me?' (Job 6:13).

job_6_14_21.name: Friends like a vanishing brook
job_6_14_21.desc: Subject turns entirely to the friends: "A despairing man should have the kindness of his friend"; the brook simile is developed to "For now you are of no help; you see terror, and you are afraid"

job_6_14_speech.name: Job at Job 6:14
job_6_14_speech.desc: Job's statement about pity to the afflicted and forsaking the fear of the Almighty (Job 6:14).

job_6_15_speech.name: Job at Job 6:15
job_6_15_speech.desc: Job's complaint that his brothers are as faithless as wadis, as seasonal streams (Job 6:15).

job_6_16_speech.name: Job at Job 6:16
job_6_16_speech.desc: Job's description of the brooks: 'darkened because of the ice and the inflow of melting snow,' (Job 6:16).

job_6_17_speech.name: Job at Job 6:17
job_6_17_speech.desc: Job's words on the brooks vanishing: 'but ceasing in the dry season and vanishing from their channels in the heat.' (Job 6:17).

job_6_18_speech.name: Job at Job 6:18
job_6_18_speech.desc: Job's observation: 'Caravans turn aside from their routes; they go into the wasteland and perish.' (Job 6:18).

job_6_19_speech.name: Job at Job 6:19
job_6_19_speech.desc: Job's words about the troops of Tema and companies of Sheba (Job 6:19).

job_6_1_30.name: Job's reply to Eliphaz
job_6_1_30.desc: One speech framed by "Then Job replied:" and running to the chapter's end without a new speaker.

job_6_1_7.name: My grief outweighs the sand
job_6_1_7.desc: Speech formula opens: "Then Job replied:"; the unit is bound by "For then it would outweigh the sand of the seas" and "For the arrows of the Almighty have pierced me", closing with the food images of tasteless meat (v.6-7).

job_6_20_speech.name: Job at Job 6:20
job_6_20_speech.desc: Job's account of disappointment: 'They are confounded because they had hoped; their arrival brings disappointment.' (Job 6:20).

job_6_21_speech.name: Job at Job 6:21
job_6_21_speech.desc: Job's reproach: 'For now you are of no help; you see terror, and you are afraid.' (Job 6:21).

job_6_22_30.name: What have I asked of you? Teach me
job_6_22_30.desc: Direct challenge in questions to the friends: "Have I ever said, Give me something?"; "Teach me, and I will be silent"; closes with the appeal "But now, please look at me" and "Is there iniquity on my tongue?"

job_6_22_speech.name: Job at Job 6:22
job_6_22_speech.desc: Job's rhetorical question: 'Have I ever said, Give me something; offer me a bribe from your wealth;' (Job 6:22).

job_6_23_speech.name: Job at Job 6:23
job_6_23_speech.desc: Job's rhetorical question: 'deliver me from the hand of the enemy; redeem me from the grasp of the ruthless’?' (Job 6:23).

job_6_24_speech.name: Job at Job 6:24
job_6_24_speech.desc: Job's plea: 'Teach me, and I will be silent. Help me understand how I have erred.' (Job 6:24).

job_6_2_speech.name: If only my grief could be weighed
job_6_2_speech.desc: If only my grief could be weighed and placed with my calamity on the scales!

job_6_3_speech.name: it would outweigh the sand of the seas
job_6_3_speech.desc: For then it would outweigh the sand of the seas — no wonder my words have been rash.

job_6_4_speech.name: the arrows of the Almighty have pierced me
job_6_4_speech.desc: For the arrows of the Almighty have pierced me; my spirit drinks in their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me.

job_6_5_speech.name: Does a wild donkey bray over fresh grass,
job_6_5_speech.desc: Does a wild donkey bray over fresh grass, or an ox low over its fodder??

job_6_6_speech.name: Job at Job 6:6
job_6_6_speech.desc: Is tasteless food eaten without salt, or is there flavor in the white of an egg??

job_6_7_speech.name: Job at Job 6:7
job_6_7_speech.desc: My soul refuses to touch them; they are loathsome food to me.

job_6_8_13.name: Wish for death, and no strength left
job_6_8_13.desc: New optative opening: "If only my request were granted and God would fulfill my hope"; runs through the questions "What strength do I have, that I should still hope?" to "success is driven from me?"

job_6_8_speech.desc: If only my request were granted and God would fulfill my hope!

job_6_9_speech.name: God would be willing to crush me
job_6_9_speech.desc: That God would be willing to crush me, to unleash His hand and cut me off!!

job_7_11_16.name: I will not restrain my mouth
job_7_11_16.desc: "Therefore I will not restrain my mouth" binds the resolve to what precedes but announces a new act of complaint, developed as accusation — "You must keep me under guard", "You frighten me with dreams" — and closed with "Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath."

job_7_14_speech.desc: Job's complaint that God scares and terrifies him.

job_7_16_speech.name: Job at Job 7:16
job_7_16_speech.desc: Job says he loathes life, asks to be let alone, and calls his days vanity.

job_7_17_21.name: What Is Man, That You Should Try Him
job_7_17_21.desc: A fresh question reframes the whole case: "What is man that You should exalt him?", followed by "Will You never look away from me" and the closing plea "Why do You not pardon my transgression... but I shall not be."

job_7_17_speech.name: Job at Job 7:17
job_7_17_speech.desc: Job questions why God magnifies man and sets his heart upon him.

job_7_18_speech.name: Job at Job 7:18
job_7_18_speech.desc: Job continues questioning why God visits and tries man every moment.

job_7_19_speech.name: Job at Job 7:19
job_7_19_speech.desc: Job asks how long God will not depart from him.

job_7_1_6.name: Life as a Hired Labourer's Drudgery
job_7_1_6.desc: Opens with a general question about mankind, "Is not man consigned to labor on earth?", and the simile "like a hireling he waits for his wages" is applied to Job in the third person before any address to God; God is not spoken to at all here.

job_7_20_speech.desc: Job confesses sin, addresses God as watcher of mankind, and complains of being a mark and burden.

job_7_21_speech.name: Job at Job 7:21
job_7_21_speech.desc: Job asks why God does not pardon and take away his sin, and says he will sleep in the dust.

job_7_4_quote.name: ‘When will I get up?' But the night drags on,

job_7_7_10.name: Remember that my life is but a breath
job_7_7_10.desc: The address turns: "Remember that my life is but a breath" and "You will look for me, but I will be no more" — the first second-person words in the chapter; the unit closes on the finality of the grave, "He never returns to his house."

job_7_pattern_days_are_vanity.name: My Days Are Vanity and Fleeting
job_7_pattern_days_are_vanity.desc: "months of emptiness" and "My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle" recur as "Leave me alone, for my days are a breath."

job_8_10_speech.name: Will they not teach you
job_8_10_speech.desc: 'Will they not teach you and tell you, and speak from their understanding?' (Job 8:10)

job_8_11_19.name: The rush and the withering plant: the hypocrite's hope
job_8_11_19.desc: Shifts to third-person parable questions, "Does papyrus grow where there is no marsh?" applied by "Such is the destiny of all who forget God," ending "yet others will spring from the dust"

job_8_11_speech.name: Does papyrus grow where there is no marsh
job_8_11_speech.desc: 'Does papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Do reeds flourish without water?' (Job 8:11)

job_8_12_speech.name: While the shoots are still
job_8_12_speech.desc: 'While the shoots are still uncut, they dry up more quickly than grass.' (Job 8:12)

job_8_13_speech.name: Bildad at Job 8:13
job_8_13_speech.desc: Such is the destiny of all who forget God; so the hope of the godless will perish: (Job 8:13).

job_8_14_speech.name: Bildad at Job 8:14
job_8_14_speech.desc: His confidence is fragile; his security is in a spider’s web. (Job 8:14)

job_8_15_speech.name: Bildad at Job 8:15
job_8_15_speech.desc: He leans on his web, but it gives way; he holds fast, but it does not endure. (Job 8:15)

job_8_16_speech.name: Bildad at Job 8:16
job_8_16_speech.desc: He is a well-watered plant in the sunshine, spreading its shoots over the garden. (Job 8:16)

job_8_17_speech.name: Bildad at Job 8:17
job_8_17_speech.desc: His roots wrap around the rock heap; he looks for a home among the stones. (Job 8:17)

job_8_18_denial.name: Bildad at Job 8:18
job_8_18_denial.desc: it will disown him, saying, I never saw you. (Job 8:18).

job_8_18_destruction.name: he is uprooted from his place
job_8_18_destruction.desc: If he is uprooted from his place (Job 8:18).

job_8_18_speech.name: Bildad at Job 8:18
job_8_18_speech.desc: If he is uprooted from his place, it will disown him, saying, I never saw you. (Job 8:18)

job_8_19_speech.name: Bildad at Job 8:19
job_8_19_speech.desc: Surely this is the joy of his way; yet others will spring from the dust. (Job 8:19)

job_8_1_22.name: Bildad's first speech
job_8_1_22.desc: Framed as a single speech by "Then Bildad the Shuhite replied" at verse 1, with no further speaker change to the chapter's end

job_8_1_7.name: Bildad's rebuke: God does not pervert justice
job_8_1_7.desc: New speaker formula, "Then Bildad the Shuhite replied" then rebuke "How long will you go on saying such things?" and the rhetorical question "Does God pervert justice?" with conditional promise "But if you would earnestly seek God and ask the Almighty for mercy"

job_8_20_22.name: God will not cast away the perfect man
job_8_20_22.desc: "Behold, God does not reject the blameless" resumes direct address to Job, "He will yet fill your mouth with laughter," closing on "the tent of the wicked will be no more"

job_8_20_speech.name: Bildad at Job 8:20
job_8_20_speech.desc: Behold, God does not reject the blameless, nor will He strengthen the hand of evildoers: (Job 8:20)

job_8_21_speech.name: Bildad at Job 8:21
job_8_21_speech.desc: He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with a shout of joy. (Job 8:21)

job_8_22_speech.name: Bildad at Job 8:22
job_8_22_speech.desc: Your enemies will be clothed in shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more. (Job 8:22)

job_8_2_speech.name: “How long will you go on saying such things?
job_8_2_speech.desc: 'How long will you go on saying such things? The words of your mouth are a blustering wind.' (Job 8:2)

job_8_3_speech.name: Does God pervert justice?
job_8_3_speech.desc: 'Does God pervert justice? Does the Almighty pervert what is right?' (Job 8:3)

job_8_4_speech.name: When your children sinned against Him
job_8_4_speech.desc: 'When your children sinned against Him, He gave them over to their rebellion.' (Job 8:4)

job_8_5_speech.name: But if you would earnestly seek God
job_8_5_speech.desc: 'But if you would earnestly seek God and ask the Almighty for mercy,' (Job 8:5)

job_8_6_speech.name: if you are pure and upright
job_8_6_speech.desc: 'if you are pure and upright, even now He will rouse Himself on your behalf and restore your righteous estate.' (Job 8:6)

job_8_7_speech.name: Though your beginnings were modest
job_8_7_speech.desc: 'Though your beginnings were modest, your latter days will flourish.' (Job 8:7)

job_8_8_10.name: Ask the former generations
job_8_8_10.desc: Turn to a new appeal: "Please inquire of past generations," with parenthetic "(For we were born yesterday...)" and closing "Will they not teach you and tell you"

job_8_8_speech.name: For enquire of the former age
job_8_8_speech.desc: 'Please inquire of past generations and consider the discoveries of their fathers.' (Job 8:8)

job_8_9_speech.name: we were born yesterday
job_8_9_speech.desc: 'For we were born yesterday and know nothing; our days on earth are but a shadow.' (Job 8:9)

job_9_10_speech.name: Job at Job 9:10
job_9_10_speech.desc: He does great things beyond searching out, and wonders without number.

job_9_11_speech.name: Job at Job 9:11
job_9_11_speech.desc: Were He to pass by me, I would not see Him; were He to move, I would not recognize Him.

job_9_12_speech.name: Job at Job 9:12
job_9_12_speech.desc: If He takes away, who can stop Him? Who dares to ask Him, What are You doing??

job_9_13_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:13
job_9_13_speech.desc: God does not restrain His anger; the helpers of Rahab cower beneath Him.

job_9_14_21.name: I would not dare answer him
job_9_14_21.desc: Turns from God's power to Job himself with "How then can I answer Him", and stays on the first person: "Even if I were righteous, my mouth would condemn me"

job_9_14_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:14
job_9_14_speech.desc: How then can I answer Him or choose my arguments against Him??

job_9_15_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:15
job_9_15_speech.desc: For even if I were right, I could not answer. I could only beg my Judge for mercy.

job_9_16_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:16
job_9_16_speech.desc: If I summoned Him and He answered me, I do not believe He would listen to my voice.

job_9_17_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:17
job_9_17_speech.desc: For He would crush me with a tempest and multiply my wounds without cause.

job_9_18_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:18
job_9_18_speech.desc: He does not let me catch my breath, but overwhelms me with bitterness.

job_9_19_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:19
job_9_19_speech.desc: If it is a matter of strength, He is indeed mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon Him??

job_9_1_13.name: No man can win a case against God
job_9_1_13.desc: Opens with the speech formula "Then Job answered and said" and the question "how can a mortal be righteous before God?"; a hymn of participles follows, "He moves mountains ... He shakes the earth", speaking of God in the third person

job_9_20_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:20
job_9_20_speech.desc: Even if I were righteous, my mouth would condemn me; if I were blameless, it would declare me guilty.

job_9_21_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:21
job_9_21_speech.desc: Though I am blameless, I have no concern for myself; I despise my own life.

job_9_22_24.name: He destroys the perfect and the wicked alike
job_9_22_24.desc: Marked as a summing-up: "It is all the same, and so I say, ‘ He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.’", a new charge about God's dealing with all men

job_9_22_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:22
job_9_22_speech.desc: It is all the same, and so I say, He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.

job_9_23_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:23
job_9_23_speech.desc: When the scourge brings sudden death, He mocks the despair of the innocent.

job_9_24_speech.name: Job's speech in Job 9:24
job_9_24_speech.desc: The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; He blindfolds its judges. If it is not He, then who is it??

job_9_25_31.name: My days flee and I cannot comfort myself
job_9_25_31.desc: New subject introduced by "My days are swifter than a runner"; the address then turns to God directly, "I know that You will not acquit me", "then You would plunge me into the pit"

job_9_2_speech.name: Job at Job 9:2
job_9_2_speech.desc: Yes, I know that it is so, but how can a mortal be righteous before God??

job_9_32_35.name: There is no umpire between us
job_9_32_35.desc: Bound to what precedes by "For He is not a man like me", and closes the speech with the wish "Let Him remove His rod from me... but I am not so in myself"

job_9_3_answer_claim.desc: If one wished to contend with God, he could not answer Him one time out of a thousand.

job_9_4_speech.name: Job at Job 9:4
job_9_4_speech.desc: God is wise in heart and mighty in strength. Who has resisted Him and prospered??

job_9_5_speech.name: Job at Job 9:5
job_9_5_speech.desc: He moves mountains without their knowledge and overturns them in His anger.

job_9_6_speech.name: Job at Job 9:6
job_9_6_speech.desc: He shakes the earth from its place, so that its foundations tremble.

job_9_7_speech.name: Job at Job 9:7

job_9_8_speech.name: Job at Job 9:8

job_9_9_speech.name: Job at Job 9:9

'man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment' (Heb 9:27).

justified_by_faith.name: justified by faith
justified_by_faith.desc:
A verdict the New Testament pronounces on Abraham, in Paul's letters. 'Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.' (Rom 4:3), against works explicitly: 'If Abraham was indeed justified by works, he had something to boast about, but not before God.' (Rom 4:2). Galatians 3:6 says it again in the same words.

Paired with [[justified_by_works]], the letter of James on the same man and the same deed. James gives his own frame for how the two go together: 'I will show you my faith by my deeds' (Jas 2:18), and of Abraham, 'his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did' (2:22). Both letters are there, each in its own words.

Hebrews 11 is a third voice, and it does not say quite the same thing as Paul. Paul argues that Abraham was justified by faith; Hebrews says he acted by faith — 'By faith Abraham, when called ... obeyed' (11:8), 'By faith he dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country' (11:9). The claims are close and they are not identical, and flattening one into the other would lose the difference.

What makes it belong here anyway is 11:17. Hebrews attributes to faith the same deed James names: 'By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac on the altar', and 'justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar' (Jas 2:21). One act at Moriah, which all three letters cite.

justified_by_works.name: justified by what he did
justified_by_works.desc:
A verdict the letter of James pronounces on Abraham, in as many words: 'Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar?' (Jas 2:21), generalised at 2:24 — 'a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone'.

Paired with [[justified_by_faith]]. The letter names its author only as James (Jas 1:1), and which James is a reading the text does not settle.

The deed it rests on is the one Hebrews 11:17 gives as an act of faith, and James joins the two in his own words: 'You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did' (Jas 2:22). All three writers cite the same act at Moriah.

korah_son_of_izhar.desc:
'Now Korah son of Izhar, the son of Kohath son of Levi ... They came together against Moses and Aaron' (Num 16:1-3).

**A Levite objecting that the whole congregation is holy** -- 'You have taken too much upon yourselves! For everyone in the entire congregation is holy' (16:3) -- which is an argument from a premise the book elsewhere grants.

Numbers 26:11 adds, without comment, that the children of Korah did not die. Eleven psalms carry their name in the title.

Four requests in two verses and every one of them asks to be acted upon: show, teach, lead, teach again. Nothing is asked for that could be got alone.

led_by_the_spirit.name: led by the Spirit
led_by_the_spirit.desc:
'For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.' (Rom 8:14), and the next verse names what that is not: 'For you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry, Abba! Father!' (8:15).

Romans 8 works by opposition throughout — flesh against Spirit at verses 1, 4, 5, 9 and 13, death against life, bondage against adoption. Five 'not X but Y' constructions in thirteen verses.

It also gives the Spirit something no other passage does: 'the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words' (8:26). An action attributed to the Spirit alone. Elsewhere the Spirit is given, sent, poured out, received or fallen upon; here it acts, and on its own initiative.

let_judgment_run_down_as_waters.desc:
'But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.' (Amos 5:24).

**Here the word means justice done now, not a verdict at the end**, and the sentence is a demand rather than a warning. It closes a passage rejecting feast days and offerings, which puts it with the other subtractions from sacrifice.

let_me_die_with_the_philistines.name: let me die with the Philistines
let_me_die_with_the_philistines.desc:
'Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines.” Then he pushed with all his might' (Judg 16:30).

His last prayer asks for one thing and the text states the motive without softening it: 'so that with one vengeful blow I may pay back the Philistines for my two eyes' (16:28). The book then records the count — more at his death than in his life — and stops.

let_him_not_deceive_himself_with_trust_i.desc: Let him not deceive himself with trust in emptiness

let_there_be_light.name: Let there be light
let_there_be_light.desc:
'And God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.' (Gen 1:3).

**The first thing made is made by speaking, and it is light.** Darkness is already there -- 'darkness was over the surface of the deep' (Gen 1:2) -- so the light arrives into it rather than replacing a blank. v4 then divides them rather than removing one.

John 1:4-5 takes up the same two in the same order and adds a verdict the chapter does not reach: 'The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it'

'Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus' (Phil 2:5), introducing the passage that runs down to 'obedient to death — even death on a cross' (2:8).

**The instruction is to adopt a mind rather than to think a thought**, and what follows is not an argument but a description of a descent.

man_shall_not_live_by_bread_alone.name: Man shall not live on bread alone
man_shall_not_live_by_bread_alone.desc:
'It is written: Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.' (Matt 4:4), quoting Deut 8:3.

**Named as a quotation and not word for word.** Deuteronomy has 'man does not live on bread alone' and 'from the mouth of the LORD'; Matthew has 'shall not live on bread alone' and 'the mouth of God'. Only, alone; the LORD, God. Matthew says 'It is written' and then does not write it as it is.

That pattern runs through his citations and is worth a reader seeing rather than smoothing.

man_who_had_his_fathers_wife.name: the man who had his father's wife
man_who_had_his_fathers_wife.desc:
'It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father’ s wife' (1Cor 5:1).

He is an individual here for the same reason the woman taken in adultery is: the text describes an individual, whether or not it can name him. What it does not hold is the instruction about him. Paul tells the congregation to 'Expel the wicked man from among you' (5:13), and that is an instruction rather than an event — the letter does not report whether it was carried out.

The text offers something that reads like the sequel and never says it is one. 2 Corinthians 2:6-7: 'This punishment which was inflicted by the many is sufficient for such a one; so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive him.' A punishment inflicted, a man restored, in a later letter to the same church — and no verse connects the two. Many readers join them; the text declines, and records the possibility here where it can be weighed.

mark_3_22_30.desc: Begins with the scribes' accusation 'He is possessed by Beelzebul' and runs through Jesus' parabolic rebuttal and the warning on blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, closing with the reason 'Jesus made this statement because they were saying, He has an unclean spirit'

mark_3_22_claim.name: He is possessed by Beelzebul
mark_3_22_claim.desc: The charge of the scribes: "He is possessed by Beelzebul ... By the prince of the demons He drives out demons".

items.label: was answered by
items.name: How can Satan drive out Satan?

mark_3_23_question.name: How can Satan drive out Satan?
mark_3_23_question.desc: Jesus's answer, spoken "in parables": "How can Satan drive out Satan?"

mark_3_24_saying.name: If a kingdom is divided against itself
mark_3_24_saying.desc: "And if a kingdom be divided against itself, it cannot stand."

items.label: is the ground for
items.name: How can Satan drive out Satan?

mark_3_25_saying.name: Jesus at Mark 3:25
mark_3_25_saying.desc: Jesus's second figure in the Beelzebul answer: "If a house is divided against itself, it cannot stand."

items.label: is an instance of
items.name: if X be divided against itself, X cannot stand

mark_3_26_saying.name: Jesus at Mark 3:26
mark_3_26_saying.desc: "And if Satan is divided and rises against himself, he cannot stand; his end has come."

mark_3_27_saying.name: unless he first ties up the strong man
mark_3_27_saying.desc: "no one can enter a strong man's house to steal his possessions unless he first ties up the strong man. Then he can plunder his house."

mark_3_28_saying.name: Jesus at Mark 3:28
mark_3_28_saying.desc: "Truly I tell you, the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies, as many as they utter".

mark_3_29_saying.name: Jesus at Mark 3:29
mark_3_29_saying.desc: "But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin".

mark_3_30_saying.name: He has an unclean spirit
mark_3_30_saying.desc: The charge the narrator gives as the reason for Jesus's warning: "Jesus made this statement because they were saying, He has an unclean spirit"

mark_3_31_35.name: Jesus' true family
mark_3_31_35.desc: Returns to the family scene set up in v.20-21 with 'Then Jesus’ mother and brothers came' and closes with the definition 'whoever does the will of God is My brother'

items.label: recounts
items.name: True family of Jesus (“who is my mother?”)

mark_3_32_speech.name: the multitude at Mark 3:32
mark_3_32_speech.desc: What the multitude sitting about him told him: "Your mother and brothers are outside, asking for You."

mark_3_33_question.name: “Who are My mother and My brothers?”
mark_3_33_question.desc: Jesus's answer to the multitude: "Who are My mother and My brothers?"

mark_3_34_speech.name: Here are My mother and My brothers!
mark_3_34_speech.desc: Spoken as "Looking at those seated in a circle around Him".

mark_3_35_saying.name: Jesus at Mark 3:35
mark_3_35_saying.desc: "For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother."

items.label: is the ground for
items.name: Here are My mother and My brothers!

mark_3_3_speech.name: Stand up among us
mark_3_3_speech.desc: Jesus to the man with the withered hand: "Stand forth."

mark_3_4_question.name: Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good
mark_3_4_question.desc: "Is it lawful on the Sabbath day to do good or to do harm? To save a life or to kill?" -- and "they were silent".

mark_3_5_speech.name: Stretch out your hand
mark_3_5_speech.desc: Jesus to the man: "Stretch out your hand."

mark_3_7_12.name: Crowds and healings by the sea
mark_3_7_12.desc: 'Jesus withdrew himself...to the sea' opens a new scene of multitudes and healings, closing with 'But He warned them sternly not to make Him known'

mark_3_9_instruction.name: to have a boat ready for Him
mark_3_9_instruction.desc: Jesus's word to his disciples, "to have a boat ready for Him so that the crowd would not crush Him".

mark_4_10_12.name: Purpose of speaking in parables
mark_4_10_12.desc: they asked Him about the parable... to those who are outside, all things are done in parables

mark_4_11_saying.name: Jesus at Mark 4:11
mark_4_11_saying.desc: Jesus's answer about the parables: "The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to those on the outside everything is expressed in parables," (Mark 4:11).

items.label: is grounded on
items.name: they may be ever seeing but never perceiving

items.label: speaks of
items.name: the mystery of the kingdom of God

mark_4_12_saying.name: they may be ever seeing but never perceiving
mark_4_12_saying.desc: "so that, they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven." (Mark 4:12).

mark_4_13_20.name: Explanation of the sower
mark_4_13_20.desc: Do you not understand this parable?... The sower sows the word... Still others are like the seeds sown on good soil

mark_4_1_2.name: Setting: teaching by the sea
mark_4_1_2.desc: Once again He began to teach beside the sea... taught them many things in parables

mark_4_21_25.name: Sayings on the lamp and measure
mark_4_21_25.desc: Does anyone bring in a lamp to put it under a basket... Pay attention to what you hear

mark_4_26_29.name: Parable of the growing seed
mark_4_26_29.desc: The kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground... the harvest has come

items.label: is an instance of
items.name: "So is/like the kingdom of God..." parable formula

mark_4_30_32.name: Parable of the mustard seed
mark_4_30_32.desc: To what can we compare the kingdom of God?... puts forth great branches

items.label: is an instance of
items.name: "So is/like the kingdom of God..." parable formula

mark_4_33_34.name: Summary of parabolic teaching
mark_4_33_34.desc: With many such parables Jesus spoke the word to them... explained everything to His own disciples

mark_4_35_41.name: Calming the storm
mark_4_35_41.desc: Let us cross to the other side... Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?

mark_4_3_9.name: Parable of the sower
mark_4_3_9.desc: Listen! A farmer went out to sow his seed... He who has ears to hear, let him hear

mark_4_9_saying.name: He who has ears to hear, let him hear
mark_4_9_saying.desc: Jesus's word closing the parable of the sower: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." (Mark 4:9).

mark_5_14_20.name: Aftermath in the country
mark_5_14_20.desc: 'Those tending the pigs ran off and reported this' shifts to the reaction of the townspeople and the healed man's departure, ending 'all men did marvel'

mark_5_1_13.name: Jesus casts demons into swine
mark_5_1_13.desc: Scene opens 'They came to the other side' and closes with the herd 'choked in the sea', a complete encounter with the unclean spirit

mark_5_1_20.name: The Gadarene demoniac
mark_5_1_20.desc: Bounded by the crossing 'On the other side of the sea' (v1) and the return crossing 'passed over again by ship' (v21)

mark_5_21_24.name: Jairus pleads for his daughter
mark_5_21_24.desc: 'A synagogue leader named Jairus arrived' introduces a new petitioner, ending as 'Jesus went with him'

mark_5_25_34.name: The woman with the issue of blood
mark_5_25_34.desc: 'And a certain woman' begins a new figure inserted into the journey, closing with Jesus' words 'Go in peace and be free of your affliction'

mark_5_35_43.name: Raising of Jairus's daughter
mark_5_35_43.desc: 'While He was still speaking, messengers from the house of Jairus arrived and said' resumes the interrupted errand, ending with the charge 'that no one should know about this'

mark_6_14_16.name: Herod's speculation about Jesus
mark_6_14_16.desc: opens 'Now King Herod heard about this' introducing new subject, and closes with Herod's verdict 'John, whom I beheaded'

mark_6_14_29.name: Herod and John the Baptist
mark_6_14_29.desc: unified account of Herod's reaction to Jesus's fame explained through the story of John's death

mark_6_17_29.name: Death of John the Baptist
mark_6_17_29.desc: 'For Herod himself had ordered that John be arrested and bound and imprisoned' begins an explanatory flashback, closing with burial 'they came and took his body and placed it in a tomb'

mark_6_1_6.name: Rejection at Nazareth
mark_6_1_6.desc: opens with 'went on from there and came to His hometown' and closes with 'And He was amazed at their unbelief. And He went around from village to village, teaching the people' marking transition to new scene

mark_6_30_34.name: Apostles return; compassion on the crowd
mark_6_30_34.desc: 'gathered around Jesus' marks return from mission, ending with 'he began to teach them many things' before the feeding scene

mark_6_35_44.name: Feeding of the five thousand
mark_6_35_44.desc: begins with disciples noting 'By now the hour was already late' and the need for food, ends with tally 'about five thousand men'

mark_6_45_52.name: Walking on the water
mark_6_45_52.desc: 'Immediately Jesus made His disciples get into the boat' begins new scene at sea, closing with 'for they had not understood about the loaves, but their hearts had been hardened'

mark_6_53_56.name: Healing at Gennesaret
mark_6_53_56.desc: 'When they had crossed over, they landed at Gennesaret' opens new locale, running to the chapter's close describing healings

mark_6_7_13.name: Sending out the twelve
mark_6_7_13.desc: begins 'Then Jesus called the Twelve to Him and began to send them out' and closes with the disciples' mission accomplished: 'They cast out many demons ... and healed them'

mark_7_14_16.name: Public parable to the crowd
mark_7_14_16.desc: Addressed to 'all the people': 'Hearken to me, everyone of you' ending with the parable formula 'let him hear'

mark_7_14_23.name: Teaching on true defilement
mark_7_14_23.desc: Begins with 'called the crowd to Him' and closes with the summary 'All these evil things come from within, and defile the man'

mark_7_17_23.name: Private explanation to disciples
mark_7_17_23.desc: Scene shifts: 'After Jesus had left the crowd and gone into the house, His disciples inquired about the parable', and he explains through to v.23

mark_7_1_13.name: Dispute over handwashing tradition
mark_7_1_13.desc: Opens with a new group arriving: 'Then the Pharisees and some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem gathered around Jesus' and closes the topic with 'Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down'

items.label: contains
items.name: Jesus answers on tradition vs commandment

mark_7_1_5.name: Pharisees raise the complaint
mark_7_1_5.desc: Sets the scene and ends with their direct question: 'Why do Your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders'

mark_7_24_30.name: The Syrophoenician woman's daughter healed
mark_7_24_30.desc: New scene marker 'From there he arose and went away into the borders of Tyre and Sidon' through resolution 'the demon was gone'

mark_7_31_37.name: Healing of the deaf man who could hardly speak
mark_7_31_37.desc: New scene marker 'Then Jesus left the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee' through the crowd's astonished verdict 'He has done all things well'

mark_7_6_13.name: Jesus answers on tradition vs commandment
mark_7_6_13.desc: Marked by 'Jesus answered them' and runs through the Corban example to 'And you do so in many such matters'

mark_8_10_13.name: Pharisees demand a sign
mark_8_10_13.desc: 'He got into the boat' begins a new scene; 'The Pharisees came forth... seeking of him a sign' introduces new actors; ends with departure 'to the other side'

mark_8_14_21.name: Warning about the leaven, misunderstood
mark_8_14_21.desc: 'Now the disciples had forgotten to take bread' shifts subject; closes with 'Do you still not understand?'

mark_8_1_9.name: Feeding the four thousand
mark_8_1_9.desc: 'In those days the crowd once again became very large, and they had nothing to eat. Jesus called the disciples to Him' opens the scene; it closes with 'he sent them away'

mark_8_22_26.name: Healing the blind man at Bethsaida
mark_8_22_26.desc: 'When they arrived at Bethsaida, some people brought a blind man' opens a new scene; closes with the command 'Neither go into the town'

mark_8_27_30.name: Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi
mark_8_27_30.desc: 'Then Jesus and His disciples went on to the villages around Caesarea Philippi' begins new setting; question 'Who do people say I am?' opens dialogue; ends 'And Jesus warned them not to tell anyone about Him'

mark_8_31_33.name: First prediction of the passion and rebuke of Peter
mark_8_31_33.desc: 'Then He began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer' begins new teaching; ends with rebuke 'Get behind Me, Satan'

mark_8_34_38.name: Teaching on taking up the cross
mark_8_34_38.desc: 'Then Jesus called the crowd to Him along with His disciples, and He told them' opens a new address to the crowd; runs through the closing warning about being ashamed 'when He comes in His Father’s glory'

mark_9_14_29.name: Healing the boy with a spirit that makes him mute
mark_9_14_29.desc: When they returned to the other disciples, they saw a large crowd - new scene with a fresh crowd and a father's request, running through the healing and private question 'Why couldn’t we drive it out?'

mark_9_1_1.name: Kingdom coming with power
mark_9_1_1.desc: Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God arrive with power - a standalone saying preceding the transfiguration scene.

mark_9_2_8.name: The Transfiguration
mark_9_2_8.desc: After six days Jesus took with Him Peter, James, and John ... He was transfigured before them; closes with the voice from the cloud and 'they saw no one with them except Jesus'.

mark_9_30_32.name: Second prediction of death and resurrection
mark_9_30_32.desc: Going on from there, they passed through Galilee...because He was teaching His disciples. He told them, The Son of Man is being handed over to the hands of men - marks a new journey and teaching, ending 'they did not understand this statement'.

mark_9_33_37.name: Who is the greatest / the child
mark_9_33_37.desc: Then they came to Capernaum. While Jesus was in the house, He asked them, What were you discussing on the way? - new location and question opens this unit, running through the child illustration.

mark_9_38_41.name: The exorcist not of their company
mark_9_38_41.desc: John said to Him, Teacher, we saw someone else driving out demons in Your name - new speaker John raises a distinct issue, resolved by 'he will never lose his reward'.

mark_9_42_50.name: Sayings on offense, cutting off, and salt
mark_9_42_50.desc: Whoever will cause one of these little ones to stumble...it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck - shifts to warnings about causing sin, repeated refrain 'where their worm never dies, and the fire is not quenched', ending with salt saying 'Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another.'

mark_9_9_13.name: Descending the mountain: Elijah and the resurrection
mark_9_9_13.desc: As they were coming down the mountain, Jesus admonished them...And they asked Jesus, Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first? - new topic of discussion begun by 'And they asked Jesus'.

medan.name: Medan
medan.desc: Son of Abraham and Keturah. 'she bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan' (Gen 25:2).

meditate_day_and_night.name: meditate on it day and night
meditate_day_and_night.desc:
'This Book of the Law must not depart from your mouth; meditate on it day and night' (Josh 1:8), and 'on His law he meditates day and night' (Ps 1:2).

**Two books, the same object and the same phrase**, and neither marks the other.

meditation.name: meditation
meditation.desc:
'meditate on it day and night' (Josh 1:8), and 'on His law he meditates day and night' (Ps 1:2).

Both of the text's main statements about it name the same object and the same frequency: the law, day and night. It is not an emptying in these verses but an occupation with a text.

megiddo.name: Megiddo
megiddo.desc: City where Ahaziah of Judah died fleeing Jehu, and where Josiah was slain by Pharaoh Neco.

melchishua.name: Melchi-shua
melchishua.desc: Son of Saul; slain with his father at Gilboa.

melchizedek.name: Melchizedek
melchizedek.desc: King of Salem and priest of God Most High.

melita.name: Malta
melita.desc: Island where Paul was shipwrecked on the voyage to Rome.

melzar.name: the steward
melzar.desc: Steward set over Daniel and his companions.

men.name: men
men.desc: 'The Nephilim were on the earth in those days-and afterward as well-when the sons of God had relations with the daughters of men. And they bore them children who became the mighty men of old, men of renown.' (Gen 6:4).

men_of_jabesh_gilead.name: the men of Jabesh-gilead
men_of_jabesh_gilead.desc: The inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead who acted together, rescued by Saul and later retrieving his body.

men_of_jericho.name: Men of Jericho
men_of_jericho.desc: Named in Nehemiah 3 for one reason: they built a part of the wall of Jerusalem.

items.name: wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD

men_who_took_strange_wives.desc: Examined by Ezra and the heads of the families, and recorded each of them identified by name (Ezra 10:16-17).

menahem_son_of_gadi.desc: Killed Shallum and reigned as king of Israel.

mene_mene_tekel_upharsin.name: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN
mene_mene_tekel_upharsin.desc:
'Now this is the inscription that was written: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN.' (Dan 5:25), with the reading given word by word over the next three verses.

The one place the text decodes a text rather than a picture. The words are weights and the interpretation puns on them — numbered, weighed, divided — and they are kept untranslated so an English reader sees exactly what Belshazzar saw: letters that mean nothing until somebody says what they mean.

mephaath.name: Mephaath
mephaath.desc: Levitical city given to the Merarites out of Reuben (Josh 21:36).

mephibosheth_son_of_jonathan.name: Mephibosheth
mephibosheth_son_of_jonathan.desc: Son of Jonathan, grandson of Saul; lame in both feet; shown kindness by David.

mephibosheth_son_of_saul.name: Mephibosheth
mephibosheth_son_of_saul.desc: Son of Rizpah and Saul; handed over to the Gibeonites.

merab.name: Merab
merab.desc: Elder daughter of Saul; given to Adriel the Meholathite instead of David.

merchants_neh3.name: Merchants
merchants_neh3.desc: Named in Nehemiah 3 for one reason: they repaired a part of the wall of Jerusalem, the sheep gate.

mercy.name: mercy
mercy.desc:
'I desire mercy, not sacrifice' (Hos 6:6) -- **a verse Jesus quotes twice in Matthew** (9:13, 12:7), both times against people arguing from the law.

Micah 6:8 puts it in a set of three requirements and Matthew 5:7 makes it reciprocal: 'blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy'.

items.name: Mercy & Restoration (major theme)

micaiah_son_of_imla.name: Micaiah
micaiah_son_of_imla.desc: Prophet who foretold Ahab's death at Ramoth-gilead.

michael_archangel.name: Michael
michael_archangel.desc: The archangel; contended with the devil about the body of Moses, and fought the dragon.

michael_father_of_sethur.name: Michael
michael_father_of_sethur.desc: Father of Sethur, the Asherite spy.

michal.name: Michal
michal.desc: Younger daughter of Saul; loved and married David, later given to Palti.

michmethah.name: Michmethath
michmethah.desc: A point on the border of Ephraim (Josh 16:6) and of Manasseh (Josh 17:7), near Shechem.

middin.name: Middin
middin.desc: Town of Judah, in the wilderness list.

midian.name: Midian
midian.desc: Son of Abraham and Keturah; father of Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. 'she bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian' (Gen 25:2); 'The sons of Midian were Ephah' (Gen 25:4).

midian_region.name: Midian
midian_region.desc: Where Moses fled from Pharaoh and lived as a shepherd with Jethro.

midianites.name: the Midianites
midianites.desc: Nomadic nation descended from Abraham's son Midian; oppressed Israel until Gideon's rout of them.

migdal_gad.name: Migdal-gad
migdal_gad.desc: Town of Judah, in the lowland list.

migdol.name: Migdol
migdol.desc: Landmark near which Israel camped by the sea before Pharaoh's army overtook them (Exod 14:2).

mightier_than_i.name: more powerful than I
mightier_than_i.desc: Assessment of the one coming after John, Mark 1:7.

mighty_men_of_old_men_of_renown.name: the mighty men of old, men of renown
mighty_men_of_old_men_of_renown.desc: "who became the mighty men of old, men of renown" (Gen 6:4)

miletus.desc: Port city where Paul met with the Ephesian elders.

milk_object.name: milk
milk_object.desc: Milk served to the three men.

mind.name: mind
mind.desc:
'be transformed by the renewing of your mind' (Rom 12:2).

The text treats it as something that can be exchanged rather than improved. Paul asks for another one — 'Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus' (Phil 2:5) — and claims it already: 'we have the mind of Christ' (1Cor 2:16). Romans 8:6-7 sets two of them against each other, carnal and spiritual, and calls one of them death.

It is also one of the four things the first commandment asks for, alongside heart, soul and strength (Mark 12:30).

my_father_and_your_father.name: my Father, and your Father
my_father_and_your_father.desc:
'go and tell My brothers, I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.' (John 20:17).

One sentence, both framings, kept apart. It would have been shorter to say our Father, and the verse does not. The possessive is repeated — my Father, and your Father; my God, and your God — so the sentence joins the two relations and declines to merge them.

John's Father is almost always the Son's ('To this very day My Father is at His work', 5:17); Matthew's is almost always the hearers' ('your Father in heaven'). This is the one verse that says both at once, and it is spoken to a single named person on the morning of the resurrection.

The verse is recorded; the reading is left.

my_god_has_shut_the_lions_mouths.name: My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions
my_god_has_shut_the_lions_mouths.desc:
'My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me' (Dan 6:22).

What gets him into the den is a habit, not a confrontation. He hears the decree is signed and goes home and prays as he had done 'before' — windows open toward Jerusalem, three times a day (6:10). The text is careful to say he changed nothing.

The king spends the night fasting and comes at dawn, and it is he who asks whether the God has delivered (6:20). The rescue is narrated as an answer to somebody else's question.

my_god_shall_supply_all_your_need.name: my God will supply all your needs
my_god_shall_supply_all_your_need.desc:
'And my God will supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus.' (Phil 4:19).

The measure is the supplier rather than the need, which is the same move Rom 8:32 makes from the other direction: 'He who did not spare His own Son ... how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things?'

my_grace_is_sufficient.name: my grace is sufficient for you
my_grace_is_sufficient.desc:
'My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.' (2Cor 12:9), closing with 'when I am weak, then I am strong' (12:10).

**An answer to a request that was refused.** Paul asks three times for the thorn to be removed and this is what he is given instead, which is the context the verse is most often quoted without.

my_heart_rejoices_in_the_lord.name: My heart rejoices in the LORD
my_heart_rejoices_in_the_lord.desc:
'At that time Hannah prayed: My heart rejoices in the LORD' (1Sam 2:1).

Almost none of it is about the child she asked for. After the first verse it turns to reversal, and stays there: the full hire themselves for bread and the hungry cease, the barren bears seven (2:5), and 'He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them among princes' (2:8).

Mary's song at Luke 1:46-55 does the same thing in the same order — opens on her own soul, turns within two verses to reversal, and ends on the mighty put down and the hungry filled. Luke does not say so.

my_lord_and_my_god.name: my Lord and my God
my_lord_and_my_god.desc:
'Thomas replied, My Lord and my God!' (John 20:28).

The strongest confession in the gospels comes from the man who refused to believe it. Eight days earlier he had named his terms exactly — the print of the nails, and his hand in the side (20:25) — and the text does not record him taking them up.

The reply moves the subject off him: 'blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed' (20:29).

my_might.name: my might
my_might.desc: Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might

my_servant_david_their_shepherd.name: My servant David will be their shepherd
my_servant_david_their_shepherd.desc:
'I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them. He will feed them and be their shepherd.' (Ezek 34:23).

Said roughly four centuries after David died, in the middle of a chapter condemning the shepherds of Israel for feeding themselves. Ezekiel 37:24 repeats it and Jeremiah 30:9 has the same thing.

It is the clearest place a man's name is used for something other than the man, and what it means by it — a descendant, a return, a figure — is exactly the argument.

my_sheep_hear_my_voice.name: My sheep listen to My voice
my_sheep_hear_my_voice.desc:
'My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me.' (John 10:27).

Three clauses and the following comes last, after the hearing and the being known. It is the shepherd figure of Ps 23 with the direction of travel stated: in the psalm the sheep is led, here the sheep follows.

my_soul_does_magnify_the_lord.name: My soul magnifies the Lord
my_soul_does_magnify_the_lord.desc:
'Then Mary said: My soul magnifies the Lord,' (Luke 1:46), opening the longest speech any woman is given in the New Testament.

**Almost none of it is about her.** After two verses it turns to what God does generally, and what it says he does is reversal: 'He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty' (1:52-53).

It is built almost entirely out of older material -- Hannah's song at 1 Samuel 2 most of all -- and Luke does not say so.

items.label: draws on
items.name: My heart rejoices in the LORD

my_strength_is_made_perfect_in_weakness.name: My power is perfected in weakness
my_strength_is_made_perfect_in_weakness.desc:
'But He said to me, My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.' (2Cor 12:9).

The answer to a request refused three times (2Cor 12:8). It is the only place where Paul reports asking for something and being told no with a reason attached, and the reason is not that the thing asked for was wrong.

items.label: is drawn on by

my_thoughts_are_not_your_thoughts.name: my thoughts are not your thoughts
my_thoughts_are_not_your_thoughts.desc:
'For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways, declares the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts' (Isa 55:8-9).

**Two verses that say the same thing twice, and the second is not a repetition.** v8 denies that they are the same; v9 says how they differ, and gives a measure -- the distance between the heavens and the earth.

It belongs with the path verses because it supplies their reason. Prov 3:5 says lean not on your own understanding and does not say why; this says why. Ps 25:4 asks to be shewn his ways, which is a request that only makes sense if they are not already known.
aka: neither are your ways my ways

mystery_babylon_the_great.name: MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT
mystery_babylon_the_great.desc:
'And on her forehead a mysterious name was written: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.' (Rev 17:5).

The capitals are the text telling you it is an inscription and not a description. The chapter then gives one key — 'And the woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth' (17:18) — and no more.

Which city is the whole of a very old argument. What the text records is that a name was written, that it was written on a forehead, and that the name is called a mystery.

new_creature.name: a new creation

'Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!' (2Cor 5:17), and again at Galatians 6:15 where it is set against circumcision as the thing that actually counts.

It states a completed change and gives no process. Nothing here says how, or when, or whether it can be undone — only that old things are passed away.

The neighbouring figures each supply a different half. [[born_again]] gives it a birth, [[buried_with_him_by_baptism]] gives it a death and a raising, and [[old_man_and_new_man]] gives it a change of clothes. Scripture never puts two of them in the same sentence, and that is worth knowing before deciding they are one doctrine.

no_man_comes_unto_the_father.name: No one comes to the Father
no_man_comes_unto_the_father.desc:
'I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.' (John 14:6).

An exclusive claim. Three verses later the same conversation gives the other half: 'Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father' (14:9), answering Philip's request to be shown him.

The two verses are usually read together and are doing different things — 14:6 is about access and 14:9 about sight.

no_man_puts_new_into_old.name: No one puts the new on the old

no_respecter_of_persons.name: God does not show favoritism
no_respecter_of_persons.desc:
'I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism' (Acts 10:34), said by Peter in the house of Cornelius, and stated flatly by Paul at Romans 2:11: 'For God does not show favoritism'.

Two writers, two arguments, one conclusion, and neither cites the other. Peter reaches it by watching the Spirit fall on Gentiles; Paul reaches it by reasoning about law and judgment. Acts 10:36 names Jesus — 'preaching peace by Jesus Christ' — but the saying itself is about God.

noah_daniel_and_job.name: Noah, Daniel, and Job
noah_daniel_and_job.desc:
'then even if these three men-Noah, Daniel, and Job-were in it, their righteousness could deliver only themselves' (Ezek 14:14), and the same three again at 14:20.

Chosen as a limit case, and the answer given is nothing. The question the chapter is arguing is how far one person's righteousness reaches on somebody else's behalf, and the three names are picked because they are the strongest examples available — a man who survived the flood, a man who survived the lions, and a man who survived everything. Even they, the verse says, would deliver 'neither son nor daughter' (14:20).

The three are not otherwise associated anywhere in Scripture. Ezekiel puts them together and nothing else does.

noah_lived_after_the_flood_350_years.name: after the flood, Noah lived 350 years
noah_lived_after_the_flood_350_years.desc: After the flood, Noah lived 350 years.

noahs_ark.name: the ark
noahs_ark.desc:
'Make for yourself an ark of gopher wood' (Gen 6:14).

Scripture itself makes it a figure, and says which of. 1 Peter 3:20-21 moves from eight souls saved by water to 'this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also' — and then immediately qualifies what it means, 'not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God'.

A reader should know the English is doing something the original does not. This and the ark of the covenant are different words.

noahs_household.desc: "Go into the ark, you and all your family" (Gen 7:1); "Noah went into the ship with his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives with him" (Gen 7:7).

nobles_and_rulers_of_judah.desc: The men Nehemiah called to account for exacting usury of their brothers during the famine, and made to restore the lands, vineyards, olive groves and houses they had taken (Neh 5:7-12).

Not X but Y again, and the X being ruled out is confession. The two verses after it rule out more: prophesying, driving out demons, many miracles, all done in the name, all answered with 'I never knew you' (7:23).

now_you_dismiss_your_servant_in_peace.desc:
'Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace.' (Luke 2:29).

**A man asking permission to die, having got what he was promised.** The promise was that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ (2:26), and what he has seen is an infant carried in by two poor parents with a pair of birds to offer.

Anna is in the same scene and gets three verses and no quoted words -- 'Coming forward at that moment, she gave thanks to God and spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem' (2:38).

o_wretched_man_that_i_am.name: What a wretched man I am
o_wretched_man_that_i_am.desc:
'What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!' (Rom 7:24-25).

The question is asked as a cry and answered in the next breath, and the answer is a person rather than a method. What follows immediately is the summary that hands the argument to chapter 8.

oath_of_david_to_saul.desc:
'So now, swear to me by the LORD that you will not cut off my descendants or wipe out my name from my father’s house. So David gave his oath to Saul' (1Sam 24:21-22), sworn at the mouth of the cave in En-gedi.

Sworn by the man being hunted to the man hunting him, and asked for by the hunter -- Saul has just conceded 'Now I know for sure that you will be king' (24:20).

obedience.desc:
'obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams' (1Sam 15:22).

Samuel ranks obedience above sacrifice; Hosea 6:6 ranks mercy above it; Psalm 51:17 replaces its content with a broken spirit. Three writers, three centuries apart, each subtracting from the same practice.

offering_for_the_house_of_god.desc: 650 talents of silver, a hundred talents of silver vessels, a hundred talents of gold, 20 gold bowls and two articles of fine polished bronze -- given by Artaxerxes, his counselors, his leaders, weighed out to twelve priests at Ahava and weighed again at Jerusalem to the same total (Ezra 8:25-34).

old_gate.desc: A named section of the wall of Jerusalem, rebuilt in the account of Nehemiah 3.

old_man_and_new_man.name: the old self and the new self
old_man_and_new_man.desc:
'to put off your former way of life, your old self ... and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness' (Eph 4:22-24), with the same pair at Colossians 3:9-10.

Put off, put on — something the reader does, repeatedly if need be.

Which sits oddly beside Romans 6:6, where the old self is not put off but executed: 'our old self was crucified with Him'. The same words, two figures — a garment in Ephesians and a body in Romans.

Colossians 3:10 reaches back to Genesis in passing: the new self is 'renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator'.

on_these_two_commandments_hang_all_the_l.name: All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments
on_these_two_commandments_hang_all_the_l.desc:
'All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.' (Matt 22:40).

The verse that makes the pair a pair. Without it there are two quotations; with it there is a claim about the whole -- that the rest depends on these, which is a statement about how the law is to be read rather than an addition to it.

Mark has a different ending: the scribe agrees, says it is 'more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices', and Jesus tells him he is not far from the kingdom of God (Mark 12:32-34).

orpah.desc: Moabite woman, wife of Chilion, sister-in-law to Ruth.

othniel.desc: Son of Kenaz, brother of Caleb; first judge of Israel; defeated Cushan-rishathaim.

our_father_is_old.desc: the elder daughter's assessment of Lot: "Our father is old" (Gen 19:31).

our_father_in_heaven.name: Our Father in heaven
our_father_in_heaven.desc:
'So then, this is how you should pray: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name.' (Matt 6:9).

The one prayer given as a form, given twice, and the two versions differ: Luke 11:2 is shorter and its clauses are ordered differently.

Our, not my. Every other address to the Father in the gospels is singular on one side or the other — the Son's Father or the hearers' Father — and this is the plural the hearers are told to use.

our_people.name: our people
our_people.desc: Those Paul calls 'ours' in Titus 3:14, who are to learn to maintain good works.

out_of_egypt_i_called_my_son.name: Out of Egypt I called My Son
out_of_egypt_i_called_my_son.desc:
'When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son.' (Hos 11:1), quoted at Matt 2:15.

In Hosea the son is Israel, named in the same verse, and the sentence looks back at the exodus. Matthew applies it to one child leaving Egypt rather than a nation, and states it as fulfilment. Both readings are on the page.

owners_of_jobs_land.name: its tenants
owners_of_jobs_land.desc: The owners of the land mentioned in Job 31:39.

pallu.name: Pallu

palm_of_deborah.desc: Site between Ramah and Bethel in mount Ephraim where Deborah held court.

palti_son_of_raphu.name: Palti
palti_son_of_raphu.desc: Spy sent from the tribe of Benjamin.

paphos.name: Paphos
paphos.desc: City on Cyprus, seat of the proconsul Sergius Paulus; scene of the blinding of Elymas.

parable_of_the_lost_sheep.name: the parable of the lost sheep
parable_of_the_lost_sheep.desc:
'If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go out to search for the one that is lost?' (Matt 18:12).

Told twice to opposite audiences. In Matthew it answers the disciples asking who is greatest; in Luke 15:4 it answers the Pharisees murmuring that he receives sinners. Same figure, two arguments.

parable_of_the_sower.name: the parable of the sower
parable_of_the_sower.desc: Named by Jesus himself: 'Consider, then, the parable of the sower:' (Matt 13:18). He gives the key in the same breath at Luke 8:11 -- 'Now this is the meaning of the parable: The seed is the word of God' -- and Matthew 13:19-23 reads the four soils as four hearings of it.

parable_of_the_tares.name: the parable of the weeds in the field
parable_of_the_tares.desc: Named at Matt 13:36, when the disciples ask for it: 'Explain to us the parable of the weeds in the field.' The key follows in three verses: 'The One who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The field is the world, and the good seed represents the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, and the enemy who sows them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the harvesters are angels' (Matt 13:37-39).

parable_of_the_unmerciful_servant.name: the parable of the unmerciful servant
parable_of_the_unmerciful_servant.desc:
'Because of this, the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants.' (Matt 18:23) -- **the comparison marker is explicit**, which is rarer in the teaching than the parables suggest.

It answers a counted question. Peter asks whether to forgive seven times and is told 'Not seven times, but seventy-seven times' (18:21-22), and the parable follows on 'therefore'. The application is stated outright at 18:35: 'That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart.'

paralytic_lowered_through_roof.name: The Paralytic Let Down Through the Roof
paralytic_lowered_through_roof.desc: a paralytic whose four friends broke open a roof to lower him before Jesus.

pass_over.name: pass over
pass_over.desc: 'But my brothers are as faithless as wadis, as seasonal streams that overflow' (Job 6:15).

passed_from_death_unto_life.name: crossed over from death to life
passed_from_death_unto_life.desc:
'whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life.' (John 5:24).

**Three claims in one sentence and all three are in the present tense** -- has, does not come, has passed. The last is the striking one: a completed crossing, stated of someone still speaking to him.

passover.name: the passover
passover.desc: Kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, a memorial of the Lord passing over the houses of the Israelites.
