where_were_you_when_i_laid_the_foundatio.name: Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth
where_were_you_when_i_laid_the_foundatio.desc:
'Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding.' (Job 38:4), spoken 'out of the whirlwind' (38:1).

**The answer to thirty-five chapters of argument is four chapters of questions, and none of them is about the argument.** Job's complaint is never addressed; what he is given instead is an inventory of things he did not make and cannot do.

His reply concedes the form rather than the content: 'Surely I spoke of things I did not understand' (42:3).

white_strakes.name: white inner wood
white_strakes.desc: the white stripes Jacob peeled in the rods

where_you_go_i_will_go.name: wherever you go, I will go
where_you_go_i_will_go.desc:
'Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you. For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.' (Ruth 1:16).

**Said by a Moabite to her mother-in-law**, which is worth holding on to, because it is read at weddings and it is not addressed to a husband. What is being promised is a change of people and of God, by someone with no obligation left to anybody.

who_shall_separate_us_from_the_love_of_c.name: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ
who_shall_separate_us_from_the_love_of_c.desc:
'Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?' (Rom 8:35).

Seven candidates in v35, then ten more in v38-39 -- death, life, angels, principalities, powers, things present, things to come, height, depth, and 'any other creature', which closes the list by refusing to be one. The answer is never given as a name; it is given as an exhaustion of names.

those_he_predestined_he_also_called.name: those He predestined, He also called
those_he_predestined_he_also_called.desc:
'And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified.' (Rom 8:30).

Four links, each taking up the last word of the one before, and every verb in the past tense including the final one. v29 supplies what the predestining is toward: 'to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers.'

whosoever_shall_call_on_the_name_of_the_.name: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD
whosoever_shall_call_on_the_name_of_the_.desc:
'And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved' (Joel 2:32), quoted at Acts 2:21 by Peter at Pentecost and again at Rom 10:13.

**Both New Testament quotations change the last word.** Joel says delivered; Acts and Romans say saved. Recorded rather than reconciled -- it is the same promise arriving with a different ending twice, by two writers, from one source.

whosoever_will_save_his_life_shall_lose_.name: whoever wants to save his life will lose it
whosoever_will_save_his_life_shall_lose_.desc:
'For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it' (Mark 8:35).

Four times in the gospels, and a fifth in different words. Matt 16:25, Mark 8:35 and Luke 9:24 give it almost identically; Luke 17:33 repeats it in a wholly different setting, with no cross mentioned; John 12:25 recasts it as loving and hating one's life. Few sayings in the gospels are attested this often.

In Matthew, Mark and Luke 9 it follows immediately on taking up a cross (Mark 8:34). In John it follows immediately on a seed dying to bear fruit (John 12:24). The saying itself never explains the paradox — it states it, four times, and leaves the two placements to say what it is for.

wisdom.name: wisdom

James 3:17 then describes what arrives — first pure, then peaceable, gentle, accommodating. Set against that, 1 Corinthians 3:19 says the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight, and 1:24 calls Christ the wisdom of God, so the word is doing two jobs and Scripture marks which is which.

'With the jawbone of a donkey I have piled them into heaps. With the jawbone of a donkey I have slain a thousand men.' (Judg 15:16).

It is a couplet, and he is making a joke — the Hebrew puns on the word for donkey and the word for heap, which the translation cannot carry. The very next thing that happens is that he is thirsty and complains to God about it (15:18).

with_the_mind_i_serve_the_law_of_god.name: with my mind I serve the law of God
with_the_mind_i_serve_the_law_of_god.desc:
'So then, with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.' (Rom 7:25).

**The last sentence of the chapter, and the one Rom 8:2 picks up.** It ends the argument where it began -- divided, serving both -- after the thanksgiving rather than before it, which is why the chapter does not resolve on the note it was heading for.

Rom 8:1 opens with 'therefore' and this is what it points back at. Rom 8:2 then repeats 'the law of sin' from this verse word for word and puts a different law against it.

The Spirit bears witness with our spirit (Rom 8:16); the Spirit bears witness because the Spirit is truth (1John 5:6); the disciples are to be witnesses after receiving power (Acts 1:8). works.desc:
'not by works, so that no one can boast.' (Eph 2:9). 'For we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works' (Eph 2:10).

One word, and the text does not change it. Works of the law (Gal 2:16, Rom 9:32), works of the flesh (Gal 5:19), good works (Eph 2:10) — the qualifier moves and the noun does not. Eph 2:9 and 2:10 use it bare, consecutively, once to exclude and once to command.

works_of_the_flesh.name: The acts of the flesh
works_of_the_flesh.desc:
'The acts of the flesh are obvious:' (Gal 5:19), and seventeen follow across three verses.

The counterpart, and the text builds it as one: two lists in one paragraph, seventeen against nine, and Galatians 5:17 sits between them saying what the relation is — 'the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are opposed to each other'. The text itself states the opposition, which is rare.

The two lists are not built alike, though, and the asymmetry is in the text. The works close with 'and such like' (5:21) — explicitly open-ended. The fruit closes with 'Against such things there is no law'. One list says there are more; the other says the law has nothing to say about these.

works_of_the_law.name: works of the law

yahweh.desc:
'in the day that the LORD God made them' (Gen 2:4), the first of 4,968 occurrences — far and away the commonest name for God in the Hebrew scriptures.

Gen 1:1 is not this name. The creation account opens with Elohim and the LORD God appears first at Gen 2:4.

you_pay_tithe_of_mint_and_anise_and_cumm.name: You pay tithes of mint, dill, and cumin
you_pay_tithe_of_mint_and_anise_and_cumm.desc: 'You should have practiced the latter, without neglecting the former' -- the tithe is upheld in the same breath that it is used against them.

you_serpents_you_generation_of_vipers.name: You snakes! You brood of vipers!
you_serpents_you_generation_of_vipers.desc:
'You snakes! You brood of vipers! How will you escape the sentence of hell?' (Matt 23:33).

**The verse that puts the two words together.** John calls the Pharisees and Sadducees a generation of vipers at Matt 3:7 and the word serpent is nowhere near it; Jesus uses the same address at Matt 12:34 and again here, and here alone he sets serpents beside it.

So a reader going from the vipers of Matt 3:7 to the serpent of Genesis 3 travels through Matthew rather than through Eden. Nothing in Matt 3:7 reaches back to the garden; Matt 23:33 is what joins the vocabularies, and it joins them without explaining either.

what_you_intended_against_me_for_evil_go.name: what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good
what_you_intended_against_me_for_evil_go.desc:
'As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this-to preserve the lives of many people.' (Gen 50:20).

**Both halves are asserted and neither is withdrawn.** The brothers meant evil; it is not reinterpreted as something else. What is added is a second intention running through the same events, and the verse holds the two without explaining how they fit.

He says a version of it twice, the first time much earlier and more gently: 'Now, do not be distressed or angry with yourselves that you sold me into this place, because it was to save lives that God sent me before you' (45:5).

your_father_which_is_in_heaven.name: your Father in heaven
your_father_which_is_in_heaven.desc:
'In the same way, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.' (Matt 5:16), and the phrase repeats through Matthew in that exact shape.

Matthew's Father is the hearers' Father, and John's is the Son's, and the difference is not incidental: it is the possessive, and it is consistent across both books. Matthew says your Father and your heavenly Father to a crowd; John has Jesus say my Father more than thirty times.

What is claimed of him here is domestic and attentive rather than sovereign — he sees in secret (6:4), knows what is needed before he is asked (6:8), feeds birds (6:26), notices a sparrow fall (10:29), and is unwilling that one little one should perish (18:14).

rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_servant.name: Servant (Role pattern: Servant): Jesus washing feet (John 13) — John 13:3–5
rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_servant.desc: Servant — in Jesus washing feet (John 13), a row of the role pattern “Servant”: John 13:3–5. knowing “the Father had delivered all things into His hands … so He got up … laid aside His outer garments … began to wash the disciples’ feet”

rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_servant.name: Servant (Role pattern: Servant): Jesus washing feet (John 13) — John 13:13–16
rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_servant.desc: Servant — in Jesus washing feet (John 13), a row of the role pattern “Servant”: John 13:13–16. “You call Me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so … no servant (δοῦλος) is greater than his master” — the text calls the disciples servants, and Jesus the Lord who does their task

rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_sufferi.name: Suffering (Role pattern: Servant): Jesus washing feet (John 13) — John 13:2
rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_sufferi.desc: Suffering — in Jesus washing feet (John 13), a row of the role pattern “Servant”: John 13:2. the devil had put it into the heart of Judas to betray Him

rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_sufferi.name: Suffering (Role pattern: Servant): Jesus washing feet (John 13) — John 13:18
rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_sufferi.desc: Suffering — in Jesus washing feet (John 13), a row of the role pattern “Servant”: John 13:18. Psalm 41:9 fulfilled: “has lifted up his heel against Me”

rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_sufferi.name: Suffering (Role pattern: Servant): Jesus washing feet (John 13) — John 13:21
rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_sufferi.desc: Suffering — in Jesus washing feet (John 13), a row of the role pattern “Servant”: John 13:21. troubled in spirit: “one of you will betray Me”

rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_sufferi.name: Suffering (Role pattern: Servant): Jesus washing feet (John 13) — John 13:27–30
rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_sufferi.desc: Suffering — in Jesus washing feet (John 13), a row of the role pattern “Servant”: John 13:27–30. Satan entered into Judas; he went out, “Judas went out into the night.”

rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_sufferi.name: Suffering (Role pattern: Servant): Jesus washing feet (John 13) — John 13:4
rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_sufferi.desc: Suffering — in Jesus washing feet (John 13), a row of the role pattern “Servant”: John 13:4. “laid aside” (τίθημι) His garments: John’s verb for “I lay down My life” (10:11, 15, 17, 18)

rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_vindica.name: Vindication (Role pattern: Servant): Jesus washing feet (John 13) — John 13:19
rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_vindica.desc: Vindication — in Jesus washing feet (John 13), a row of the role pattern “Servant”: John 13:19. “so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He” (ἐγώ εἰμι) — the betrayal foretold becomes the proof

rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_glory_1.name: Glory (Role pattern: Servant): Jesus washing feet (John 13) — John 13:31–32
rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_glory_1.desc: Glory — in Jesus washing feet (John 13), a row of the role pattern “Servant”: John 13:31–32. “Now the Son of Man is glorified” (δοξάζω five times), said when Judas had gone out

rcell_servant_jesus_washing_feet_glory_2.name: Glory (Role pattern: Servant): Jesus washing feet (John 13) — John 13:12

rolepat_warfare.name: Role pattern: Spiritual warfare
rolepat_warfare.desc: A role pattern: Submission to God, the powers, opposition, resistance, God's help, and standing. Submission comes first in the text (James 4:6–10; 1 Peter 5:5–10).

number_forty.name: forty
number_forty.desc: Forty also appears as ages, armies and measures. This card gathers the spans of forty days or forty years the text counts, the phrases that repeat, and the places where the text itself sets one forty beside another.

number_twelve.name: twelve
number_twelve.desc: Twelve also counts years, cities, cubits and thousands. This card gathers the sets of twelve the text counts — the tribes, things numbered for the tribes, the Twelve — and the places where the text itself sets one twelve beside another.

sactgroup_proclamation.name: Speech-act group: Proclamation
sactgroup_proclamation.desc: Speech that declares or directs: bearing witness, confessing faith, promising, warning, summoning, commanding.

sactgroup_confrontation.name: Speech-act group: Confrontation
sactgroup_confrontation.desc: Speech that meets another head on: rebuking, accusing, defending, taunting, boasting, refusing.

sactgroup_forms.name: Speech-act group: Set forms of speech
sactgroup_forms.desc: Recognised shapes of speaking: the riddle, the call and its answer, the lament over a city, last words.

the_christ.name: the Christ
the_christ.desc:
'We have found the Messiah' (which is translated as Christ) (John 1:41): the text glosses Messiah as Christ (also John 4:25). Who in the text says that Jesus is the Christ, and in whose words, is on this card: the narrators and authors; Peter, Andrew, Martha, an angel and Paul; and Jesus' own answers when asked (Mark 14:62; John 4:26; Matt 26:64).

Luke gives no yes to the question: asked 'If You are the Christ, tell us', Jesus answers 'If I tell you, you will not believe. And if I ask you a question, you will not answer' (Luke 22:67-68); to the next question, 'Are You then the Son of God?', 'You say that I am' (22:70), and the council says, 'Why do we need any more testimony?' (22:71).

theme_creation.name: Creation (major theme)
theme_creation.desc:
The major theme Creation: The making of the heavens, the earth, the sea and all that is in them. A reading: every passage it names resolves to a verse in the Berean text.

**Doug Egge's note.** The theme is Creation: God's making and ordering of the world, "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Gen 1:1), and every core concept below begins there. It also reaches forward, because later scripture carries the idea on, and Paul above all ties the first creation to a new one: "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation" (2 Cor 5:17); "What counts is a new creation" (Gal 6:15); "The creation waits in eager expectation" and "will be set free from its bondage to decay" (Rom 8:19, 21); "All things were created through Him and for Him" (Col 1:16). Isaiah had already said "I will create new heavens and a new earth" (Isa 65:17), and the Bible ends "Behold, I make all things new" (Rev 21:5). The later passages extend the theme; they do not replace the original creation it is about. The graph's node for the word "creation" keeps to the word and does not join Genesis to Revelation on its own.
